#3658. Bonfire of the Neocons: The MAGA Finger-Pointing Begins

Good afternoon from Washington, where foie gras is now illegal and the local Stasi is going door-to-door to check that every citizen has downloaded Bluesky.

The town, one of the bluest in the country, is in a state of stunned ecstasy as it struggles to process the mind-bending midterm election results. Democrats won the House, the Senate, and a majority of governorships, penetrating deep into historically red strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina. During a book party for Sophia Bush at The Jefferson hotel on Wednesday night, the actor nearly cried as she delivered a toast to the results—and to her new bestseller.

On the right, the finger-pointing has already begun. In this edition of Party Animals, you can read my dispatch from a night out with the DC Republicans in mourning and the Democrats celebrating in cocktail-fueled delirium. Plus, a MAGA civil war reignites over Iran, with Vice President JD Vance already wading into the factional fight that could determine the future of the party.

Also mentioned in this issue: Marc Thiessen, Curt Mills, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott, James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Mark Mitchell, Matt Walsh, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be drowned in cocktail-fueled delirium. Praise will be run as a Democrat south of the Mason-Dixon Line.

The morning after the generational Republican midterm collapse that Party Animals is dubbing Blue Tuesday, JD Vance put on his political-analyst cap. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy X post. “The president himself said so last night.”

Never mind that Vance’s referenced war is one that his own administration started and is currently presiding over. Vance has often tried to cast himself as an outside observer of the Trump administration, its preeminent reply guy on social media and podcasts—a clever, if often ludicrous, pose for the vice president.

The Vance post was the highest-level opening salvo in a civil war that had been brewing for some time. It erupted into the open on Tuesday night as the results began to spell doom for Republicans and the blame started flying with velocity. The internecine battle is between the “America First” faction of the Trump movement and those who have supported the war in Iran, the latter labeled by detractors—with a sneer—as neocons.

The day before the blue tsunami, hopeful MAGA devotees attended a campaign rally in Ohio.

“The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” wrote Matt Walsh in a post on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.” As the dire results came down, even some on the right who had cheered on the war came to see, in the cold glow of their screens, the political devastation it had wrought. “Iran War is clearly catastrophically unpopular and has to end,” posted Will Chamberlain, who had spent the last few months loudly dismissing the war’s critics as subliterate simpletons.

On social media, MAGA luminaries shared a screenshot of an infamous op-ed written by Iran war booster Marc Thiessen, whose headline confidently claimed earlier this year: “There is no US downside to striking the Iranian regime.” Fox host Mark Levin lashed out at critics blasting his support for the war, insisting it had nothing to do with the results. Reality would seem to differ. One NBC News exit poll found that 74% of voters said Iran was a “crucial or major factor in how they voted.”

“It was the Iran war, stupid,” said Curt Mills, the executive director of The American Conservative, in an interview with Party Animals. Speaking about Thiessen and Levin, Mills was unsparing: “Professional liars. Professional liars. Not analysts, not honest people, and, honestly, not very invested in the future of the country.”

I asked Mills, who praised Vance’s statement, if it was not strange for the vice president to speak out against the administration while serving in it. “What option does he really have if he wants to keep his job, stop the war, and maybe run for president? I mean, it is strange. It is unprecedented in some ways,” he said. “Is it working? Maybe.”

In restaurants and barrooms across the capital, the ruling party’s apparatchiks watched and agonized as Democrats mounted a historic midterms rout.

The How: The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and colleagues have the definitive account of how Trump lost the midterms for Republicans, packed with genuinely shocking reporting that reveals exactly what went wrong at each turn.

Rockstud the Vote: My colleague José Criales-Unzueta trained his gimlet eye on a photo posted by Free Press reporter Olivia Reingold from a Democratic election night party in Michigan and found some suspicious discrepancies in the leather straps of a smoking heel.

Ballroom Blues: Read Shawn McCreesh’s New York Times dispatch from Trump’s strange walk of shame around the White House ballroom construction site the morning after the midterms. “Inside his concrete chrysalis,” McCreesh writes, “everything was still beautiful.” 💔

Department of (Deeply Unpopular) War: Amid a flurry of anonymous quotes from Trump officials and allies laying blame for the midterms on Pete Hegseth, the president tells Jonathan Karl of ABC News that he’s standing by his defense secretary—for now, at least.

Of Mics and Men: In the wake of Patrick Bet-David’s election night stream, Vanity Fair’s Dan Adler has a biting eulogy for the manosphere: “Donald Trump’s 2024 tour of the Joe Rogan–dominated podcast circuit heralded the makings of a new mainstream media. But in the MAGA midterm wreckage, the idea of the manosphere as a political force has shattered.”

A Few Good Streamers: VF’s Abigail Sylvor Greenberg spoke with Hasan Piker and his lawyer, who promised that Piker’s $75 million defamation lawsuit against Scott Jennings is only the beginning.

Russell Brand trial: The star comedian turned right-wing podcast lounge lizard was found guilty in a London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Musk in the barrel: Elon Musk, who just torched nearly half a billion dollars in an effort to keep Republicans in power, now faces the wrath of Democrats. The New York Times has a handy guide to the coming storm. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Senator Ed Markey.

#3657. Former PlayStation Boss Thinks Sony Is Solving The Wrong Problem With PS6

Sony confirmed last week that development on its "next-generation" PlayStation platform will pick up speed in 2027, but not everyone is convinced the world needs a PS6 right now. In an interview with The Trophy Room, former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden said true innovation would come from finding a way to lower the price of the PS5, allowing more potential buyers to enter the market.

"I think we have enough power in the machine. The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200, it's to make another PS5 for $300. Now, that would be true innovation," Layden said, while also remarking how the PS5 generation saw price increases over time, not reductions.

Compared to previous generations, the PS5 has only gotten more expensive in the six years that it has been on the market, rising from $400 to $600 for the PS5 Digital Edition, while the PS5 with a disc drive has increased from $500 to $650. The PS5 Pro has seen the biggest increase in the few years it has been around, as the beefier machine has jumped from its original price of $700 to $900. Various factors are to blame, but one of the biggest is the global memory shortage that has hit all fields of technology, thanks to AI data centers eating into the world's supply.

A PS6 that costs over $1,000 will be out of reach for many consumers, and as Layden believes, it likely won't be as big a graphical leap forward as we've seen in previous PlayStation generations. While the difference in video game graphics between the PS1 and the PS2 was especially noticeable, later consoles have shown diminishing returns, and Layden believes the graphical quality of PS6 games will be even harder to notice. "These are the differences that only dogs can hear," Layden said about the reported increase in teraflops and ray-tracing power the PS6 will supposedly offer.

"What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is don't iterate the console. Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that. The silicon is fine, the operating system is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."

As the current generation continues, Sony has also sought to extend the PS5's lifespan with new ideas, like a PS5 Pro-inspired upscaling tech called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR). While it's only available for two games currently, QSSR could give the PS5 plenty of staying power in the current gaming generation and the next.

Over a decade after Boy Meets World ended in 2000, a spinoff series was developed for Disney Channel and called Girl Meets World. But even after Girl ended in 2017, there were still some characters that fans wanted to see more of. That’s all the more reason I'm so excited to hear Will Friedle and Matthew Lawrence talking about their own spinoff idea. And, seriously, I need a network exec to hear them out!

Cory Matthews and Shawn Hunter may have been one of the most perfect best friend pairings, based on their exploits in Boy Meets World. However, those two characters' older brothers, Jack and Eric, are also truly a bromance deserving of attention. During a recent episode of Pod Meets World, Matthew Lawrence, who played Jack, said during a press junket that he was asked about a Jack/Eric spin-off series. Will Friedle dropped some very positive thoughts on the prospect, and they make me giddy:

I think you could still do it. Jack and Eric come together. It’s the new Odd Couple!

Yes! This needs to come together. For those who don’t know, Neil Simon’s play The Odd Couple is about two mismatched roommates, and Jack and Eric definitely fit that bill. While Jack is the logical straight man of the duo, Eric is the zany eccentric. As the two characters (and the actors who played) were so yin and yang, a spinoff would definitely make for some entertaining TV.

Lawrence went on to explain that a Jack/Eric spinoff was once in the cards, but the relationship between the creators and Disney “kind of fell apart.” Also, Lawrence recently told EW he could see the duo, both in their 40s, forced back together after going their separate ways. Lawrence continued to say on the podcast that if a potential spinoff isn’t picked up by television, he has an excellent idea of how a micro spin-off series could work, and I’m loving it:

If anything, it’s like the new YouTube in a sense that these days, as you see with Obsession and all of these things that are coming, I mean, that’s kind of the new groundlings when you talk about comedy. The new spot where they bring out shows. So maybe if we even start, maybe it’s like, build it and they will come.

It’s true that YouTube has become the new platform for creatives to bring their ideas to fruition before they hit the big or small screens. If there's enough attention, it would be so interesting to see if this possible BMW offshoot could hit streaming one day.

Friedle said himself he’s “totally down” for a spinoff, so I'm feeling somewhat hopeful that the two might try to see this through. The last time fans saw Jack’s big one-time return on Girl Meets World, he reunited with Eric. However, it was revealed that Jack was a high-ranking executive at an environmentally harmful firm, which clashed with Eric's position as a newly elected senator. However, the iconic duo mended fences at Eric’s niece’s school dance, with Jack admitting that his friendship with his old pal was “the best choice” he ever made.

This TV show idea seems better than a previously proposed spin-off idea that came while Boy Meets World was still airing. Friedle revealed he almost left the ABC/Disney sitcom when creator Michael Jacobs pitched a “young Friends” idea for Eric to move to L.A. and meet new friends there. While it’s always amusing to see Eric’s humorous interactions, I’d rather see a straight man/funny man dynamic between him and Jack.

Now that the idea of a Jack/Eric spinoff has been brought up, this Boy Meets World fan is keeping her fingers crossed that it comes to fruition. Given that mismatched roommate shows like The Big Bang Theory, 2 Broke Girls, Perfect Strangers have been successful, why not give Jack Hunter and Eric Matthews a shot?

In the meantime, fans can watch Eric and Jack's dynamic on Boy Meets World and Girl Meets World by streaming them with a Disney+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3655. Bug Hall Defends GoFundMe After Being Told to 'Stop Impregnating' His Wife

The Little Rascals star Brandon “Bug” Hall is addressing backlash over launching a GoFundMe page before the arrival of baby No. 6 with his wife, Jill.

Hours after Hall, a self-described “radical Catholic extremist,” created a fundraising campaign on Thursday, November 5, asking for financial assistance for his family’s camper van and bills, one X user called out his family planning and suggested getting a 9 to 5 gig to make ends meet.

“Put your pride down and get a real job. This is embarrassing, stop impregnating your wife when you can’t even keep your family afloat,” the user wrote. “Set your priorities straight, practice NFP. If you don’t want advice then stop putting your business online.”

The actor fired back, simply tweeting, “I’m going to keep impregnating my wife 👍.”

A second user responded to Hall’s thread writing, “Don’t beg us for money then.”

Hall, 41, reposted a story about his clapback on Monday, November 9, and doubled down on his response. “I should have added ‘For God and country’ 🤣💪⚜️,” he wrote via X.

Hall made a name for himself as a child actor, playing Alfalfa in 1994’s The Little Rascals.

The following year, he starred in The Big Green and in 2002 he acted alongside Lindsay Lohan in Disney Channel’s Get a Clue. Hall’s most recent credit is in 2024’s Cabrini where he played Christopher Weddington.

Despite continuing to work in the entertainment industry on and off for decades, Hall revealed he “self-cancelled” six years ago, calling himself a “medieval moralist” who is dedicated to raising six children with his pregnant wife, whom he wed in 2017, while following a Catholic extremist religion.

Hall announced nine months ago that his family planned to live off the grid on a rural property in Arkansas that consists of one RV.

Earlier this month, Hall revealed via his GoFundMe page that he needed help despite his best efforts to be self-sufficient.

“It’s now six years since I self-cancelled, and I have avoided doing one of these in all that time,” he wrote on the page. “I always said this was my choice, and so I didn’t want to offload the glorious burden of it unless there was no other choice. Well here we are.”

Hall explained that his brood was “a few materials short of having things working right, and I’ve fallen a little behind on the few bills we have,” pointing to his phone bill and propane costs for the camper as some of the unexpected fees he can’t afford.

“We’re all overjoyed to be where we are, and we’re even enjoying roughing it, but baby six is less than a month away, and I really need some help getting the last few things buttoned up beforehand,” he continued.

Hall noted that he wanted to “finalize everything” over the next two weeks so he can “take some work until the baby arrives.”

The former child star added, “Times are hard for everyone, and I’m no more deserving than anyone else, but I ask in your charity that you help where you can, whether monetarily, by sharing this, or by prayer and sacrifice for the Hall-Barnetts of the Holy Cross. Viva Cristo Rey ⚜️.”

Hall has raised more than $27,000 as of Monday after asking for $2,000.

Hall received additional backlash when the site remained live after he previously claimed he would take it down once the goal was met.

The Subterranea star, however, alleged on Monday that the GoFundMe was paused for review and he hasn’t been allowed to take it down as planned.

Hall then told one X user who suggested he accept the full $27,000 donation that he would indeed reap the benefits of the page still being live.

“Oh I am, brother. I argued with multiple friends who tried to convince me to keep it up. I told each of them that a man always does what he says,” Hall replied. “The automated lockdown because of petty leftists is clearly God’s will. I’m going to get my tractor/sawmill and get to work building.”

#3653. Bob Dylan Meets Pope Leo in a Black Hoodie and Polka-Dot Tie

Yes, I was there. Not at his meeting with the pope, of course, but at the controversial Bob Dylan concert held at the Unipol Dome in Milan.

The legendary singer-songwriter has a discography that stands the test of time, but his recent decision to perform in near darkness hasn’t exactly been celebrated. With a black hood pulled up that almost completely conceals his face and only a few dim lights illuminating the stage, the impact of seeing one of the greatest artists of the 20th century was greatly diminished. From the stands, I couldn’t even zoom in on my phone because it was sealed in a bag at the entrance.

Eventually, I accepted it. Dylan intentionally created this experience, expressing his desire to distance himself from the audience. Far from a technology-forward performance, the Nobel Prize laureate, whose face has become a central figure in modern history, sang nonstop from under a hood for more than an hour and a half.

Dylan has worn the hood for at least the last two years, likely because he wants the audience to focus on his music rather than on him as a public figure. But does it have the same effect when meeting with the pope, especially when he isn’t performing?

The singer was received by Pope Leo XIV at the Apostolic Palace, dressed as if it were a stop on his tour: black sweatshirt, hood up, black gloves, black pants, and a loosely tied polka-dot tie. The ensemble was completed by an umbrella—also black—being used as a cane.

Andrea Monda, editor in chief of the Vatican newspaper L’Osservatore Romano, and Reverend Antonio Spadaro, an official from the Vatican’s Ministry of Culture, which sponsored this meeting, as it had done in July with Patti Smith, escorted Dylan. The two Americans came together in a tableau that is destined to become iconic.

The contrast bordered on the surreal: The Pope's characteristic white robes and Dylan's reclusive black hood. As always, the memes were quick to follow. Some compared Dylan to Palpatine from Star Wars, while others saw a parallel to the final encounter in the game Assassin’s Creed II.

It’s amusing to see them visually contrasted, because their personalities overlap in many ways (and not just because of their American origins). Pope Leo wrote the foreword to a book on disarmament, quoting a 1963 protest song by Dylan titled “Go Away You Bomb.” As for Dylan, he has embarked on a spiritual journey over the years that has brought him closer to the Christian faith.

Pope Leo XIV meets Bob Dylan on November 4, 2026, in Vatican City, Vatican.

“I’m a religious person,” he said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal—“I read the scriptures a lot, meditate and pray, light candles in church. I believe in damnation and salvation, as well as predestination. The Five Books of Moses, Pauline Epistles, Invocation of the Saints, all of it.”

So, is wearing a hood in the presence of the Pope a provocation? Probably not: If anything, it’s consistent with how he has made his recent public appearances.

The brief, 10-minute meeting was private, during which the two exchanged gifts. The Pope gave Dylan a rosary. The musician reciprocated with a signed copy of Chronicles–Volume One, Dylan’s autobiography. The hood stayed on throughout the meeting, turning a gesture of artistic consistency into something that, to outsiders, might look like a defensive maneuver.

Perhaps this is the intended paradox: Dylan has spent his career evading labels, yet precisely when he tries to hide, his goes viral. In many ways, it’s an act of loyalty to himself. At 85, with a career that has left an indelible mark on music and politics, he continues to defy conventions. At least he took off his gloves to shake the Pope’s hand.

Warning! The following contains spoilers from the 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way episode "Hakuna Ma-Drama." Stream the episode with an HBO Max subscription, and read at your own risk!

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way finally showed Andi Wallace and Nigel having a heart-to-heart about boundaries in their relationship, and I think it unintentionally revealed why this relationship may never work. Andi is ready for a relationship with a deep emotional connection, and it doesn't seem like Nigel is willing to do that.

TLC teased the first part of Nigel and Andi's conversation ahead of the episode, but now that we have the full context, I have thoughts. Can Nigel really be jealous of Andi texting other men, when he's seemingly unwilling to offer her anything different than what he does with all his lovers? Let's talk this out.

The latest episode of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way to air amid the 2026 TV schedule brought up something that I'm not even sure Andi realized in the moment. While Nigel went after her for texting other men, he defended his relationships with other women as they were purely physical with limited to zero texting beyond that. Minutes later, Andi mentioned that he wouldn't text her when he's with other women, and Nigel argued that he would rarely text anyone, period.

I personally found that exchange to be telling. Since the start, I've had trouble figuring out how Nigel's relationship with Andi is different than any of his other part-time lovers. Based on their conversation about texting, I'm beginning to get the feeling that it isn't, which feels like a major problem.

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way fans are still on the fence about whether Andi or Nigel are still together at this point. That's been even more uncertain since the revelation that Andi had been on Tinder and was embracing her side of ethical non-monogamy.

90 Day Fiancé's Angela Deem Drops Cryptic Message About Michael When Asked About Hunt For Love

I'm now wondering if the reason their relationship feels so ambiguous is due to Nigel treating Andi like she's a part-time lover. To be fair, if she ended up returning to the United States like some believe, that feels like a part-time romance. Is Nigel wrong for treating someone that way when he can only roam grocery stores with them barefoot once in a blue moon?

Also, I wouldn't be surprised if Andi realized she just wasn't going to get the emotional connection from Nigel that she desperately craved. It doesn't sound like his part-time lovers are getting that treatment either, which could just mean that it's not something he's ever going to give a partner. These two just may be a bad match, but we'll just have to wait and see.

#3651. GTA 6 Jacket That Costs $3,000 Sells Out Immediately

Much of the IRL marketing and promotion for Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has taken place in Miami, but the developer isn't ignoring other parts of the world. The British retailer Selfridges, an upscale department store, hosted a takeover of its flagship London store today, November 9, and among the items on sale was a £2,500 ($3,300 USD) varsity jacket inspired by GTA 6--unsurprisingly, it's sold out already.

IGN reported that the the takeover included a blue Grotti Cheetah Classic car from the game, along with GTA 6 logos and imagery throughout the store. Selfridges is offering more than 60 themed items, including clothing, bags, shot glasses, luggage tags, a cigar ashtray, and more.

The Goodtime State Varsity Jacket is adored with the logos for Rockstar and the game itself, while the sleezes are emblazoned with imagery from the game. The back of the jacket is the real showstopper, though, featuring an alligator in sunglasses having a drink. Check out more images on the Selfridges website.

Richmond basketball player Jack McCaffery, son of legendary coach Fran McCaffery, has been placed “on indefinite medical leave” after being diagnosed with Hodgkin’s Lymphoma.

“Jack was seen by medical staff at Richmond earlier this week, and following his evaluation, he traveled home with his parents and was admitted to the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania,” the school said in a statement on Sunday, November 8. “He will remain there and has begun a course of treatment under the care of the doctors and nurses at Penn Medicine.”

Jack, 20, transferred to Richmond in April after playing his freshman year at Butler University.

The basketball player’s father, Fran, currently coaches at Penn University following a legendary career at the University of Iowa.

“We are grateful to the Richmond coaching staff and medical team for their prompt response, and to Kevin Mahoney and the doctors and nurses here at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania,” Fran, 67, said in a statement on Sunday. “He is in great hands and our family feels blessed to be here, where Jack’s care is directed by this world-class care team.”

Penn Medicine’s Dr. Alison Wakoff Loren acknowledged “any cancer diagnosis is distressing, especially at a young age.”

“But we are confident in Jack’s treatment plan and Penn Medicine’s team of lymphoma experts,” Loren continued in a statement. “Hodgkin’s lymphoma mainly affects young people in their 20’s, but it is a highly curable form of cancer, thanks to years of dedicated research. #3648. Scott Colom’s Mississippi Votes Are Still Rolling In—and So Are the Views on His Viral Campaign Ads

In an era when short-form-video political messaging reigns supreme, it might be a tiebreaker, and even kingmaker, in Mississippi’s Senate midterm race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom narrowly leads incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as ballots continue to be counted on Thursday, November 5.

On October 13, Colom’s campaign released an ad that opens with a clip from a televised February interview featuring Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer and former agriculture commissioner, responding to a question about rising beef prices by offering that Mississippians “have so many proteins to choose from.” The ad then cuts to a man grilling burgers. “Pick another protein?” he asks. “Sheee-it. I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad appears to have been made by content creator Ryan Sayles. Vanity Fair has reached out to Sayles as well as Colom’s campaign for comment.

The message, which highlighted the Colom campaign’s commitment to cost cutting, capitalized on Hyde-Smith’s gaffe to the tune of more than 2.8 million views between X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook within the first 36 hours, according to the Clarion-Ledger. Former president Barack Obama’s video endorsement emphasizing Colom’s “Christian faith,” released just a day earlier, earned just over 700,000 views on the platforms in nearly double the time.

Colom currently has the edge in the historically deep-red state: If elected, he would become the first Democratic Mississippi Senator in more than 40 years—as part of the blue wave that swept the 2026 midterms, in which Democrats seized back control of both the House and Senate from MAGA-era Republicans. In Mississippi, which President Trump won by roughly 20 points in 2024, Hyde-Smith was favored to win. That is, until mid-October, when one of Colom’s campaign ads went viral, turning the Southern enclave into a surprise battleground state.

The day before Halloween, Colom made waves when he paid tribute to the Oscar-winning Ryan Coogler film Sinners, casting himself and his twin brother, Andrew, as fictional twins Smoke and Stack Moore, both portrayed by Michael B. Jordan in the movie. The film, which was set in the 1932 Mississippi Delta, follows the Black brothers as they try to keep white vampires away from their juke joint. The ad, titled “Sinators,” and released by Colom on October 30 with the disclaimer that “this is a joke!” shows the two men guarding a door as a blonde woman, who seems to be a proxy for Hyde-Smith, tries to enter. Colom says the duo have to “hold her off until the sun rises on Election Day” in the ad, which garnered more than 380,000 views on X alone prior to the November 3 election, as reported by the Sun Herald. If Colom wins, he would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era (1865–1877). VF has reached out to Coogler for comment on Colom’s campaign ad.

Colom’s attention-grabbing content hasn’t come without controversy. During the campaign, the candidate was compelled to delete another ad that featured an artificial-intelligence-generated depiction of Hyde-Smith running away from reporters after the state attorney general Lynn Fitch threatened legal action against him. (Fitch, a Republican, helped support Texas’s lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results, and was also counsel for the petitioner on Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the case which ultimately overturned Roe v. Wade.)

Shortly before the release of the Sinners ad, but after the AI dustup, the Senate Majority PAC, the flagship super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on a broadcast TV and digital ad campaign for Colom. “It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement to The Hill.

Colom, a local prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, seeking her second full term in the Senate, had a past connection heading into this political stand-off. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for federal judge in 2023, citing his support for transgender rights and his having previously been boosted by a George Soros–linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press. Colom told ABC News this “has nothing to do with the run for me…. As a Christian, I forgive her. It’s about the people in Mississippi.”

Since Mississippi elections do not have an automatic recount process, the opponents face a potential legal challenge over the results of their Senate race, in which Colom holds a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith. Colom later echoed a similar sentiment. “It’s not about me. It’s about the people in Mississippi,” the smiling Colom told reporters while speaking to constituents at a local establishment on Thursday morning. “They decided to go in a new direction.”

#3647. Cops Arrest Dad For Leaving 6-Year-Old In Line Overnight To Save Spot For Pokemon Cards

A South Carolina man has been arrested after allegedly leaving his six-year-old daughter in line at Target at 1 AM to save his spot for Pokemon trading cards.

As relayed by ABC News, witnesses said they saw John-Michael Dooley, 35, give his daughter a pillow and a blanket at around 1 AM last week before leaving her. After about an hour, customers, concerned for the girl, notified police.

It’s one of the most talked-about films this fall for a reason, but…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Writer and director Martin McDonagh's latest movie, Wild Horse Nine, had a triumphant run across film festival season before landing in theaters nationwide this weekend on the 2026 movie schedule. I’ve been excited to see it since I first saw the trailer, or really, since I heard the movie was getting made. I’m a big fan of most of McDonagh's work, and the cast includes some of my favorites, like John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, and Parker Posey. And there is a lot to love about the film. However, I can’t shake the feeling that I really didn’t care about Chris (Malkovich) and his fate, and that makes it hard to think of Wild Horse Nine as one of the best movies of the year.

As with some of McDonagh's other high water marks, specifically In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin, Wild Horse Nine brings what I appreciate most about his work: a dysfunctional friendship. It’s that friendship and the banter between Chris and Lee (Rockwell) that I love about the movie. The dialogue is crisp, biting, and hilarious. It’s also touching. They don’t hate each other like the characters in the other two movies I mention. They love and respect each other. They trust each other with their lives (literally).

I also love the ridiculous premise of the movie and the over-the-top nature of it. Chris was JFK’s assassin, for example. Often I would hate that kind of plot point, but here, it’s just ridiculous enough to make sense. I also love that most of the movie takes place in an exotic location. Easter Island is a unique place, and you don’t often see movies set there. Every time there is a giant moai in the background or a wild horse (though they have nothing to do with the title, apparently) on the road, it adds to the surrealness of it all. I loved all that.

Chris is dying. He’s got cancer, and he is dealing with dementia. He knows he’s not long for the world and decides he’s going to go out on his terms, with an assist from his loyal partner, protege, and friend, Lee. Lee, meanwhile, is working with their boss, MJ (Buscemi), to take Chris out anyway. This is the heart of the movie, the motivation that keeps Lee and Chris going, but I, frankly, didn’t care.

That might sound cold-hearted, but I didn’t. I didn’t feel an emotional attachment to what should have been the emotional center of the movie. I almost feel bad saying this, but despite the great dialogue and the cool setting, the movie didn’t move me at all. It all just passed over me like a “good hang” rather than a film that tugged at me. It felt empty to me in that respect.

Wild Horse Nine is going to get a ton of attention come award season, and let me say that I am all in on Malkovich getting nominated and finally winning a long-deserved Oscar for his work here. I hope McDonagh is nominated for best director, too. I certainly hope Rockwell gets his flowers as well. However, this isn’t the best movie I’ve seen this year, and I’ll likely be pulling for another movie come Oscar time.

Hugh Scott is the Syndication Editor for CinemaBlend. Before CinemaBlend, he was the managing editor for Suggest.com and Gossipcop.com, covering celebrity news and debunking false gossip. We've seen Mario, karts, Mario on a kart, and lots more since Lego first teamed up with Nintendo, and at long last, everyone's favorite talking green dinosaur is getting his chance in the spotlight--not you, Denver. Never you.

#3644. Inside Ye’s Yeezy Runway Show in Los Angeles After His Antisemitism Scandals

Once I clawed my way through the crowd of leather pilot jackets and passed the overzealous security guards who checked my ticket thrice, I walked through a borehole into the new Yeezy flagship store in Los Angeles’s Koreatown, where Ye stood off in the corner talking to some professional cool kids. Hundreds of people gathered on Wednesday night inside the white, brightly lit, cavernous space connected by tube-like passages for his label’s first runway show in four years. Rappers Big Sean, Kid Cudi, Rich the Kid, and A$AP Nast showed up—so did influencers Quenlin Blackwell and Fai Khadra. The streamer N3on, Ye’s daughter North, and his wife Bianca Censori also attended. And there were hundreds of unticketed fans waiting outside, hoping to get in.

“I’ve been waiting for a Yeezy show for a minute,” Kid Cudi told a camera crew on his way inside. “It’s just beautiful to see my big bro back out there doing his thing.” The musician’s team said he was “on hiatus” when Vanity Fair reached out for comment afterward. A woman standing next to me online started loudly complaining as people tried to cut her. “I just wanna see Ye,” she moaned.

And there were some other attendees who seemed more interested in making their own content. “I’m trying to network,” N3on told his Kick audience on a livestream from the show. “Everyone’s here bro…I’m looking for some collabs.”

The show started with the sound of the first note (E6) of the piano part at the beginning of Ye’s song Runaway. Models marched around a giant mound in the middle of the room in leather trench coats, militaristic jackets, shorts cut like briefs, and monochrome combat uniforms in shades of bone, charcoal, black, and red. Some of the models wore chunky combat boots that rose up the calf; others balanced on thin stilettos, including a pair of knee-high cream boots that looked like they belonged to a space-age dominatrix. It was utilitarian and a bit fetishy. The pacing of the runway walks was relentless, as if Ye was hitting you over the head with this concept until you thought it was cool. After the show, Ye walked out to a standing ovation, wearing an all-black leather outfit, black military boots, and a huge gold tiger-shaped belt buckle.

There is something fascinating about the fact that Ye can still draw adoring crowds like this one in Koreatown, and sell out football stadiums while other artists find themselves on black lists for doing way less (Javier Bardem, for example, claims he’s lost roles and brand endorsement deals because of his opposition to the war in Gaza). Ye’s last major runway show was in October 2022, during Paris Fashion Week, when he sent models down the runway wearing shirts emblazoned with the words “White Lives Matter.” The stunt led to a public confrontation with then Vogue fashion editor Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, whom Ye proceeded to attack online after she criticized the collection (Vogue, like Vanity Fair, is owned by Condé Nast). The whole thing, plus his breakup with Adidas (a brand that was started by two former members of the Nazi party) over a series of antisemitic comments, amounted to a huge fall from grace for someone who once enjoyed the patronage of Anna Wintour and helped reshape the next generation of streetwear.

One reason for Ye’s continued commercial viability is, of course, his artistic prowess. There are certain artists who become too big to fail, not because they’re too wealthy or too powerful, but because their old work has become so deeply embedded in popular culture that people can’t let it go, while their new work continues to push boundaries. That might be the case for Ye—even if this latest show wasn’t particularly groundbreaking or original. If I’m being generous, the new line was giving Boots, the Netflix military dramedy set in the ’90s about a gay marine. But, given what we know about Ye, parts of the show could’ve also been interpreted as skinhead-coded. And it certainly didn’t feel like I experienced a display of genius—a term we need to stop using to describe Ye. He probably doesn’t need us to put him on that pedestal (his ego is big enough), and I remain skeptical that a truly great artist can be capable of spewing so much hate. Art is about empathy.

I suppose most of the people cheering at Wednesday’s show had learned to compartmentalize. They had found a way to separate the designer who completely changed the sneaker game and ushered in a new era in streetwear from the guy who declared his love for Hitler, threatened to go “DEFCON 3” on Jewish people, and released a song called “Heil Hitler.” Or perhaps they really believed the apology Ye published as an advertisement in The Wall Street Journal earlier this year, in which he attributed his antisemitic behavior in part to bipolar disorder and a brain injury. Or maybe the antisemitism never bothered them in the first place.

I was asked to cover this show because I’m based in LA—I’m typically not a style correspondent. But still, I was plenty curious to see what Ye was up to. On the drive over, I thought about the ethics of covering his first big commercial venture since 2022. Maybe I would be giving him exposure he didn’t deserve. Or, maybe my presence amounted to some kind of tacit endorsement. But I dismissed that thought because I knew plenty of Jews who went to Ye’s concert at NRG Stadium in Houston last week, and I didn’t equate their attendance with bigotry. But it raises a lot of interesting questions about the politics of art and fandom. Does going to see the Michael Jackson movie mean you don’t believe the sexual abuse allegations against him? Do I have to forgive Ye’s antisemitism if I want to keep The College Dropout and My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy in my listening rotation? Maybe it’s kind of similar to how carnivores need to be okay with the murder of animals if they’re going to eat meat. I guess I’d have to be willing to forgive Ye in some sense if I plan to keep singing “couldn’t afford a car, so she called her daughter Alexis,” out loud on the StairMaster at Equinox.

Whatever one thinks of Ye personally, his influence on fashion and music is undeniable. The muted colors, exaggerated proportions and futuristic sneakers that helped define Yeezy have spread through the industry. His fingerprints are all over contemporary fashion, including the celebrity brands that followed in his wake. (Cough cough: Skims and SKYLRK).

Wednesday’s show, titled Season 01, was billed as a reset for Yeezy. So, it makes sense that the show took place in something of a primordial cave. But it’s going to be hard for him to ditch some of the baggage he’s accumulated over the last few years. Standing outside the show was a man wearing a navy suit, white shirt, red tie, and Trump ’28 hat—a loud reminder that Ye hobnobbed with white supremacists like Nick Fuentes and ran for president with the far-right conspiratorial political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos as his campaign manager.

Ye perfectly summed up my feelings about him in one of his own songs. “I miss the old Kanye, straight from the Go Kanye.”

I've watched enough behind-the-scenes footage from Denis Villeneuve's book-to-screen adaptation of the Dune series to know making Arrakis convincing takes a lot of sand. But hearing Zendaya and Robert Pattinson describe what filming the final installment in the movie franchise was like has me reaching for a glass of ice water. Apparently, playing people who live on a desert planet involves wishing you weren't on one.

Zendaya and Pattinson joined their co-stars for a conversation with The New York Times about Villeneuve's trilogy finale, which arrives on the 2026 movie schedule in December. Zendaya, who reprised Chani for the film, said the blazing sun made acting with her face difficult. Between the heat and the early calls for makeup and prosthetics, it was anything but relaxing. As she tells it:

The hardest thing is to just meditate through the heat. There's scenes where the sun is so bright that I am trying to give another facial expression other than [Zendaya scrunches up her face as if in pain] and I physically can't. [Laughs] I was just pouring sweat, trying to focus, keep my eyes open as much as I can. You've got to get ready and set up before the sun starts coming up, while it's still cool, and also we had to get into the prosthetics of it all. No one earlier than Rob.

I Didn’t Expect Jason Momoa To Name Drop Disneyland While Describing Filming In The Desert For Dune 3

I'm sorry, but if the weather is physically preventing me from making facial expressions, I'm calling it a day. Seriously, I have enough trouble concentrating when the air conditioning goes out. Zendaya still has to convey Chani's complicated feelings about Paul Atreides while the sun tries to cook her through her costume.

Then there's Pattinson, who joins the franchise as Scytale. You'd think a newcomer might find the machinery overwhelming when it sounds like something from an amusement park. Instead, the actor seemed delighted by an elaborate sequence, explaining:

The desert is just another level. There's this one sequence where I'm in this spaceship, on a gimbal, on the edge of a sand dune, and we had this 350-foot-long model of a sandworm. The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own "Dune" theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all. There are no negatives.

A 350-foot sandworm model? I love details like that. Villeneuve could presumably leave plenty of the spectacle to visual effects, but building something that enormous gives the actors a very real piece of Arrakis to react to. Of course, Pattinson's declaration that there were "no negatives" came with a fairly disgusting exception. He continued:

Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them. He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress.

"Bulbous sweat bubbles" is an image I would have happily gone my entire life without imagining. Still, I appreciate how much he enjoyed working with Villeneuve, even if his body apparently found a brand-new way to perspire.

Dune: Part Three picks up nearly two decades after Paul's rise to power and concludes Villeneuve's adaptation of Frank Herbert's saga. It's due in theaters December 18, going head-to-head with Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday. Judging by these cast stories from the making of Dune, the performers earned every minute we'll spend sitting comfortably in an air-conditioned auditorium. I'll gladly watch the sandworms, with my wildly themed popcorn bucket in hand, from the comfort of a reclined theater seat.

#3641. DC Studios Is Getting A Marvel Veteran To Replace James Gunn And Peter Safran

DC Studios co-presidents James Gunn and Peter Safran have officially announced they'll step down, and Marvel veteran Jeremy Latcham will replace them. Gunn and Safran architected the new DC Universe of films and TV series, and they also had ambitious plans to expand the DCU into video games. Latcham is no stranger to superhero cinema, with credits on several of Marvel's biggest projects, including Spider-Man, Guardians of the Galaxy, and Avengers.

"Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface," Gunn and Safran wrote in a statement (via Variety). "We're immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow."

Following the relaunch of the DC Universe in film, Gunn later spoke about the potential of cross-platform storytelling, saying actors would portray their characters across all forms of media—including video games. "We have a couple of little DC games coming out. But we also have talked about–and in early stages of planning--some bigger things," Gunn said in 2025. "One thing in particular I’m excited about, but it does take time."

We never got to hear David Corenswet reprise his role as Superman in a video game, and since then, big changes have happened behind the scenes. Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery was approved earlier this year, leading to a merger between Warner Bros. Interactive (the WB division that publishes video games based on the company's IP) and Paramount Games Studio.

While the ambitious plans for the video game side of DC Studios never materialized, Gunn and Safran were still busy building a new DC Universe for the big and small screen. Three feature films were released--Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface--while the TV side saw multiple animated and live-action projects like Lanterns, Creature Commandos, and Peacemaker. Next year's big project is the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, which Gunn wrote and co-directed, and The People v. Gorilla Grodd is an upcoming series that will see Skyler Gisondo back as Jimmy Olsen.

On the video game side, Rocksteady is rumored to be working on a new single-player Batman game.

#3640. Bachelor's Andi Dorfman Reveals Son's Name, Meaning After 'Gnarly' C-Section

The Bachelor alum Andi Dorfman has shared her newborn son’s name one day after announcing his birth.

“Welcome to the world … Hudson McGraw Hart 💙,” Dorfman, 39, wrote via Instagram on Monday, November 9, alongside hospital photos with husband Blaine Hart and their baby boy.

The reality TV alum continued, “8 lbs 2 oz and 21 inches of pure love and snuggles and already melting our hearts and making me quickly understand what everyone means when they say there’s something so special about being a boy mama 🥹.”

Dorfman then shared the sweet meaning behind their son’s name.

“Named Hudson after mom’s favorite place, NYC, and McGraw to carry on a special family name on Dad’s side,” she explained.

Dorfman also shared more details about her birth experience.

“Thank you for all the well wishes, everyone is recovering well (side note: c sections are quite gnarly!!)” she wrote. “We are so grateful for a healthy growing family and this sweetest little love we never knew we needed 🧸.”

Dorfman and Hart, 40, announced their son’s birth on Sunday, November 8.

“Absolutely head over heels in love 💙,” Dorfman wrote via Instagram alongside a photo of their son’s tiny foot wearing a hospital bracelet.

Dorfman also shared a video of herself and Hart heading into the hospital on Sunday.

Dorfman and Hart are also parents to daughter Harper, 22 months. The couple announced their pregnancy with baby No. 2 in June.

“Harper, the BIG SIS coming this fall! So grateful for baby #2 to join the crew. These are truly what our dreams are made of 🥹🥰,” Dorfman captioned photos from her maternity shoot at the time.

Dorfman later reflected on expanding her family in a post last month.

“I can’t believe we are soaking in the last few weeks of just us three 🥹,” she wrote. “I find myself holding Harper a little tighter lately and feeling bittersweet knowing this chapter is coming to an end. It feels like for so long it’s just been us three (even thought it’s only been less than two years) and honestly, I am sad/emotional knowing things will never be exactly like this again. But I remind myself of the excitement that awaits us: Harper gets to be a big sister, Blaine gets to raise a son and we as a family get to become a fearsome foursome!”

Dorfman first rose to reality TV fame on season 18 of The Bachelor in 2014. Later that year, she led The Bachelorette season 10.

Dorfman reconnected with Hart in 2021 after previously meeting him through a mutual friend 15 years earlier. The couple got engaged in 2022 and tied the knot in 2023.

#3639. Carrie Coon on ‘The Gilded Age’, ‘The Liberation’, and Parenting

Carrie Coon and I are supposed to be talking about her new film, The Liberation—a gripping drama about a suburban mother who leaves her family to join an all-woman cult in the 1980s. But when we meet for tea at the London West Hollywood hotel, it doesn’t take long for our conversation to turn to general doom and gloom. Between the moment I order a custom-made ginger tea—which I’m now calling “the Carrie Coon special”—and when it arrives at our table, we’ve already started talking about fascism in America, how hard it is for an actor to find enough work to earn health insurance, global warming, and the devastating fires in Los Angeles.

“I don’t do small talk anymore. I’m not good at it,” says Coon, taking a sip from her own ginger tea—a blend she started having this restaurant make for her after getting hooked on it while filming The White Lotus in Thailand. “I’m just like, ‘So we’re all going to die. How you feeling about that?’”

But even when she’s talking fire and brimstone, Coon’s charming warmth keeps the conversation from being too dark and stormy. If Coon were leading a cult, I might join. She’s funny and empathetic; she makes this sweet, quick “aww” sound if you compliment her or share something she’s sympathetic with. Maybe Coon, who was raised in Ohio, simply can’t shed her Midwestern sensibility, even though she transforms onscreen into characters with much harder, and sometimes pricklier, outer shells. Coon has earned four Emmy nominations for playing the stubborn small-town cop Gloria Burgle in Fargo, the lonely lawyer Laurie Duffy in The White Lotus, and twice for the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell on The Gilded Age, which just debuted its fourth season on HBO.

Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector in season 2 of The Gilded Age.

She reveals a different side of herself in The Liberation, Guy Nattiv’s drama that opens in limited (and Oscar-qualifying) release November 6 before going wide January 8. Her character, Rita Cooper, is a Holocaust survivor whose trauma and stagnation in her family life cause her to abandon her husband (Tracy Letts, Coon’s real-life husband) and two daughters (Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young) for an all-female spiritual group led by a charismatic leader named Ricki (Lily James).

The film is a strong showcase for Coon as she transforms both physically and emotionally. When Rita joins the commune, she loses weight and her identity as she falls further under Ricki’s spell. “People are struck by me playing someone who feels weaker or more frail, because I’m often put into roles where I’m strong, verbal, intellectual, brassy,” says Coon. “I think it’s unusual for them to see that level of vulnerability in my performances. But of course, I think of myself as capable of all that.”

I nervously admit to Coon that when I watched The Liberation, I was troubled to find that, as a mother of two young kids, I could understand Rita’s choice—to leave behind all the demands and burdens of family and household, to run to a place where you could focus solely on yourself. It’s hard to say this out loud.

Coon makes that sympathetic “aww” sound. “We all have that moment. It’s a fantasy, but haven’t we all thought, ‘I could leave right now; what would happen if I just didn’t come back?’” she says. “That’s why I found her so compelling, because she walked away from her family and chose to invest in her self-actualization and her healing in the ’80s. It’s a really risky choice, but, I suppose, just undeniable for her.”

Coon and Letts, who married in 2013—in a hospital where Letts had just received emergency gallbladder surgery—have two kids together who are now five and eight years old, just a few years ahead of my own. Juggling life as a working mother can be challenging, especially in invisible ways. “I think a lot of the cognitive load is so heavy, and people don’t really understand,” says Coon.

Carrie Coon, Leslie Bibb, and Michelle Monaghan in The White Lotus.

When Coon was cast in the third season of HBO’s hit The White Lotus, playing a woman who goes on a luxury vacation with her two longtime best friends, she was gone for a total of 10 weeks. At the time, her daughter was only three. “That was very hard, and that was a very difficult decision,” she says. “I’m not sure it was a great decision, ultimately. I don’t know if we would do it again the same way.”

She’s had other moments of feeling spread too thin, especially just before she went to film His Three Daughters—the 2023 movie that cast Coon, Natasha Lyonne, and Elizabeth Olsen as three sisters who reunite to care for their ailing father. “I turned to Tracy and said, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I can’t do both things,’” she remembers. Maybe as her kids get older— “little kids, little problems, big kids, big problems,” she says—she will actually have to shift her focus. “In this world where we have no schema to navigate the challenges they’re facing, I would have to take a step back again and be with them,” she says. “I don’t know. It’s hard to say.”

Elizabeth Olsen and Carrie Coon in His Three Daughters.

Coon and Letts’s kids joined them for part of the time while they filmed The Liberation in Vancouver. During the first half of the movie, Coon wore hip pads and other body-shaping additions to make Rita seem more weighed down by her responsibility and the trauma of having been a child in a concentration camp. Coon says she could also lean into the exhaustion she already felt: “We were co-sleeping in a little apartment, and it was not easy,” she says. “And so I was like, ‘Great, I don’t have to look like anything. I could just be tired.’ So I kind of allowed that exhaustion I normally feel, which I try to overcome in my daily life, just to creep in more.”

When Rita leaves her family for the isolated commune, Coon’s environment also shifted: She moved to a new filming location, and her family left town. In the mornings, she’d swim or stretch. She’d also lost 10 pounds and shorn her hair for the role, transforming from Rita into Naya—the new name Ricki gives her character, a common practice in cults. “Carrie’s a very, very strong, physical actress,” says Nattiv. “Rita is the matriarch of her family. She’s a strong woman, intelligent—and then she’s not. She loses everything. It was amazing to see how she shifts between Naya and Rita.”

Nattiv based The Liberation on his grandmother Rita—who really had been in a concentration camp as a child, and joined a commune in her adult life. Rita had given testimony to Yad Vashem, the World Holocaust Remembrance Center; Coon watched it as she prepared to play the role. She also watched and listened to hours of testimonies of women who had been in concentration camps in Poland, learning “the sort of very specific way that particular trauma is held in the body, the challenge of speaking the unspeakable.”

I wondered if watching so many hours of these stories, so much horror and pain, was difficult. “Well, if I’m really honest, I found that I was drawn to listening to them instead of the news,” says Coon. “I started listening to them as a comfort, because they were a story of resilience. Thinking about the unspeakable atrocities that were happening around me in my very own country with my own tax dollars—and yet here are people on the other side of something like that, articulating those stories and what they learned.”

The present political climate is ever-present in Coon’s mind, as well as on her social media accounts. (A few of her more recent X posts: “Failed president,” “Close the camps,” “The president has nothing but ‘tranny’ jokes. How pathetic. How empty.”) For the past few weeks, she’s been encouraging people to vote, especially her fellow Ohioans. As she admitted, she’s not one for small talk.

Carrie Coon (center) with Odessa Young, Bella Ramsey, Sharon Taylor, and Tracy Letts in The Liberation.

“It’s absurd. It’s untenable,” she says. “We’re in a really precarious moment because people’s lives are untenable all across the board.” She recognizes her own privilege—that she and her husband are both able to work, that they can afford childcare—but says she’s worried for actors who can’t find roles in this shrinking economy. “Even just the labor of making tapes, the free labor, there’s no protection,” she says. “We have these rules in our union, but no one’s really following those rules. What young actor is going to make that phone call and complain?”

She’s also noticing how few female-centered films get told on the biggest stages, with the biggest budgets. “What happens when you’re living in an authoritarian regime is everybody gets scared, and everybody gets safe, and everyone’s making really safe choices. It’s not what people want,” she says. “Women are tremendous economic drivers in this economy, and we still aren’t making art for them.”

Coon will do her part, with films like The Liberation. She’s wrapped work on another independent movie, Honeymoon/Funeral, a romantic comedy from Fresh Off the Boat creator Nahnatchka Khan that also stars Rebecca Ferguson and Greta Lee. Next year, Letts heads to London from April through October to do Death of a Salesman at The National, which means more maneuvering for their family unit. “We’re thrilled for him. And yet that’s going to be a really interesting time for our family,” she says. “So I don’t have as much work lined up, and I’m okay to be patient. I feel good about being patient right now.”

But she does have one wish for the future: She’d like to do a comedy. “No one’s letting me do that. My family is surprised by my career because it’s just not the way I occurred to them as a person at all. People are expecting to meet a very serious and lugubrious actress that needs a lot of special drinks or something,” she says. While taking another sip from her custom, off-menu ginger tea.

Ken Jennings isn't going anywhere as Jeopardy!'s host, but he has two famous names he's considered should he need a substitute for a day. Fans may not be surprised to hear that both of these TV personalities have been working hard amid the 2026 TV schedule. These two stars sound like entries on a wishlist, but now that Jennings has put it out there, I'd love to see both of them host the quiz series.

Jennings finally accepted the full-time hosting gig in 2023 in the aftermath of Alex Trebek's passing and various inquiries from curious fans. During a taping, Jennings was asked who'd be a fitting replacement for him in the event he has to miss shows. The first name he floated was none other than longtime Survivor host Jeff Probst. As Jennings astutely mentioned, before Probst was watching contestants battle it out in Fiji, he had a very different gig:

Well, you know who has a lot of Jeopardy! hosting experience is Jeff Probst, who hosted Rock & Roll Jeopardy! back before he was Jeff Probst. I mean, he now hosts three seasons of Survivor a year, I think, so the guy is probably busy.

Probst actually hosts two seasons of Survivor a year, both of which are filmed back-to-back in Fiji in a little under two months. As the host told Variety back in 2024, however, hosting the series is a year-round job. When he's not on the island, he's helping work on post-production, overseeing the casting process for future seasons and hosting a podcast. All this to say, he may be just as busy asJennings suggested, even if he doesn't have a third season to film.

One could argue that in the event that Probst was unavailable, Pop Culture Jeopardy! host Colin Jost could serve as a substitute. Unfortunately, for Jost, though, Jennings named-dropped the host of another hit reality TV series instead.

If Jeff Probst is too tied up in Survivor, Ken Jennings also floated RuPaul as a potential fill-in. The Drag Race host may not be any less busy than Probst, but that didn't stop the former Jeopardy! champ from name-dropping him as well:

Also, RuPaul, I think, would be pretty good.

RuPaul hasn't hosted Jeopardy or a spinoff, but all that Drag Race experience and his time mentoring many successful drag winners has to count for something. I think he'd be a great choice for a one-off, provided he has the time to commit.

It's interesting to hear Ken Jennings not mention Mayim Bialik, as she co-hosted with him for years before he become the sole host. Perhaps he's privy to some info that she's not willing to return to Jeopardy, or he just thought that would be a boring answer to give to the audience. We can only speculate.

For now, it's a non-issue. Ken Jennings is solidly in the role as host, despite pushing off full-time hosting duties for years. It's kind of hilarious, considering everyone, including Alex Trebek, assumed he'd end up in the role, and that he ultimately embraced his fate years later.

Jeopardy! airs on weekdays in syndication, so check their local listings for when and where to watch it. We'll also keep an eye out to see who may substitute for Ken Jennings should he need a day off in the near future, and if Jeff or Ru end up getting tapped for it.

#3637. GTA 5’s Trevor Should Be In GTA 6 Sitting On The Toilet To “Pass The Torch,” Actor Says

Steven Ogg famously portrayed the wildcard character Trevor in Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 5, and he wishes Rockstar brought the character back for GTA 6.

Speaking to Principle Magazine, Ogg said it would have been a nice moment to "pass the torch" to have Trevor show up at the beginning of GTA 6 "sitting on the toilet" or doing some "weird thing" like walking around having something fall on his head, knocking him to the ground.

In short, Ogg said he wanted Trevor to have some kind of "acknowledgement" that Trevor's story is over and it's time for Jason and Lucia to take center stage in GTA 6. Ogg said it could have been a nice full circle moment because, in GTA 5, Trevor's first scene shows him bashing Johnny Klebitz from GTA 4.

"I’m not a fan of all of the reboots and the sequels. I don’t get the … the hunger for that, but there is, because it makes money and that’s why people do it," he said.

Ogg went on to say things have come so far since GTA 5, so he wanted to see how characters from GTA 5 could look in GTA 6, given the technical improvements from the past decade.

"So, I’d be curious. But you know, not my duck, not my bottle. Not my monkey, not my cage," he said.

Also in the interview, Ogg pushed back against the online theories that he is no fan of GTA and Trevor. He said he's always been proud of Trevor and proud of what Rockstar created. He doesn't play GTA 5, but he said people are out of line for taking his soundbites about GTA 5 and spinning them into a belief that he's no fan of GTA or his character. He acknowledged he didn't like how people would call him Trevor, and not Steven, in real life, though.

"That’s been all blown out of proportion. Or that I hate GTA and now I’m starting to embrace it more. No, it’s just early on, there was a lot of people calling me Trevor. And I’d be like, 'Well, my name is Steven,'" he said. "So I could never understand that. So it’s always like 'What’s your name, David? Okay, Nolan.' It doesn’t make sense if you know someone’s name and you’re calling them someone else’s name. I don’t get it. And I understand people associate with characters and connections," he said. "At these Comic Cons, they’re not Documentary Cons. So I couldn’t be these people. I mean, I couldn’t even be Trevor, because he’s a cartoon. Simon [from The Walking Dead] was a human on a TV show, at least. Yeah, it’s just one of those things. It’s like… [scratches head]. It’s like me calling you, you know, Barbara."

Trevor was one of the three playable characters in GTA 5, alongside Michael (Ned Luke) and Franklin (Shawn Fonteno). Ogg, in particular, landed some notable acting roles after GTA 5, appearing in the TV shows Better Call Saul, Snowpiercer, and Westworld, along with the films Emancipation and Unabomber.

Trevor was apparently going to be in more content for GTA 5, as Ogg said Rockstar canceled Trevor-centric DLC that would have featured a James Bond-like story. Rockstar reportedly canceled the DLC so it could instead focus more on GTA Online, which is known to basically print money.

GTA 5 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#3636. Switch 2 Just Had Its Best Sales Week Of 2026, And It’s All Because Of Zelda

Nintendo just released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake for Switch 2, and the themed console that Nintendo debuted with the game has, perhaps unsurprisingly, sold incredibly well.

Circana's Mat Piscatella shared new data that confirms the Switch 2 just had its best sales week of 2026 so far, based on dollar sales, thanks to the 40th Anniversary Edition console. The $520 console launched on October 29, and Circana's reporting period for the week ended on October 31.

The special-edition console sports a geometric design inspired by the Zelda series, with a large Triforce symbol on the dock. The accompanying Joy-Cons feature the game's classic green and gold color scheme, along with specific designs based on the RPG series.

The system doesn't include a copy of the game, which launched on November 5, and is priced at $60 digitally and $70 on a physical cartridge.

Sales of the 40th Anniversary Edition console helped lift total spending on hardware in the US for the week by 81% compared to the same week in 2025.

The Ocarina of Time remake has been a huge hit critically, scoring a 9/10 here at GameSpot. It's the highest-rated game of 2026 so far. Nintendo has not revealed any sales numbers for the game, however.

#3635. Inside PS, The Private Members-Only Terminals at LAX, Miami, and Paris Airports

There are 10 terminals at the Los Angeles International Airport. One through nine are for the general public: terminal one for Southwest, terminal two for Virgin Atlantic, the international hub in the numberless terminal B. Each one is packed with weary, edgy travelers lined up for security, coffee, or a meal. You arrive at your terminal via rideshare and depart via rideshare—so long as your ride is a premium black car. If it isn’t, you must take a 20-minute bus ride to a parking lot called “LAX-it,” where you wait amongst the hordes for your UberX to arrive as it slowly inches through crippling traffic.

The 10th terminal promises to deliver you from this misery. It’s around the back of the airport complex, off the 105 in El Segundo, next to several cargo holds and a Gate Gourmet facility where airplane meals are carted off to various jets on the tarmac. When you arrive, no one asks for a boarding pass. A security guard checks your name off a list, and a valet whisks away your bags with care before you’re ushered into your own private suite with amenities galore: squishy velvet couches and boucle chairs, Assouline coffee table books, free iPhone chargers, and chocolate-covered almonds and gummy bears. A fridge comes with sparkling waters and canned matcha drinks—a far cry from the plastic Dasani bottles found at Hudson News. A private bathroom boasts Le Labo soaps.

While you’re waiting for your flight, you can get a manicure, a table massage, or even a haircut. You can request a pair of Normatec Elite compression boots (retail price: $1,099) to help with your circulation before takeoff. Or if you are feeling more social, you can head to “the Salon,” where abstract art hangs on the wall and chandeliers dangle from the ceiling. Order the coconut chia pudding or bagel-and-lox platter if you’re there for breakfast, duck confit agnolotti or a Mediterranean chicken panini on house-made ciabatta for lunch. For dinner, there’s a New York strip, and caviar service is always available.

When it’s time to go, you’ll pass through a private security check with a dedicated TSA agent. Then you’ll climb in a BMW (suitcases already loaded) which drives you across the tarmac directly to your plane. Forget boarding with Zone 8 or gatechecking your carry-on.

The Salon at PS at LAX, designed by Elle Decor A-List interior designer Cliff Fong.

This is PS at LAX—a private, members only terminal at Los Angeles International. It’ll cost you to get in: One-time access to the Salon (and nothing else) without a membership is priced at $1,295. For frequent fliers, an annual baseline membership starts at $1,250 and goes up to $4,850. Private suites cost an additional $3,650 or $4,950 for four people, depending on the type of membership.

Unsurprisingly, it’s become a see-and-don’t-be-seen hub for LA celebrities wary of attracting the camera-wielding masses at commercial airports (and the paparazzi that stake out the terminal). Gigi Hadid, Gabrielle Union, Hailey Bieber, Jamie Foxx, and Kourtney Kardashian are just some of the famous faces that are known to frequent PS at LAX.

But this year, PS is pushing beyond the Hollywood stars eager to escape the clutches of Deuxmoi. In the past six months, the firm has opened private terminals in Miami (taking over the historic Pan-Am space) and Dallas. Paris is coming in early 2027. The seclusion, the gourmet food, and the luxurious interiors (curated by Elle Decor A-List designers Jean Liu for Dallas and Cliff Fong for Miami and LA) are all nice draws, but there's another reason PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter cites for why customers are willing to shell out thousands of dollars on top of a first-class ticket.

The Atlanta airport on March 23, 2026. Government shutdowns have caused disastrous scenes at American commercial terminals.

Because, well, it has been. The last fiscal year has seen three government shutdowns, the longest of which lasted for 76 days. TSA Deputy Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill told Congress that the agency experienced the longest security wait times in its 24-year history during the shutdown that stretched from February 14 to April 30, 2026. Some airports, including Atlanta, had lines up to five hours long. The logistical meltdowns hit at a time when air travel has never been more popular: In 2025, nearly 907 million people flew commercially in the United States. Belouizdad Porter says that those disruptions led to a direct increase in PS customers.

The growing crowds at airport lounges also nudged some travelers over the edge. Credit card companies long ago realized that offering lounge access enticed new customers, with Chase, American Express, Citi, Capital One, and more getting in the game. But demand exceeded square footage, and many of those lounges suffered from overcrowding and subpar service, selling the dream of an aero oasis that never was.

“There have never been more airport lounges,” David Mack writes in the New York Times, “Yet there also have never seemed to be more lounges that are not worth the hassle…Sometimes the lines for the lounges are the longest in the airport.”

(Though the only thing worse than an overcrowded airport lounge might be getting stranded outside. Reddit is currently up in arms about the obscene food prices at the newly renovated Burbank Airport in California—price tag: $1.3 billion—where a cheese and bean burrito costs $25.)

Another contributing factor? The rising costs of private jets. While the terms “one percent” or “.1 percent” are often thrown around when it comes to PJ owners, the reality is only 0.003 percent of America’s population can afford even fractional ownership. Demand for private aircraft surged after the pandemic, raising prices, and now the average net worth of those who own a jet is $190 million. For those with fractional ownership, it’s $140 million. Yet there are still plenty of mere decamillionaires looking to dodge the misery of the airport. As Sartre put it: Hell is other people.

Previously, “You could either fly round-trip first class for $6,000 but deal with the airport, the friction, and the crowd,” Belouizdad Porter says. “Or you could fly private round-trip and it's $200,000.” PS operates somewhere in between. “I think there’s a real appetite for that middle ground: the convenience of private aviation without the commitment or expense of chartering an entire plane,” says Lucie Kittel, founder of luxury travel advisory firm Domino Travel.

And besides, even if you do reach the level of private jet ownership, you still can’t always avoid the flying masses. A midsize jet that fits six to nine people costs between $10 and $20 million dollars and can fly 2,000 to 3,000 nautical miles. If it’s on the shorter end of that range, it can just make a trip from New York to California—but not to Europe. There’s also the issue of safety: The country is currently facing a pilot shortage, and more experienced candidates often work with mainstream airlines who can provide higher salaries. Larger planes can also better navigate rough weather.

Carriers like United and Delta know all of this, which is why they’re beefing up their luxury experiences. Delta recently announced it was investing over $1 billion in retrofitting its premium cabins, and new Delta One Terminals at JFK and LAX allow first-class ticket holders to avoid overcrowded TSA lines and the standard lounge. “Most of my clients flying out of JFK are choosing Delta One,” Kittel adds, “and they love the experience.”

Thanks to the artificial intelligence boom—the latest phase of a 15-year bull market for stocks—there’s been an explosion of multi-multi-millionaires in America. While not all of them can fly private, they certainly can devote large sums of money to separating themselves from the hoi polloi. Both startups like PS and established players are now competing for that sub-ultra-wealthy dollar.
