#3634. When Is Joran van der Sloot Getting Out of Prison? His Expected Release Date

More than two decades after Natalee Holloway vanished on a high school graduation trip to Aruba, the man who confessed to killing her is back in the spotlight thanks to a new Netflix docuseries — and her mother is still fighting to see him formally charged with her murder.

Joran van der Sloot admitted to bludgeoning the 18-year-old Alabama teen to death as part of a 2023 proffer agreement, nearly 20 years after Natalee was last seen leaving a nightclub with him. With Netflix’s three-part docuseries Taken: Natalee Holloway now streaming, viewers are once again asking where van der Sloot is, how long he will remain behind bars and when he will be released.

Van der Sloot is currently in custody at Challapalca prison in Peru. He is serving a 28-year sentence for the 2010 murder of 21-year-old Peruvian college student Stephany Flores Ramírez, which is running concurrently with a 20-year U.S. federal prison sentence for extortion and wire fraud. Under that arrangement, he is expected to be released in 2045.

Holloway disappeared on May 30, 2005, while celebrating her high school graduation in Oranjestad, Aruba. She was last seen leaving the Carlos’n Charlie’s nightclub and getting into a car with van der Sloot and brothers Deepak Kalpoe and Satish Kalpoe. Van der Sloot was quickly named a suspect after the accounts he gave to authorities didn’t line up.

All three men were arrested in June 2005 on suspicion of kidnapping and murder, then released without charges that September. They were arrested a second time in November 2007 and released one month later. Aruban officials reopened the case in 2008 after Dutch crime reporter Peter R. de Vries released hidden-camera footage in which van der Sloot described Holloway’s death, but the case fell apart when officials couldn’t corroborate his statements.

Five years after Holloway vanished, van der Sloot killed Flores Ramírez in Lima, Peru. He fled to Chile but was arrested in June 2010. That same month, he was indicted in the United States on federal wire fraud and extortion charges tied to a March 2010 meeting with Natalee’s mother, Beth Holloway, during which he demanded money in exchange for information about Natalee’s disappearance.

Van der Sloot pleaded guilty to the federal extortion charges in 2023 and was sentenced to 20 years. As part of the plea deal, he finally admitted to killing Natalee and agreed to share information about her death. Aruba enforces a 12-year statute of limitations for homicides, meaning the window to convict him there has expired.

Van der Sloot married Leidy Figueroa in July 2014 at the Peruvian prison where he is still serving his sentence. His attorney confirmed to CNN that Figueroa was an accountant and had one child at the time of their wedding. The couple welcomed a daughter on September 30, 2014, just three months after they tied the knot.

His attorney confirmed to the Daily Mail in 2023 that van der Sloot was divorcing Figueroa and moving on. “Joran had a bunch of girlfriends,” his lawyer said at the time. “Lots of girls used to visit him.”

Even with van der Sloot’s confession in hand, Beth says she is not finished pursuing accountability for her daughter’s death. “The nightmare’s over, right? But I’m not done yet,” she told Tudum after the November 4, 2026, premiere of Taken: Natalee Holloway.

Beth has spent the past two years working with Netherlands attorneys Royce de Vries and Annemiek van Spanje to file a murder complaint against van der Sloot with Dutch authorities. “I’ve been working busy behind the scenes, got the murder complaint,” she said. “And now we’re working on, hopefully, murder charges. So I’ve been busy, but one step at a time.”

She said she feels confident in her legal team, noting that Royce has a personal connection to the case because he is the son of Peter R. de Vries, the Dutch investigative journalist whose 2008 reporting documented van der Sloot admitting to his involvement in Natalee’s murder. “I know this is a legacy to his father,” Beth said of Royce. “He’s going to finish this job.” She added that a Dutch prosecutor is “obtaining all the documents” and “getting all Natalee’s case files.”

Beth has also reflected on what the long investigation cost her and why the word “closure” has never fit. “The not-knowing is the never-ending nightmare. And with that nightmare, you endure endless scammers, theories, investigations that are swirling around you, and they never cease because you can never say it’s over,” she said. She added that she now feels at peace “because the nightmare of not knowing what happened to Natalee is over, and the endless scammers, the endless taunting of her killer, they’re over.”

Getting formal murder charges against van der Sloot, she said, is her “new mission.”

#3633. Susie Wiles Is Out. What Will Trump Do When He Runs Out of Women to Fire?

You know how after millions of people make clear that they despise not just your political project but also you personally, the logical response is to triple down on the specific things they hate?

That’s Donald Trump’s signature move. Three days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats—nine if you feel bullish on Mississippi and Alaska—and secured a House majority, winning 253 seats and counting, the president announced that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, would be replaced by Stephen Miller.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Even though polls indicating a blue wave proliferated before the election, this particular outcome still comes as a surprise. After all, Wiles had apparently proven her ability to ride out storms before—including everything that rocked Trump’s 2024 campaign, which Wiles managed, and her choice to sit for 10 interviews with Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple in 2025, during which she discussed Elon Musk’s drug use and JD Vance’s true motives for embracing Trump. “Despite his travails, Trump needs Wiles and almost everyone around him knows it,” Whipple recently wrote in a follow-up story tracing rumors of Wiles’s imminent axing.

But now Wiles’s luck has finally run out. Why? Perhaps because she is, in the end, a woman.

Trump’s first term was marked by all sorts of chaos, including frequent arrivals to and departures from the White House. (Remember Omarosa?) But it doesn’t take Jessica Fletcher to detect that this time around, there’s a distinct pattern when it comes to whom Trump is willing to toss aside when the going gets rough. The scalps of the no-scalps era all have barrel curls. As Texas representative Jasmine Crockett observed in April, “He will throw the incompetent women under the bus a lot faster than the incompetent men.”

On March 5, following an uprising against the administration’s mass-deportation effort that culminated in two protesters being killed by ICE agents in Minnesota, Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem was axed. After wrath over the administration’s botched handling of the Epstein files, Attorney General Pam Bondi was fired in April.

Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s labor secretary, resigned later that month amid a misconduct investigation. Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, who couldn’t sell Trump’s disastrous war with Iran, submitted her resignation in May, after her husband was diagnosed with cancer. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt stepped down—of her own accord—in August. Following an embarrassing Wall Street Journal investigation, Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece—and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.—was forced to resign last month.

Though you may have already forgotten all about her, Katie Zacharia had perhaps the least distinguished tenure of all: She gave her first briefing as Trump’s new press secretary on a Tuesday and was forced out by Friday of the same week. Shortly before Wiles’s ouster this week, Harmeet Dhillon, who helped kill DEI after joining the civil rights division of Trump’s Justice Department, announced she was stepping down.

All this, and Pete Hegseth still has a job.

What are we to make of the fact that Trump’s departed all happen to harbor two X chromosomes? Could it be, perhaps, that President “Grab ’Em by the Pussy” has a problem with women—even the loyalists who are largely responsible for helping him claw his way back into the White House in the first place? (Does Trump win, or even run, in 2024 without Wiles? It’s a possibility I’d like to see Rodham author Curtis Sittenfeld explore in an upcoming novel.)

The one thing we can be sure about is that, as of right now, there are only three women left in Trump’s 21-person Cabinet. The members of that trio—Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Kelly Loeffler, administrator of the Small Business Administration—might want to watch their blowout. (So should Natalie Harp.) Perhaps after they go, Trump will start employing the principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion while stabbing his allies in the back.

#3632. MacBook Neo 2 is coming, and Apple reportedly expects a massive hit

Apple has a MacBook Neo 2 planned for early 2027, per Mark Gurman, and a new report from Digitimes indicates the company is expecting it to be a massive hit.

When the MacBook Neo debuted earlier this year, it became an instant hit.

Driven primarily by MacBook Neo, Apple set a new record for its best ever sales week among first-time Mac buyers.

But as popular as the first MacBook Neo has proven, it sounds like Apple is planning for its successor to be an even bigger hit.

Apple has given suppliers a shipment forecast of 16 million MacBook Neo units for 2027, about double the nearly 8 million units expected in 2026, according to supply-chain sources.

16 million units for 2027 is a huge increase from MacBook Neo’s 2026 numbers.

A small portion of that increase can be attributed to the MacBook Neo being on sale for longer in 2027. The original Neo arrived in March 2026, so 2027 will have the advantage of January and February sales.

But those two extra months can’t come anywhere close to accounting for the doubling of units. Especially since they’re slower periods for consumer electronics sales.

With reporting pointing to a MacBook Neo 2 launching in early 2027, it sounds like Apple is confident the Neo will prove even more popular in the year ahead.

Ones of Matt Damon’s 2026 movie releases, The Odyssey, couldn’t stop breaking records after its debut this past July. At present, Damon's name is also being mentioned amid awards season conversations. Still, as the star comes off his big year, he's speaking honestly about what he considers to be the low points of his career.

The Good Will Hunting star was recently asked when he knew The Odyssey would be a hit, and he admitted that moment came when he saw the movie for himself. Decades earlier, Damon had those same instincts, as he explained to GQ. However, in those cases, the results weren't nearly as strong as they are now. While discussing one particular slump, Damon named one of the films he had on the docket in 2000:

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And Will was, as he is now, the biggest star. And so it’s like, it’s not Will’s fault. [Laughs]

While The Legend of Bagger Vance may have had one of the best golf scenes in Hollywood history, it was definitely a box office bomb, grossing $39.5 million globally against a reported production budget of $80 million. Not to mention, the sports-drama film has low critics' score of 43% on Rotten Tomatoes. In the long run, it didn't hurt the careers of Damon, Smith or Theron, but I can understand why the Bourne star would've been shaken by the reception at that time.

Damon, unfortunately, experienced another setback after the release of Bagger Vance. There's another failed movie of Damon's that he's still not over, and it was released in 2000 as well:

And then I did All the Pretty Horses with Billy Bob [Thornton], and that was a whole fraught experience. There were different ideas between the studio and between Billy Bob about what the movie should be, and so it ended up getting cut in a way that wasn’t to Billy’s liking and it didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

I can imagine how frustrating that must have been to envision what you wanted your movie to be, only for the studio to take over. With that, it's hard not to wonder what could have been if Billy Bob Thornton had had his way. Ultimately, All the Pretty Horses was another bomb for Damon, as it made only $18.1 million worldwide on a budget of $57 million. As for its critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, it's at 33%, as of this writing.

Considering the Saving Private Ryan star's immense success, it's now somewhat wild to think about Damon worrying about his acting career, but it happens. He'd later experience a huge lull with no job offers, until Steven Soderbergh approached him about The Informant! The Ocean’s alum was so happy that he even offered to write the screenplay. While Scott Z. Burns ended up with the screenwriter role, Damon was still honored to be offered this leading role after a long career stretch.

It's so refreshing that Matt Damon has no problem looking back on the rougher points of his career. It’s also not unheard of for actors to look down on their own movies, but Damon speaks more diplomatically about Bagger Vance and All the Pretty Horses. I can imagine setbacks being hard to think about, but I get the sense that they've served as fuel for his career. And just look at him now. He's the lead of one of the biggest movies of all time and could even land himself some awards over the next few months.

#3630. Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Best Replacement Has 11,000+ ‘Very Positive’ Reviews on Steam

Death’s Door combines the best elements of Soulslikes and dungeon crawlers

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake was released last week, nearly three decades after the original came to Nintendo 64. Plenty of newcomers are discovering the greatest game ever for the first time (raises hand) on Nintendo Switch 2. However, as it’s a Switch 2 exclusive, plenty of gamers might be left feeling like Squidward watching everyone else have fun and frolic in Hyrule.

Like so many great pieces of art, the original Ocarina of Time and other Zelda games have inspired legions of developers to make their own dungeon-crawling Zelda-likes, like Tunic and Hyper Light Drifter. The best of the bunch might be Acid Nerve’s hit Death’s Door, and it’s available right now on all platforms. Originally released in 2021, it’s amassed a dedicated fan base, as indicated by its over 11,000 Very Positive player reviews on Steam.

Death’s Door is a lot like if Dark Souls and The Legend of Zelda were mashed together — with some bureaucratic nightmares thrown into the mix. You play as a crow with a big sword who collects souls for the Reaping Commission. He travels through various dungeons on the way to collecting three Giant Souls needed to open the titular Death’s Door. You’ll gradually uncover a conspiracy about the afterlife while exploring a realm untouched by death.

That realm is both bleak and beautiful. One level will take you to a mansion and its grounds dotted with orange-leaved trees (perfect for autumnal vibes), while another will have you canvassing a lush forest on the way to battle the Frog King. The color of those levels contrasts with the dour bureau, which is mostly rendered in black and white and feels as stuffy and draining as any office job.

Your crow will acquire various magical abilities that open up opportunities for exploration in Metroidvania-like ways, like using a bomb spell to destroy breakable walls. Those abilities really come in handy during combat, which is the highlight of the game. Like a Soulslike, Death’s Door is difficult, and you’ll need to become a master of the dodge-roll to survive against its aggressive enemies. The crow acquires a handful of weapons with different abilities and combos, though none as trusty as his classic sword.

Thankfully, even if you perish, you retain your experience points (called “souls,” of course), so Death’s Door is a bit more forgiving than its Soulslike contemporaries. It’ll still kick your butt, however.

Death’s Door was beloved at launch and was nominated for several end-of-year awards. It won a handful, like Best Indie Game at the Golden Joysticks. It sold over 100,000 copies in its first week after launch, though Acid Nerve hasn’t released updated sales figures since.

In fact, Acid Nerve has been largely quiet since Death’s Door came out. The small studio hasn’t announced what game it’s working on next, or if it is developing a new game at all. As fans have pointed out, six years passed between the studio’s Titan Souls in 2015 and Death’s Door, so it wouldn’t be too shocking if the studio announced something for next year. Still, plenty of Death’s Door players count it among their favorite games, and are eagerly awaiting whatever Acid Nerve serves up next.

At least they’ll always have Death’s Door to play. It was released on Windows PC and Xbox consoles in July 2021 before expanding to Nintendo Switch and PlayStation consoles five years ago in November 2021. It remains one of the best Zeldalikes around, and is worth checking out if you can’t get your hands on Ocarina of Time, or for when you finish the new remake and are in the mood for more Zeldalike adventures.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3629. How the ‘Glee’ and ‘Girls’ Revivals Can Avoid Mistakes Made by Other TV Reboots

The blue-tinged afterglow of the 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both the House and Senate, unleashed a burst of online millennial optimism. Some have credited a pair of newly revived Obama-era coming of age TV shows that often got political themselves, Ryan Murphy’s Glee and Lena Dunham’s Girls, with being a precursor to the Blue Wave.

But for all of the internet’s excitement for new episodes of Glee and Girls , no one said aging beloved characters (who is Hannah Horvath at 40?), or addressing the current sociopolitical moment (will Sue Sylvester in a MAGA hat be inevitable?!) would come without risk. How do the Girls and Glee reboots meet nostalgic expectations while delivering something new and prescient about where the world is now? Perhaps Dunham and Murphy can draw lessons about aging gracefully in adaptation from revivals that have aired before them.

Ahead, a guide to do’s and don’ts for the return of generational TV, from the second coming of Sex and the City to Roseanne’s rocky renewal.

Riding a high from his Emmy-nominated shows including Ted Lasso and Shrinking (Apple TV), plus Rooster (HBO), series creator Bill Lawrence relaunched Scrubs, now airing its second season on ABC, into a post-Abbott Elementary landscape—where network TV craves workplace comedies for its airwaves. It seems that the folks behind Glee and Girls, respectively, have found the right moment to return to TV. Murphy has spoken about Glee’s recent streaming resurgence for younger audiences, and Dunham is coming off a headline-making book tour for her bestselling memoir Famesick, written about her time making Girls 1.0.

Rather than write themselves out of the show’s controversial final season, in which most of the show’s central cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, Sarah Chalke, were sidelined in favor of an entirely new group of characters, the creative team opted to retcon the entire ninth season and start fresh for the reboot. That means Glee can freely pretend its own flashforward—in which Rachel Berry is a surrogate mother for fellow Glee Club pals Kurt and Blaine could be abandoned. And maybe Shoshanna never decided she was too good for the rest of the Girls and they can all be dysfunctional friends again…right?

A political sketch titled “Oh Honey,” which reunited original cast members Debra Messing, Eric McCormack, Sean Hayes, and Megan Mullally in support of Hillary Clinton ahead of the 2016 presidential election, may not have prevented a Donald Trump presidency. But it did garner millions of views online, earning the attention of top NBC brass who hoped to capitalize on the nostalgia by relaunching Will & Grace in 2017. While the Glee Club has yet to release their own teaser, Dunham announced the Girls revival via four-way video call with cast members Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, and Zosia Mamet that promptly sent the internet into a tailspin.

While the Will & Grace revival lasted for three seasons largely because of its ability to engage with the day’s political issues, particularly as they related to the LGBTQ+ community, some felt the show became too steeped in Trumpland. In one episode, a Trump-supporting Karen even gets staunchly liberal Grace a job decorating his Oval Office. Girls and Glee will have to strike a similarly delicate balance with their own returns—incorporating the current political landscape in ways that feel natural to the narrative, as much as one can when often tone-deaf show choir kids and Brooklyn hipsters are involved.

Just as And Just Like That made a splash by murdering Mr. Big in the first episode via Peloton-induced heart attack, Glee and Girls should aim for maximum impact upon arrival. Maybe Adam Driver’s character meets his end while going method for a role and learning a dangerous new skill. As for Glee, perhaps the character played by Grammy-winning Finneas O’Connell (brother and music producer of Billie Eilish), could go up in a blaze of glory. Despite getting his start with a four-episode arc in the show’s final season, in 2020 O’Connell claimed that he’d never seen Glee, including the episodes he was in.

Taking a show outside of its comfort zone in the right ways raises the stakes—and highlights core tensions from the original series (see also: Miranda shown riding the subway for the first time). But some viewers felt And Just Like That… showrunner Michael Patrick King’s inclusion of diverse voices into the narrative veered too far outside of the shoebox with Che Diaz, the divisive podcast-cohost–slash-comedian–slash–veterinarian-office-worker that took the brunt of audience ire over freshly sober Miranda’s decision to divorce her husband Steve. New characters can become de facto villains for a series revival, particularly if they interfere with cherished dynamics from the show’s first run.

The return of Kelsey Grammer’s sitcom hero Frasier Crane was undercut by the absence of breakout supporting characters Niles and Daphne, as actors David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves did not reprise their roles for the reboot. Luckily, the core four of Girls have already signed on for their five-episode revival, and several Glee alums are in talks for its reboot, including series lead Lea Michele.

In addition to some of the creative challenges facing Frasier 2.0, the former NBC sitcom was welcomed back on Paramount+, a lesser-known streaming platform in comparison to Netflix or Peacock. At least it wasn’t Helen Hunt and Paul Reiser’s Mad About You, another ’90s NBC comedy that got its grand return on…Spectrum (?!) in 2019. Girls will air on HBO’s streaming partner, Max, and Glee is in the works via Disney+ and Hulu—barring any major industry mergers.

The Roseanne reboot earned new resonance in the zeitgeist—and major ratings on ABC—for its authentic depiction of a working-class Middle America family under Trump’s first presidency. Like the original 1988 series, the revival focused on the economic and social realities of surviving as a lower-income family in America. And like Will & Grace before it, Roseanne organically, even comically, depicted familial political divides by portraying Roseanne Conner as a Trump voter and her sister Jackie as a Hillary Clinton supporter.

After series lead Roseanne Barr tweeted a racist slur about Valerie Jarrett, a senior aide to President Barack Obama, ABC Entertainment president Channing Dungey terminated the series on May 29, 2018, following its renewal for an 11th season on the network. Then, the following month, ABC announced it was ordering 10 episodes of a spin-off about the family titled The Conners, which regenerated by killing off the character of Roseanne, ending just last year after seven seasons on the air. If anything, the show’s unlikely staying power proves that if a show sticks to its DNA, it can outlast even the messiest of scandals.

The four-episode return of Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel’s mother-daughter dramedy was rightfully docked for its extended, gratuitous Stars Hollow musical involving Tony Award-winning performers (and ex-spouses) Sutton Foster and Christian Borle. But a bit of superfluous song-and-dance naturally feels right at home for Glee, and even Girls—an encore version of Marnie singing Kanye West’s “Stronger” would reach cringeworthy new depths.

The pregnancy revelation that ends Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life should have kicked the revival off, not concluded its story. Instead, A Year in the Life emphasizes just how little Rory and Lorelei have grown in the years since Gilmore Girls ended, only to leave the revival’s most compelling leap forward for its final moments—and totally unresolved. After a decade, the bait-and-switch still burns, which speaks to the divisive, and enduring, nature of TV returns themselves. As for the next chapters of Glee and Girls, may the writers’ rooms hear our post-election pleas.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

#3627. Russell Brand and Wife Laura Asked for Prayers in Podcast Before Sentencing

Russell Brand and his wife, Laura Gallacher, asked for support in their last podcast episode before he received his 10-year prison sentence.

“We’re in the UK. … Why is that?” Brand, 51, said in an October episode of their “Sunday Service With the Brands” podcast. “Fancied a trip? … The Lord brought us here.”

Later in the podcast, the pair asked listeners to “pray for us if you feel so inclined” ahead of the trial.

“For me being back here, obviously there are great challenges knowing that however we shake this down, there are people that feel aggrieved and hurt and my prayer is that this will be addressed in the coming weeks,” Brand said. “We’ll do our best to respect the important restrictions that exist around court cases to ensure that truth and justice can be done.”

Gallacher added that the couple hoped to continue with their podcast amid the trial and went on to reflect on how she is leaning on her faith.

“I suppose, more than ever, when you are faced with times of challenge, that’s when you have to find your footing and your grounding, your anchor, your God,” she said. “You need to find your connection with God. Your personal connection with God. I suppose part of, perhaps, what Sunday Service will be in the next few weeks will be a journey of how we are anchoring ourselves in faith and trust and loyalty to God during the times.”

Brand had been accused by multiple women of sexual assault, rape and emotional abuse. The allegations spanned from 1999 to 2013 and he entered a not guilty plea, denying the allegations before being tried on seven sexual offense charges.

Two months after the podcast episode dropped, news broke that Brand had been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was sentenced to 10 years and six months behind bars.

Brand reportedly showed no emotional when he was sentenced but had a brief exchange with Gallacher before he was taken away, saying, “We’ll be OK.”

Brand and Gallacher, who met before his marriage to Katy Perry, reconnected in 2015. The pair tied the knot two years later and have since welcomed three children: daughters Mabel and Peggy in 2016 and 2018, respectively, and a son in 2023.

If you have experienced sexual assault, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 for confidential support.

You Can See Everything is the most talked-about movie on the 2026 movie schedule, and for good reason. There are many WTF moments that people have latched on to. There is one, it seems, that was left on the cutting room floor that Billy Evans just told the world about via X. It turns out, according to Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, got into a wrestling match with co-director Nathan Fielder. As wild as the movie got, this was not something I expected would happen, nor would I have expected it not to make the final cut.

Fielder is known for doing a lot of, let’s say, unconventional stuff in his projects, and that certainly holds true in You Can See Everything. Evans, for his part, seems to have been all in on going for it, too. There’s that now-infamous scene of Evans in the shower, a scene that he claims wasn’t his idea, disputing the claims of co-director Lance Oppenheim. Then there is this scene, as described by Evans on X:

I really wish they'd kept the scene where I wrestled Nathan, Borat style. Full top mount. His little Canadian frame struggling beneath me. I thought he was in on the joke. Until he wasn't. Imagine realizing that in camera.

Not only that, but according to Evans, Fielder ended up in the pool at the rented beach house where Evans and Holmes lived in the weeks leading up to Holmes’ imprisonment on fraud convictions and where most scenes with Evans and Holmes were filmed. Evans explains in a follow-up tweet after being asked if the two of them were naked:

Clothed. But Lance Oppenheim asked him to: 1) stand by the edge of the pool 2) remove his phone and monitor 3) look up Then I tossed Nathan into the pool. Borat wrestling ensued. I thought it was a bit. It wasn't.

He doesn’t go further into how it wasn’t a bit, or that Fielder was surprised by it. Honestly, knowing Fielder, I’d be pretty surprised myself if Fielder wasn’t in on it with Oppenheim. I guess anything is possible.

Evans also teased that there is a lot more that didn’t make the movie, saying in another tweet:

This literally wouldn't make the top 10 best deleted scenes. We didn't hold back. We showed them everything. You saw what they wanted to show you.... It was a wild experience. Hate us, [love] us, the truth or lack thereof is in the edit.

It’s hard to imagine that a director’s cut with added scenes could be better than the theatrical cut that we’ve all seen now, but if Fielder and Evans wrestling isn’t one of the top 10 best scenes left out, then I really hope the home release of You Can See Everything includes a lot more! Meanwhile, the film is closing in on a $100 million haul at the domestic box office, and that is just as astonishing as anything left out of the movie.

#3625. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Are Moving Again

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly found a new home in the Cotswolds, less than three months after their return to the United Kingdom. But anyone who thinks they’ve bought a new home will be disappointed. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who had been staying at the residence of a wealthy entrepreneur friend since August 26, have reportedly left the main house on the property to move into another residence located within the same estate, according to Daily Mail journalist Richard Eden. “They were living in the main house,” a person close to the entrepreneur told the British newspaper. “They have now moved to a property on the estate.” The move reportedly took place before Harry and Meghan left for a vacation abroad with their children.

Since the couple returned to the United Kingdom, their search for a new home in Britain has been a hotly debated topic, especially in light of their disagreements with the royal family and security concerns. The mystery surrounding their residence has fueled speculation and various theories. Where would the Sussexes choose to settle? That was the question echoing everywhere on social media and in the press. For security reasons, the details of their living arrangements have always remained confidential.

As reported by the British media, the couple and their two children had been staying at a property owned by a wealthy friend, nestled in the Cotswolds countryside—an area Harry and Meghan already knew well. In 2018, the year of their wedding, they rented a prestigious farmhouse in the region for two years—a historic property with an estimated value of 4.12 million British pounds (about $5.5 million), part of the Great Tew Estate. The residence included a four-bedroom farmhouse, a barn converted into living quarters, and a separate cottage with two additional bedrooms. The property also featured extensive grounds and a heated patio. Over the years, the Cotswolds, in the English countryside, have become a retreat for numerous celebrities, including Jeremy Clarkson, David and Victoria Beckham, and Kate Moss. A few weeks ago the Duchess of Sussex was photographed at The Three Horseshoes, a quaint pub near Burford, in the company of Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi. In 2024, DeGeneres and de Rossi left the United States to move to the Cotswolds, where they live on a large estate surrounded by greenery.

The Sussexes’ housing history in the United Kingdom, however, has been quite eventful. Before leaving the United Kingdom, the couple lived at Frogmore Cottage in Windsor, a property made available to Harry and Meghan by Queen Elizabeth II. In 2023, however, the two royals left the residence. The decision came a few months after the publication of the duke’s memoir, Spare. To renovate Frogmore Cottage, approximately 2.4 million British pounds (about $3.2 million) went into transforming two existing buildings into a single-family home. The renovations were extensive: The ceiling beams and floor structures were replaced, the electrical system was redone, new gas and water lines were installed, and a soundproofing system costing approximately 50,000 British pounds (about $67,000) was reportedly put in place. Despite the significant spend, the Sussexes left the property for good after moving overseas.

Even before settling in Windsor, Harry and Meghan lived at Nottingham Cottage, within the Kensington Palace complex. It was a rather small residence that apparently hadn’t won Meghan over. In the Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, the duchess recalled with a touch of irony that the name Kensington Palace suggested something grand, while the reality was quite different: “Kensington Palace sounds very regal, of course it does. It says ‘palace’ in the name. But Nottingham Cottage was so small!” Harry added that the house had very low ceilings and was even slightly slanted.

The new home in the Cotswolds could therefore be a practical solution for the Sussexes, at least until they figure out their plans in the United Kingdom. Meghan’s professional commitments may also take her away from England again. The duchess is expected to move temporarily to Australia next year to participate in the filming of Junior MasterChef, the cooking show she is set to cohost. Prince Harry and their two children might join her during her stay in Australia, but there’s no confirmation of that yet.

The identity of the estate’s current owner remains a mystery. He is a friend of Prince Harry’s, with whom he shares a commitment to charities that support veterans and military personnel. Apparently, the businessman would be happy to continue hosting the prince, Meghan, and their children for a long time to come. Several theories have circulated regarding the benefactor’s identity, with some speculating that he is Ian Wace, a British financier with an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion and who has long been close to Harry. He owns the Rowler Estate, a vast estate in the Cotswolds. His private life has been marked by tragedy: In 1994 he lost his first wife, Joanna, and their two young children in a car accident in Hampshire.

However, being hosted by a wealthy friend is nothing new in the Sussexes’ lives. In 2020, when they decided to step back from their royal duties and move to the United States, the couple stayed at the Beverly Hills mansion of producer and media mogul Tyler Perry. It was a Tuscan-style residence with eight bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, located within the gated community of Beverly Ridge Estates.

A few months later, in August of that same year, Harry and Meghan purchased a mansion in Montecito, California, where they settled. Surrounded by greenery, the mansion is located in a residential area frequented by some of Hollywood’s most famous stars, including Oprah Winfrey, Ariana Grande, and Brad Pitt. It is a very luxurious home that, at the time of purchase, was dubbed the Sussexes’ new palace—one the couple seems to have no intention of selling, despite their return to the United Kingdom. According to reports, the maintenance staff had continued to care for the family’s chickens.

The couple is still holding on to the California property, purchased for around $14 million, which continues to serve as one of their family homes. The estate includes a wine cellar, a movie theater, a gym, a spa, a large swimming pool, a tennis court, a wood-fired oven, a barbecue, and more than 13 and a half bathrooms.

However, this is not the only residence owned by the Sussexes. Just several years ago, Harry and Meghan purchased a home on the Portuguese coast, near the one owned by Princess Eugenie—Harry’s cousin—and her husband, Jack Brooksbank. The property is located within the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club, an exclusive residential complex with about 300 ocean-view villas in Melides, south of Lisbon.

Meanwhile, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected in Brussels on November 10 for an event dedicated to protecting children from online risks and abuse. The heart of the initiative, organized by MEP Antonio López-Istúriz White as part of a parliamentary intergroup, will be the unveiling of The Lost Screen Memorial, a video installation created in memory of children who lost their lives after falling victim to online abuse and exploitation. The installation will consist of 50 large-scale portraits of the young victims. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola is also expected to attend the ceremony.

According to reports in the British media, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint speech on the issue—which has long been a focus of the couple’s advocacy—before participating in a discussion with international activists. Among the scheduled speakers is Sandra Spitaels, the Belgian mother of Glenn, who, in 2017, took his own life at age 15 after a nude photograph of him was circulated online.

These two developments involving the Duke and Duchess of Sussex come as Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle, is at the center of a horrific legal case. He is the subject of an investigation launched following a complaint filed by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., with the Philippine police and the FBI. The younger Thomas handed over to investigators a box containing several images and videos that allegedly depicted child sexual abuse, found among his father’s personal belongings in Cebu City, Philippines.

Another discovery reportedly took place in recent days at a storage unit that Thomas Markle allegedly rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico. The facility was reportedly inspected by local police as part of an investigative operation. Meghan’s 82-year-old father has reportedly been transferred in recent days to a facility in Florida that specializes in caring for people with dementia, according to The Sun.

His move to a care facility could now complicate the investigation, particularly the possibility of questioning Thomas Markle. His cognitive condition could make it more difficult to proceed with the investigation, especially given the protections afforded to residents of specialized facilities.

Meghan, who has had no contact with her father since 2018, has not commented on the latest developments. It had previously emerged that the duchess, who had been aware of the allegations against her father since 2018, wanted to speak out publicly. One of the agents from Royalty and Specialist Protection (RaSP)—the Scotland Yard unit responsible for the security of members of the royal family and other public figures—reportedly advised her not to speak out. The agent reportedly told her, “Leave it with us, we’ll investigate it.”

Thomas Markle was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges connected to the possession of child sexual abuse material. He has previously denied possession of such material.

If your goal is to look effortlessly polished, the rich-mom trend might be for you. It’s all about finding pieces that make getting dressed feel easy while still looking put together. And when it comes to tops, a few thoughtful design details can make all the difference. Boxy sweaters may be cozy, but they can sometimes leave outfits looking a little shapeless — so we’re ready to trade them in for more flattering silhouettes that bring a little extra polish to everyday dressing.

We’re shopping tops with cinched waists that create definition, flowy batwing sleeves that drape beautifully and feminine details that give even the simplest outfit a luxe feel. The best part? The James Bond movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, with entire generations brought up on 007's adventures. Daniel Craig's Bond movies ended with No Time to Die, opening the door for a new actor to take on the mantle in the developing 26th movie by Denis Villeneuve. Fans have spent years taking bets on the next Bond, and the Oscar-nominated filmmaker recently trolled us at a recent event.

No Time to Die's ending shockingly killed off 007, a first for the long-running franchise (which is streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription). Those involved with the next movie have been keeping tight-lipped about casting, but Villeneuve spoke at the LACMA Art + Film Gala, where he spoke to the crowd and said:

With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The actor who will play the next James Bond is… And I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack.

What a tease. Clearly the acclaimed director knows that folks are dying to know who will take on the role of 007 in his James Bond movie. And what's a little light trolling among friends? Hopefully we'll get more answers about his developing blockbuster once Dune: Part Three hits theaters this December as half of Dunesday.

Denis Villeneuve's involvement in Bond 26 helping to buoy excitement for the mysterious project... even if we still don't know who will be playing the lead role. In a video from Variety's Instagram, he got honest about why he can't say much right now, offering:

I should not comment right now because every word I’m going to say is going to be scrutinized. I would just say that I’m having a great time.

The Arrival director was being cheeky at the event, but these comments show a much more sincere side of him. He's clearly thrilled to be behind the camera for the next James Bond movie, even if fans are desperate for any information regarding casting. You can see a video of him giving the above quote below:

It's been years since No Time to Die hit theaters back in 2021, fans have been curious about which actor will be passed the baton from Daniel Craig. Unfortunately we're still waiting on casting news, with fans tossing around a number of familiar names online. There are tons of rumors about who might be playing the martini-sipping agent, as well as chatter that the studio might go with an unknown rather than an established actor. Hopefully we get some answers soon.

All of the Bond movies are streaming on Amazon, and Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three hits theaters December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed that more Bond 26 info comes after that title gets its wide theatrical release.

#3620. Mass Effect Legendary Edition Finally Gets Co-op Back on PC

Mass Effect 3’s co-op mode put four players on a map, each with a class and a race, against waves of Cerberus, geth, Reapers, or Collectors. In the original trilogy, it was the only Mass Effect you could play with friends. When Mass Effect Legendary Edition compiled and remastered the games in 2021, that co-op mode didn’t make the cut. Project director Mac Walters said in 2021 that the team’s focus in releasing Legendary Edition was on the single-player experience…and that at some point the team had to draw the line. This year, that changed.

Legendary Edition Multiplayer, a free download from the modding team ME3Tweaks, both restores that missing co-op mode and adds new ways to play the game. After installing the mod, boot it up, and you’ll get a world of quality of life improvements, new content, and glitch fixes:

You’ll need a PC copy of Legendary Edition with an unmodded Mass Effect 3. Because the mod lives apart from your trilogy, setup takes a few more steps than a typical mod. ME3Tweaks says it won’t interact with the original game at all, so your settings, saves, and mods stay fully separate. To install it, download ME3Tweaks Mod Manager 10.0 or higher, import both the Launcher Mod and the main mod from Nexus, and click Install LMP. To import your Mass Effect 3 profile, run Legendary Edition once first, or EA App cloud sync may flag a conflict. Then launch from Steam, the EA App, or Mod Manager.

ME3Tweaks has been building toward an N7 Day mod release for months. The team has released mods on N7 Day before, including Pinnacle Station in 2021, a combat-focused DLC for the first Mass Effect that the remaster left out because its source code was lost. The team isn’t done working, either: We can look forward to at least three further content packs, including a Redemption map pack with remade multiplayer maps and one with the Rejection enemy faction.

But for now, with the restored co-op mode, we’ve got our hands full. Bring three friends, generate an invite from the pause menu, then pick a heavy weapon (or skip it for the extra ammo and speed). See how long your squad can hold the line. Co-op is back in Legendary Edition, and it’s a good thing, too. The Reapers have waves waiting.

Mass Effect Legendary Edition is available to play on PS4, PS5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X/S. Find the latest install and joining instructions for this co-op mod on the Legendary Edition Multiplayer page.

#3619. Meet the 20 first-place apps from RevenueCat’s Shipaton 2026

A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore.

RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people.

You can get a look at every first place winner below, and read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement for every more.

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

#3618. Vija Celmins, the Ultimate Artist’s Artist, Gets Honored by LACMA

On Wednesday, I walked down Crosby Street and stopped at an easy-to-miss building where, high above the cobblestoned street, is the studio of Vija Celmins, who’s been there for almost 50 years. It’s a classic gigantic SoHo artist loft, the kind you’ll be shocked to hear still exist—but they do. In the 1970s, the previous tenant put a Buddhist temple in the front room. Not finding anything particularly wrong with that, Celmins lived in the temple for a while.

“Then I finally thought, gee, maybe I could put a couch in here,” Celmins told me as I walked in.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s been decades since the galleries moved from SoHo to Chelsea and got replaced by boutiques. But among this warren of cast iron buildings, some of the artists who moved in during the pioneer days remain. Among them is Celmins, the masterful pop-landscapist who paints in infinite textures, taking on the universal with an obsessive tenacity. The 88-year-old is a living link to a long-gone generation, and someone always in the running when we talk about the best artists who are both still with us and who began their careers before the JFK assassination.

Approaching nonagenarian status, Celmins is still incredibly quick, with a generous, buoyant voice. She immediately hopped down the stairs of her old studio and took me over to the windows.

“I used to be able to see down the street before they built this ugly pink building—all the way to the bridge, because this was a parking lot,” she told me, referring to a building erected 21 years ago.

She walked past a print she made some years ago: a depiction of the ocean, her most famous subject, installed on the wall. She admired it in a refreshingly objective way.

“It’s so loose. Usually I tighten everything down,” she said. “I mean, it’s such a relief. I had forgotten that. And what did I do? I only made 10 of them, which is interesting, in ’16. I must have done this at… It looks like it’s a drypoint—doesn’t it look like drypoint? I mean, I did a fucking lot of oceans, as you know.”

Though not a household name, in certain circles, Celmins has attained near-mythic status. The very few people I told about this interview ahead of time were shocked she was having anyone over to her studios in Manhattan and Long Island. She works incredibly slowly, and thus has shown incredibly infrequently. This has started to change in the last few years. She had a retrospective at the Met Breuer in 2019, and in the last few years, a few shows of new work at her gallery, Matthew Marks—the blue-chip commercial concern that represents a disproportionate number of the greatest American artists.

Next year, Celmins will have a show at Dia Bridgehampton. Tomorrow, she’s the guest of honor at the LACMA Art+Film Gala, a big deal in American museumdom. It comes with a gigantic bash presided over by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow. The gala’s also honoring Denis Villeneuve, which Celmins is excited about. She’s seen the Dune movies and, like Villeneuve, is a big fan of the desert.

During my visit, she opened up a random drawer under a drawing table. There was stuff everywhere, decades of sketches and notes and Post-its. She has a constellation of postcards taped to the wall, with paintings as inspiration, ones that look nothing like Vija Celmins—Picasso, Balthus—along with photos of her heroes and her friends with pets. There’s Jasper Johns with his dog, Borges with his cat. She’s got framed artworks from friends who are mostly dead now, like a Ken Price drawing of some undulating cups—“You know Kenny Price?”—and a very kooky, absolutely amazing H.C. Westermann of a wolf with its heart throbbing in its chest, wandering through the desert. Westermann made it for her. She made Westermann a wolf drawing in return. She doesn’t know what happened to her wolf.

There are drawings of globes, sculptures of globes, her tablet paintings, more prints of the ocean, a paperweight from an insurance company in Kansas City—near where she grew up in Indiana after leaving Latvia—a wrapped-up canvas labeled “ED MOSES” on the side, and plenty of drawings of Saturn.

She moved into the SoHo place after two decades working in Venice Beach, California. While in LA, she honed and refined, and inarguably mastered, a painstakingly laborious practice of applying graphite to paper in slow, methodical marks, rendering the passage of time in hyperreal landscapes. She now mostly works in a studio on the eastern end of Long Island, where she's had a place for the last few decades. But it’s here at the SoHo studio, in the erstwhile cauldron of cutting-edge American art, where she loves to be.

“The studio out in the country is more like where I went back to painting, really,” she told me. “And here I did all these weird things.”

This wasn’t the first time we had met. A few weeks back, I was admiring the very cool Gary Hume show that Marks had up in his gallery on 24th Street when gallery director Jacqueline Tran tapped me on the shoulder and asked if I would like to meet Vija Celmins. Vija Celmins! At the public opening!

We chatted for a few moments. She seemed spry, fit, with an elastic mind. Then she invited me over for lunch—not in the city, but at her place on farmland out east. On an October morning I hopped on a Jitney, then an Uber to Celmins’s part of the hamlet, which is essentially rural, with small clapboard homes encircled by crop formations.

I arrived at the same time as my fellow visitors: Michael Govan, the director of LACMA, and his wife, the fashion executive Katherine Ross. Celmins welcomed us in and introduced us to her cat, Raymond, who immediately pounced on my cup of takeout coffee.

“Down, Raymond! He’s very friendly,” Celmins said. “He’s my son.”

Out here, in the two-room studio attached to her house, she’s been able to conjure a vision of landscape perhaps more potent than the breakthroughs she came to so many years ago. In her studio, she showed us how the raindrops on her window, as captured in her work-intensive flattened plane panorama, could take on epic qualities.

We sat down for lunch—quiche and soup from a local bakery—and Celmins started telling stories about California. She hadn’t lived there in a number of years, though the topography of the state is what willed her artwork into being. She drove out to the desert with James Turrell, with Doug Wheeler, and spent years—decades—arguing with Robert Irwin, who taught her at UCLA. Irwin called Celmins his “star student.” I’ve always liked this Bob Irwin quote about Celmins: “Vija has perfect taste. She doesn’t like anything.”

Govan told her about the museum, LACMA, and the new building that had finally been completed earlier this year after two decades of planning and fundraising. Celmins was quite curious about it all. She has a few plans for when she’s in town for the LACMA gala. She seemed intrigued about meeting her fellow honoree, director Villeneuve, and watched the Dune movies in preparation. (I heartily recommended she watch Sicario and Arrival as well.) She’s going to visit her old studio at 701 Venice Boulevard, which she hasn’t seen in decades.

“I was going to go out in the desert, but I’m not going to have time to do it,” she said. “I might have to make another trip. I really like the Death Valley desert because it’s so vast, so terrific. And they have airplanes zooming from the Air Force around really fast. I used to wave at them. They go really low, and they just go like, vvvvvrrroooooom! Right above, following the outline of the mountains.”

She’s also going to see Riko Mizuno, her Los Angeles art dealer, who is currently 94 years old. But most of her friends are gone.

“A lot of them have died, I mean, I didn’t have that many friends, but some died, and some are dying right now,” she said. “And then they moved away. Ed Moses, I knew pretty well. Billy Al Bengston. Well, Kenny Price, I loved Kenny.”

Then she mentioned Robert Therrien—“You know Bob Therrien?”—the late artist who has become quite famous for oversized sculptures that are astronomically popular on Instagram. A retrospective at The Broad this year became something of a sensation. I can’t imagine an artist more different than Celmins—but as it turns out, they had a deep mutual respect for each other.

“I met him once, and he was a very unusual person,” Celmins said. “He was really tall, and everything in his studio was like—he had a ceiling that was maybe like 25, 28 feet tall. And he had this little ladder that went up this side to this kitchen, which was this kitchen he remade from Chicago or someplace where his family used to live. I’ll show you one little thing. He gave me this.”

She got up from her chair and found the Therrian artwork on a shelf. It was a snout, bobbing up and down in a terrifying manner, attached to a curved metal rod. Just the inner part of the face of a canine, floating forever.

“It’s so disorienting. Where’s the rest of the dog?” I asked.

I thought I'd seen most of the celebrity fashion from this year's LACMA Art+Film Gala, but apparently Emma Watson had other plans. The Harry Potter franchise star may be absent from the 2026 movie schedule, but she's certainly been making memorable Hollywood appearances lately. While everyone was busy admiring the outfits worn by Nicole Kidman, Kim Kardashian and the rest of the A-list guests, Watson attended without attracting nearly as much attention.

According to Los Angeles Magazine, Watson was among the guests celebrating filmmaker Denis Villeneuve and artist Vija Celmins. While other celebrities turned heads in elaborate LACMA outfits, Watson was noticeably absent from several prominent red-carpet fashion galleries. As you can see in the Instagram story she shared (see below), the Little Women actress was dressed like a fiery work of art.

Watson wore a striking, floor-length burgundy gown that looked as though someone had poured molten red glass over silk. The fitted, glossy bodice featured a rich crimson neckline and delicate straps draped across her shoulders, while the flowing skirt shimmered with deep red and wine-colored tones. It's a gorgeous look on its own, but the really fascinating part is how the material was created.

As Watson explained in her Instagram Stories, artist Caroline Zimbalist developed the fabric using a biopolymer-based material that's heated, mixed and poured by hand directly onto silk. Plant-derived glycerin gives the material its softness and flexibility, and as the water evaporates, it bonds with the silk to create that unusual, sculptural finish. So, yes, Watson essentially wore a piece of experimental textile art to an event celebrating art. I love this take on celebrity fashion.

Honestly, this is becoming something of a pattern for Watson. Back in September, the actress made another unexpected Hollywood appearance at the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, where she wore a gorgeous little black dress with an unconventional artistic twist. That one incorporated real flowers, carefully attached to a recycled velvet garment. Watson went viral for wearing the dress, as it looked like the flowers were floating across her body. The internet certainly had some fun with that one, especially Harry Potter fans. I have to admit, this latest look is maybe a bit more magical, and my favorite. The woman seems to appreciate a dress with a little more going on than meets the eye.

For that earlier appearance, Watson worked with stylist Jared Ellner and florist Anthony Maslo on a bespoke design featuring orchids, lilies and other blooms. In an interview with Vogue, she explained that the outfit celebrated the natural world and the beauty of things that don't last forever. Even the flowers were preserved afterward. I love that kind of attention to detail, especially when so many celebrity looks disappear into the endless stream of red carpet photographs.

LACMA seems like an especially fitting place for Watson to continue exploring the connection between clothing and artistic expression. The annual event brings together filmmakers, artists and fashion designers to support the museum's programming. This year's gathering, presented by Gucci and co-chaired by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow, raised nearly $7 million.

There was plenty of fashion to admire, too. Nicole Kidman wore an elaborate Chanel ensemble inspired by Edgar Degas' Little Dancer of Fourteen Years, while Anya Taylor-Joy turned heads in an archival Pierre Cardin design. The evening also featured a performance by Rosé, making it a pretty spectacular night even before I learned Watson was among the guests.

What I particularly love about Watson and her recent appearances is that she seems more interested in the creative work behind what she's wearing than making sure she gets captured on camera. She's also been an advocate for sustainable and ethical fashion for years, so seeing her embrace pieces with an artistic story behind them feels pretty fitting.

Of course, it's been quite some time since Watson appeared in a major movie. Her last feature was 2019's Little Women, and she's spoken candidly about why she stepped away from acting. She's since devoted much of her attention to other interests, including philanthropy and her Renais gin business.

That's two surprise appearances in Los Angeles this fall, both at events celebrating art and storytelling. If Watson keeps turning up in outfits with this much thought behind them, I may need to start paying closer attention to her Instagram Stories. Clearly, the usual red carpet galleries aren't telling me everything.

The late Patrick Stewart was a celebrated dramatist, but he also had great comedic chops. It's something I don't think about often, until I saw that he wrote his own eulogy over a decade ago, and it's so hilarious.

For fans who need a break from the heartfelt tributes and touching stories, I implore you to check out his performance done for a Just for Laughs gala in 2015. Stewart took the stage to perform his own eulogy, but considering this was a comedy event, he had a twist in store for Trekkies:

Sir Patrick Stewart was more than just an actor, he was the greatest actor ever. He was also a husband, a father, and a friend. But most of all, he was an objectophile who achieved sexual congress with thousands of inanimate objects.

The audience burst into laughter because what else can you do at the end of that statement? Here's the guy who played one of the best Star Trek characters of all time, claiming he's having sex with furniture and other things.

It's something I'd never seen until after his passing, and I'm glad. All the sadness I had reading tributes and stories about his life is off to the side right now, as I listened to Stewart continue his hilarious bit:

As a boy, Sir Patrick entertained his classmates at Mirfield Secondary Modern School where he dutifully honed his craft as an actor, developing his now signature baritone voice and made sweet, secret lunch hour love to the janitor’s floor polishing machine.

It's one of those jokes that works really well because of who the one telling it is. So many co-stars have come through the woodwork in recent weeks talking about how sweet he was, and how humble an actor he was despite his fame. To think he'd have some odd, deviant behavior lurking beneath the surface as bizarre as this would be horrifying, and makes it so funny.

It's a funny eulogy, but it only worked in full if he was able to "land the plane" in terms of bringing it full circle. Fortunately the actor had the ultimate closer, revealing to the howling audience that they were sitting in chairs that he had defiled just minutes before their arrival:

In addition to winning the audience over with his wit, warmth, and humanity, Patrick also realized his final wish. Mere seconds before you, the audience entered, he rubbed his unwashed genitals on each and every seat of Montreal's Place Des Arts! Sir Patrick Stewart, you will be missed.

Many people will remember Patrick Stewart for Star Trek and X-Men, and rightfully so. That doesn't mean he didn't have memorable comedy roles, however, such as when he played King Richard in Robin Hood: Men in Tights. He also received an Emmy nomination for a guest role in Frasier, and he had a great night hosting Saturday Night Live.

There's a part of me sad that Patrick Stewart essentially worked up until his death, but also so grateful that he's left behind such a body of work to sift through. I still love hearing the touching stories and tributes about his life, but it's good to know I have this hilarious eulogy to look back on in the coming days to break up the sad moments.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family and friends of Patrick Stewart. He made us laugh and cry, and it's nice to see evidence of that on the internet for all to see and enjoy.
