#3614. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3612. Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Coolest Dungeon Hides a Secret Tribute to a Beloved Classic

Nintendo's highly anticipated remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and millions of players are reliving their childhood adventures or experiencing Link's journey for the very first time. Though the Nintendo 64 game has received a dramatic visual glow-up for the Switch 2, the remake meticulously preserves the spirit of the original — including an extended reference to a classic American novel that even Ocarina diehards may have missed the first time around.

[Ed. note: Mid-game spoilers ahead for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. If you haven't retrieved the Master Sword yet, turn back now!]

After Link collects the three Spiritual Stones and returns to Hyrule Castle Town to claim the Master Sword, we move forward seven years in time. Link is now an adult, and in order to thwart Ganon's terrifying reign, he must awaken six sages throughout Hyrule by visiting their temples and claiming their power for his own. The first of these is located just outside Link's hometown of Kokiri Village, land of the fairy folk. Though most of his youthful pals don't recognize the grown-up Link, they urge him to investigate the Forest Temple and rescue their dear friend Saria.

When Link ventures into the Forest Temple, he discovers something altogether unexpected: an eerie, luxurious old mansion inhabited by ghosts. As he enters a central room flanked by colorful torches, four ghostly Poes appear to snatch away the flames. Venturing deeper into the mansion, Link discovers that these ghoulish gals are actually four sisters: Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy.

Sound familiar? Those are the same names (and the same birth order) as the March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women. It's a timeless coming-of-age story about four sisters who have very different goals and ambitions in life, one that's been adapted countless times for stage and screen. The most recent adaptation is the 2019 film by Barbie and The Magician's Nephew director Greta Gerwig, which stars Saoirse Ronan, Florence Pugh, and Timothée Chalamet.

While you might be inclined to think this is some newfangled meddling with the localization, these were also the Poe Sisters' names in the Nintendo 64 original. (There's one exception: the second sister, Jo, was called "Joelle" in the 1998 game.) Naturally, there are plenty of "well actually" guys pointing this out in the comments of social media posts. But it's still a fun little Easter egg for players discovering it for the first time, whether or not they've played Ocarina of Time before.

If you're like me and have never played Ocarina of Time until now, be sure to check out Polygon's extensive guides and walkthroughs for the remake. Like this hidden node, there are plenty of puzzle solutions, hidden items, and valuable power-ups you can easily miss on your first playthrough.

Presley Gerber tragically passed away after working toward addiction recovery in September of this year. He left behind his famous parents, Cindy Crawford and Casamigos businessman Rande Gerber, and his sister Kaia, who have all been reeling in the wake of his death. This week, the Bottoms cast member addressed that grief head on with a viral post about grief “coming in waves.”

It’s from The Year of Magical Thinking by Joan Didion, a book with a lighthearted title that betrays its heavy subject material and that I still think about to this day. It helped me get through my mother’s battle with cancer, and I think it’s a helpful read for anyone going through it with a loved one. However, it particularly highlights grief in the face of addiction, and I would guess was especially pertinent to Gerber.

Kaia shared a post this week about the titles on grief that have been helpful after losing her brother. A separate slide included a quote from Didion that's one of the more memorable from the book.

Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief, comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate the dailiness of life.

Here's what else she's been reading in recent days, per her post.

A post shared by Library Science (@libraryscience)

Didion wrote The Year of Magical Thinking in 2005, while frequenting hospitals as her daughter Quintana Roo dealt with health issues. All of this came just shortly after losing her husband, beloved author John Gregory Dunne. The book follows Didion’s experience with grief following her husband’s death alongside her daughter’s hospitalizations and complications related to alcohol abuse. The book ends without us knowing what was next for Quintana Roo and Didion, though her daughter would pass away in August of 2005, just shortly before the author would publish the book.

Joan Didion mixes up stories about experiences she'd shared with her family over time with prose about everything she was also going through in the moment. It’s beautiful, direct, and devastating writing. I wouldn’t recommend picking it up as a beach read, but if you are going through something in your family, it’s helpful for contextualizing feelings and realizing humans are similar. We all go through the pain and anger and feelings of helplessness when we are losing a loved one.

It's not one of the author's titles that have yet made it to the big screen, but Didion’s book is powerful. I read almost 10 years ago and some of her words are still with me. It holds up years after it was published, and it’s a gripping read. I’m glad Kaia Gerber found solace in it. I hope her parents, and celebrity pals like George and Amal Clooney, have found some solace too.

#3610. Report: Apple reduces employees’ AI token allowances as Ternus moves to cut costs

Bloomberg reports that Apple has begun reducing employees’ daily AI spending limits, with some engineers seeing their allowances cut from $300 to $200, and further reductions planned across multiple teams. Here are the details.

Over the past year, tokenmaxxing, the practice of consuming as many AI tokens as possible, often as a measure of productivity, took over Silicon Valley, with companies such as Meta even introducing internal leaderboards, some unofficial, ranking employees by their AI token usage.

Tokenmaxxing emerged alongside improvements in AI agents’ coding capabilities, as tools such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor became increasingly popular among software developers.

Unsurprisingly, companies soon began to rein in token usage as the rising costs of AI tools raised questions about whether the productivity gains justified the expense. Just recently, Accenture reportedly reduced its centrally funded Claude allowance to just $29 per employee per month, requiring any additional spending to be covered by individual projects or teams.

And while there hadn’t been reports of disproportionate token usage from engineers and other employees at Apple, Bloomberg reported today that the company is also looking to rein in employees’ AI spending as part of CEO John Ternus’ broader cost-cutting efforts.

Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap for some engineers using AI models to $200 from $300, according to people with knowledge of the change. The company is now planning further cuts for some engineering teams, potentially reducing their daily allowances to as little as $100, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams, the people said. Employees who require higher allowances to perform their jobs will be able to seek exemptions from senior leadership.

It is not immediately clear which tools are affected by the new spending limits. However, Bloomberg reports that Apple employees have access to several AI services, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini. Some teams are also being encouraged to use cheaper AI models or models that run locally on their devices to reduce costs.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman had previously said that Apple was heavily reliant on Anthropic’s AI models for its internal operations, describing the company as essentially “running on Anthropic,” despite its partnership with Google to power Siri.

That came a few months after then-CEO Tim Cook encouraged employees to make greater use of AI in their daily work during an all-hands meeting, saying, “All of us are using AI in a significant way already, and we must use it as a company as well.”

Back to today’s report, Bloomberg says employee reactions to the new spending limits have been mixed. According to its sources, “few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances,” while others “see the reductions as a sign of broader cost cutting, adding to concerns about potential layoffs.”

Interestingly, the cuts come as Apple’s overall spending continues to rise. Earlier this week, Apple reported its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings, bringing its fiscal year to a close with R&D expenses up 32% to $45.8 billion, driven in part by higher infrastructure and AI costs.

Bloomberg notes that it remains unclear how much Apple will actually save through the new restrictions, particularly since some employees weren’t using their full allowances to begin with.

#3609. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

Shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. Fans of Downton Abbey were thrilled at the new series set in America (streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and we're two episodes into its fourth season on the air. The show is full of Broadway royalty, and two more stars of the Great White Way have just joined the fun. So what is it going to take to get a full-blown musical episode?

The Gilded Age Season 4 started off with a bang, with fans concerned about Marian and Larry's relationship after their tryst. The Gilded Age cast is obviously full of Broadway icons, such as Audra McDonald, Kelli O'Hara, Denée Benton, Donna Murphy, and Celia Keenan-Bolger. Milligan plays Mrs. Louisa Knapp Curtis, a journalist who is covering President Cleveland's forthcoming visit to New York. She won the Tony for her role in Kimberly Akimbo, and she also originated the role of Pamela in Head Over Heels.

Theater kids like me also likely clocked that Taylor Trensch recently made his debut on The Gilded Age as well. He's playing Oliver, the new bumbling footman for the van Rhijn household. It seems like Oliver is going to be struggling with the new gig, although I'm going to be waiting for him to belt out some tunes in every scene.

None of those titles had the amount of accomplished musical theater performers that the HBO series has, so I'd imagine that The Gilded Age would blow people away if it allowed its cast to show off their vocal talents.

I'm not the only one who has been hoping to see a musical episode of The Gilded Age. While it remains to be seen if this happens, fans were treated to Voices of The Gilded Age: The Christmas Album, which features the cast of the show singing holiday tunes. When Siri AI launched in iOS 27 earlier this fall, Apple used a waitlist to gate access. But a newly updated support document says the waitlist is no longer being used, except in “high demand” times.

If you haven’t yet enabled Siri AI on your iPhone, Apple recently made it quicker and easier to gain access.

That’s because, per updates to this support document, the company is now only using a waitlist for Siri AI in “high demand” times.

This will add you to a waitlist, and wait times can vary. Siri AI will begin to download automatically when your wait is complete.

It’s understandable that a waitlist was used initially upon iOS 27’s release. Apple needed to slowly grant access while gauging server performance. But now that we’re nearly two months into the iOS 27 rollout, it’s great that Apple is only deploying the waitlist occasionally as needed.

#3606. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

I truly cannot believe I'd ever be this hungry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Survivor's Lewis Kelly made my stomach turn with this "wtf" story about just how hungry contestants get. I'd suspected things could get dire when I've seen players give up immunity for food, but never in a million years did I think people would consider eating food they pooped out.

As we watch him try to win it all on the 2026 TV schedule, Lewis recalled a shocking story on TikTok in which someone in the tribe made a wild suggestion after Sharonda came back with corn. He explained below:

As you know corn does not fully digest when you poop. Someone in our camp noticed that we were pooping out corn kernels and thought that we could reuse them. Wanted us to pick them out of our poo, wash them, and reboil them in a pot and see if we could get a second use out of them...That merge feast came at the perfect time I have to say.

Keep in mind, Survivor contestants are getting fed more these days than they were a long time ago. I just can't imagine who was suggesting that they genuinely pick corn out of their own fecal matter, combine it, and then boil it to serve in another meal. Literally every time I type that out, I get the urge to vomit, so I'm not sure how anyone could legitimately consider it.

Survivor's Brady Got Asked About The Peeing Thing (But I Can't Get Over How Many Times He Said Brody)

Sharonda received the corn when the Dina tribe was still together, which leads me to wonder who among them suggested such a wild thing. The only thing I can think of is that Danny Kilby has gone on the record about his love of pooping in the ocean, and how it may be his preferred way of doing that. Is there any connection between these stories? We can only speculate.

It's stories like this that make me empathize more with Survivor contestants when they crash out over not being picked to eat an Applebee's reward. I would've never thought food could be such a factor, especially when the game was reduced to 26 days, but Lewis just drove home for me how desperate things can get.

The good (and perhaps most important) part of the story is that it seemed like no one was actually game to do it. Had that post-merger feast never happened, however, we might've heard about some Brodys chowing down on some "recycled" corn in a later meal. And here I thought grubs were the grossest thing someone could eat when playing Survivor.

As disgusting as it was, I do love hearing cast members tell these stories from Survivor 51 that we didn't see in the episodes. With only 90 minutes (including commercials) to tell the story each week, it's totally understandable that something like this would fall by the wayside. Had the tribe actually gone through it and done it, however, I would be upset if it was left on the cutting room floor.

Survivor continues on CBS on Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. With the remaining cast formed under one tribe, I can't wait to see what new alliances are forged. I'm also so invested in trying to figure out who won this season, because I'm still not entirely sure who is getting the winner's edit.

#3604. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3603. Apple Photos keeps getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

iOS 27’s biggest highlight is Siri AI, but the update also packs new features for apps like Messages, Notes, Wallet, and more. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Photos app in iOS 27.

Apple Intelligence powers a trio of editing tools in iOS 27’s Photos app: Extend, Reframe, and a much-improved Clean Up feature.

Extend lets users “give their subjects more breathing room,” per Apple. For example, “they can straighten a crooked horizon without cropping out anything important, or adjust the aspect ratio, and Extend will fill in the missing pieces.”

Reframe lets you adjust the framing of your image spatially. Here’s how Apple describes it:

With Spatial Reframing, users can improve the composition of a photo after it’s been taken. Spatial Reframing builds on Apple’s deep understanding of spatial models thanks to Apple Vision Pro, so users can touch and drag a photo and preview in real time how the perspective shifts — as if they’d repositioned the camera in the original scene. Using powerful image models, Spatial Reframing will only generate new content where the perspective has been shifted, ensuring the reframed photo stays consistent with the original scene.

And the Clean Up feature that debuted in iOS 18 “gets a major upgrade,” Apple says, “so users can remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex.”

iCloud Shared Albums get their first major upgrades in years with iOS 27. The timing is likely no coincidence, with the feature perfect for Apple’s new HomeView product.

Here’s an overview of what’s new, per Apple:

iOS 27 adds two new collections to the Photos app, available under Utilities.

Captured by Me exclusively contains photos taken by you. So it will filter out screenshots, photos you’ve saved from others, and so on.

Identity Documents scans through your Photos library and surfaces images that contain important reference documents, like your driver’s license or passport.

Apple says iOS 27 also adds “Album organization improvements,” but it doesn’t mention specifics.

Another new organization tool in iOS 27 is that you can add keywords to photos. Captions are still available too, but if you scroll up on a photo, near the bottom you’ll find a new ‘Add Keywords’ option.

Another upgrade perfect for HomeView involves slideshow improvements.

Apple Photos has supported quick, easy slideshow creation for years. But if you wanted to customize the automatically generated slideshows, you were out of luck.

Now in iOS 27, slideshows offer new tools for customization. You can change the transition type, set a custom length for the full slideshow and for each photo, and more.

Another welcome addition is that Apple now lets you save any slideshow as a video with one tap.

iOS 27 doesn’t contain any big changes to the design of the Photos app, so if you were hoping to go back to the pre-iOS 18 era, you’ll be disappointed. But the update does offer a variety of exciting new features that make iOS 27 a big release for Apple Photos.

Which of iOS 27’s new Apple Photos features are your favorites? Let us know in the comments.

#3602. How to get the Golden Scale in Zelda Ocarina of Time

The Golden Scale is a unique item in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake that allows Link to dive deeper. You can consider it an upgrade to the Silver Scale, an item that you obtain as young Link as you try to find Princess Ruto. However, unlike the Silver Scale, you can only get the Golden Scale after becoming adult Link.

If you would like to explore the depths of Hyrule and hunt for all the treasures hidden underwater, you should learn how to get the Golden Scale in the Ocarina of Time remake.

You obtain the Golden Scale by catching a fish longer than 60 cm in the Fishing Pond. To complete the challenge, you must travel south of Hyrule Field to Lake Hylia as adult Link. You will see that the lake is dry, and you won't be able to reach the Fishing Pond, located on the right side of the map, on your own. You will need to either ride a magic bean plant (that you need to plant as child Link next to the laboratory) or play the Scarecrow Song near the bridge at the front of the building, and then use the Hookshot on to it. Lake Hylia will also be refilled once you clear the Water Temple, so you can come back after that, too.

Once inside, talk to the Fishing-Pond Man and learn that you can earn a prize if "you catch a big enough fish." Rent a fishing rod for 30 rupees, allowing you to fish as many times as you want until you tell the Fishing-Pond Man that you're done. When preparing to cast your bait, we suggest that you aim at the middle of the pond where you can usually find big fish.

Big fish are more difficult to reel in because they resist for longer periods. Just be patient and keep moving the rod in the direction the fish is pulling. If you catch a fish that is smaller than 60 cm, you just need to toss it back and keep trying until you find the right fish.

However, if you get a fish that meets the requirements, keep it, and then go talk to the Fishing-Pond Man. Select the "I'm done" option and he will examine your fish, and you will receive the Golden Scale.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

The superhero genre is wildly popular, and fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order were shook when Guardians of the Galaxy director James Gunn pivoted to DC as the co-CEO of the studio. It's only been four years since he took the job and kickstarted the new DCU, but he and Peter Safran have already been replaced. I knew the Warner Bros. merger was going to result in some changes, but I didn't see this coming.

For the past few years, Gunn has been methodically crafting the new DCU, both in theaters and streaming with a HBO Max subscription. While the first few projects from Gods and Monsters have been released, a new report by THR claims that Gunn and Safran are stepping down as co-CEOS ,and being replaced former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham. Talk about a change in leadership.

James Gunn took to Instagram to share his own response after this news broke, shocking superhero fans. His statement starts:

Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri I used to write an draw my own comics with a mix of DC comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn't know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn't pass up the unique opportunity. I'm glad I took the job.

Per THR, Safran and Gun will end their time at co-CEOS of DC Studios on December 1st. Their four years at the studio resulted in the formation of a new shared universe, and the release of movie titles Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface, as well as TV shows Creature Commandos, Peacemaker, and Lanterns. Gunn is also directing Man of Tomorrow, which is expected to hit theaters next summer. Later in the director/writer/producer's statement on IG he got real about his time at the head of the studio, posting:

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the last. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that.) I'm always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to short breaks to unwind, and I've stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.

Gunn admits that he'll miss being the warden of the DCU, but also seems excited to go back to filmmaking rather than running the entire studio. In addition to bringing Man of Tomorrow to theaters, he's also a producer on The Batman: Part II and the forthcoming TV series The People v. Gorilla Grodd. Neither Gunn nor the report by THR give one specific reason for this change of the guard, but it certainly sounds like the Suicide Squad director is happy to be back behind the camera, rather than in a board rom.

You can see James Gunn's full statement about leaving his gig as co-CEO of DC Studios below:

Gunn's comments about missing his loved ones in some ways echoes what his wife Jennifer Holland told CinemaBlend earlier this year. Namely that he puts loved ones in his projects so he doesn't have to spend as much time away from them.

There are a few factors that might have gone into this decision. To start, there's Warner Bros.' merger with Paramount, which will likely influence a number of staffing changes for the newly formed company the Skydance Corporation. The DCU has also had a few missteps as of late. Supergirl struggled at the box office, while Lanterns was the subject of some backlash. The newest movie venture Clayface took #1 at the box office, but some people were disappointed it didn't have any real connections to Batman or the greater shared universe.

We'll just have to see how the new leadership affects the DCU as a whole, and the original plans for the shared universe. The next upcoming DC movie hitting theaters will be Man of Tomorrow, hitting theaters July 9th, 2027.

#3599. Ink Review: Danny Boyle's Tabloid Media Origin Story Will Make You Feel Sick

Journalism and media have undergone significant changes in the 21st century. The internet has altered everything and barriers are gone. The gatekeepers who used to be there to say what was or wasn't news don't exist, at least not in the way they used to. Director Danny Boyle has examined this "Give 'em what they want" tabloid media culture in his latest movie "Ink," which will make anyone who values real journalism sick to their stomach.

Adapting the play of the same name, the movie traces the origins of the British gossip rag The Sun, focusing on a group of misfit visionaries who had an idea for a new kind of news. Rather than simply report "the news," why not give people what they want instead?

Less a biopic a about Rupert Murdoch (played here by Guy Pearce) and his family, the real-life family the Roy clan on "Succession" is based off of, it focuses instead largely on Larry Lamb, played by "Sinners" star Jack O'Connell. Lamb was the man hand-picked by Murdoch to change The Sun from a fledgling paper into something, well, different. Driven by revenge and a sense of "I'll show 'em," Lamb, at least as presented by Boyle, is one of the most significant figures who shaped the modern era. And not in a good way, it probably goes without saying. But I'll say it anyway.

The story being told in "Ink" is an ugly one with grave consequences in the real world. Danny Boyle starts out by making this seem almost fun and exciting. Larry Lamb assembling his team has an "Ocean's Eleven" quality to it, with the kinetic energy of some of the director's best movies, most notably "Trainspotting."

Slowly but surely though, it all devolves into something more sinister. Even though news and journalism should probably be seen as a public good and an essential function of any democratic society, the need to make these publications profitable changes the game. Lamb and Rupert Murdoch lean into the "business" side of the news business, and that's where things get downright icky.

The tone of "Ink" shifts from a fun outsider tale to a dark story about taking something too far in pursuit of capitalist superiority. We see Larry Lamb lose the man he was, becoming a man that's difficult to respect. While the great newsroom movies in cinema history, such as "All the President's Men" and "Spotlight," make viewers feel the power of journalism, "Ink" forces the viewer to understand that power can and often is used in far less noble ways. Boyle is offering up his view of the men responsible for that shift.

By heading back to the past, namely the late '60s in the U.K., Boyle shines a light on the modern era. Podcasts. Blogs. Tabloids. Cable news. It all traces its roots back to this moment in history and it's hard not to leave this movie feeling some kind of way about our current media culture.

"Ink" also makes the viewer think about how accurate movies like "Spotlight" and other "based on a true story" movies are. Boyle and writer James Graham probably weren't too interested in getting everything exactly right, as this movie is about how a narrative can be shaped. Boyle and Graham shaped a narrative using real people who had real influence on the world as we know it. Accuracy isn't the point. It's about painting a picture.

"Ink" is a true showcase for Jack O'Connell. He's chewed the screen rather delightfully in movies like "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" in recent years. But this film allows him to be more human and take the driver's seat in a grounded movie with a killer ensemble. He's the best part of a movie that also includes an excellent Claire Foy and a good-as-ever Guy Pearce.

Pearce, in particular, deserves credit for playing Rupert Murdoch with nuance. It would be easy to turn the guy who helped create Fox News into a cigar-chomping, cartoonish villain. Pearce didn't take the easy way out.

Will "Ink" rank amongst Danny Boyle's best films? Maybe not. It's tonally uneven and about as subtle as a jackhammer. But it's also got one hell of a point to make. News is kind of like vegetables: Not the most fun, but nutritious and necessary. "Ink" shines an uncomfortable light on how we, as a society, allowed news to turn from vegetables into junk food. Eat enough junk food, you'll get sick.

"Ink" hits select theatres December 11, 2026, before releasing on Netflix on January 8, 2027.

#3598. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s no surprise that Jack Black would be in attendance at a Metallica show at Sphere in Las Vegas. After all, this is a guy who is famous for singing “You can't kill the metal” with his band Tenacious D. As someone lucky enough to have seen a few shows at the state-of-the-art venue, I can say that watching Black absolutely get down at the show, he’s a model for how I want to live. The power of music truly overtook him, and that’s the best inspiration there is. Oh, and Celine Dion was also getting down next to him, which could be the most random thing about the whole thing. Check it out:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Sporting a very scruffy beard and a backwards hat, the School of Rock star is truly dancing like no one is watching. He’s in the zone, as you might say, hanging on every lyric Metallica frontman James Hetfield is spitting out during the song "Blackened" from their legendary album ...And Justice for All. If you’ve ever seen Metallica, and I have a few times, you know that when the crowd locks in, they really lock in. There’s a reason they’re the most popular metal band in the world, despite some iffy output over the last…well… few decades, if I’m honest.

It’s their live shows, with the imagery and pyrotechnics that really set them apart, and what better venue to provide insane visuals for a frenetic Metallica show? Black is certainly loving it. As a man just a few years younger than Black and of…let’s just say…similar build, I’m left inspired. Like Black, I love seeing live music, and it’s something I never want to get sick of doing, even as I creep towards my AARP-era. Black shows no signs of slowing down, and that’s inspiring, for sure.

Speaking of inspiring, a couple of seats away from Black is none other than legendary Celine Dion, taking in the show in Las Vegas. Dion is no stranger to Sin City concerts, having performed hundreds of shows in Vegas over the years. She’s one of the city’s most enduring stars, and her show at Caesars ran for almost a decade before ending in 2019. She’s right there, headbanging along with Black and air drumming along to Lars Ulrich.

Black headbanging at a Metallica show is to be expected, but Dion? As the kids would say, that is not something I had on my bingo card. Seeing her at The Eagles, or even The Backstreet Boys at Sphere, wouldn’t be shocking, but Metallica? Yeah, I wouldn’t have seen that coming at all. It’s Black, though, who has my attention.

Black has had a big year on the 2026 movie schedule, with The Super Mario Galaxy Movie crushing at the box office in the spring, and Jumanji: Open World set to hit theaters on Christmas Day. He’ll also have A Minecraft Movie Squared on the 2027 film schedule, so finding time to release some steam at Metallica is probably perfect before the media blitz he’ll be in for over the next few months.

#3596. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet Honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,” said artist Vija Celmins as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to its programming (this year it raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as one of the first arrivals on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Celmins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin haute couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve’s leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet altogether, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I’ve never really met Denis. I’ve met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions, and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I’ve always felt that cinema is seen as a Pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would—right here, right now—announce which actor would play James Bond. The French Canadian director is helming the next Bond film, and over the past week reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift’s performance of “Love Story.” Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests, Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband, Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the “Culture Queen of Los Angeles,” she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, and starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, which, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial costar Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve’s speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mash-up of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt, or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew, and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

Odessa A'zion in a Charles & Ron + Maison Privee coat.

Tyriq Withers, Isabel May, and Homer Gere

#3594. Every Martin McDonagh-Directed Movie, Ranked (Including Wild Horse Nine)

British-Irish filmmaker Martin McDonagh has become one of cinema's foremost stewards of the tragicomedy. In a McDonagh movie, violence or death can be hilarious, or devastating, or both. He forces us to sympathize with unlikable or even evil characters by showing that even those bad eggs still have human sides. Catholicism casts its shadow over McDonagh's stories, especially in how he loves to focus on guilty, even suicidally guilty, people. He dares you to sympathize with those guilty people in spite of their horrible sins and, quite often, he succeeds.

While there are usually glimmers of hope for redemption, McDonagh's stories never end with tidy answers, either. As for his crackling dialogue, it's remarkable how adept he is at both non-sequiturs and rhythmic back-and-forth. If Quentin Tarantino had been raised in London and Galway instead of Tennessee and Los Angeles, you'd have a writer like Martin McDonagh.

McDonagh began as a playwright, producing several plays in the 1990s and early 2000s. He moved into film in 2004 with his directed short, "Six Shooter," and then jumped to features with 2008's "In Bruges." He's remained there since and has become a frequent Oscar nominee to boot. To celebrate his sixth and latest film "Wild Horse Nine" hitting theaters, here are all of McDonagh's movies, ranked!

McDonagh's first film was a short one: 2004's "Six Shooter," which is available to watch for free on YouTube. In 2006, "Six Shooter" received an Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film. It's the least of McDonagh's films by its very nature as a short, but running only 26 minutes has a positive double-edge: The script is small but airtight, like a great short story should be.

Brendan Gleeson plays Donnelly, an Irish man taking a train ride after his wife died in the hospital that morning. There's also a couple (David Wilmot and Aisling O'Sullivan) onboard reeling from the death of their infant son, as well as a very rude and loud kid (Rúaidhrí Conroy). The kid enjoys running his mouth and prodding the other passengers, and rest assured, he's holding a dark secret too.

Even with its short runtime, "Six Shooter" still has a lot of what have become McDonagh's trademarks as a storyteller. There's a death scene that'll make you jump with how abrupt it is, as well as an overall theme of grief-driven people looking to suicide for the answer. There's also a twist, seeded offhandedly in the movie's opening, that comes back and completely reframes everything at the end.

Considering the accolades "Six Shooter" earned, all the way up to the Academy, it's also a credit to McDonagh that he hasn't remade it as a full-length feature. The train ride setting benefits from the brevity, and while the twist is satisfying at 20 minutes of build-up, at 90 it might be a drag. "Six Shooter" sits well enough as is.

In "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri," McDonagh wrote a story about a tight-knit community in the vein of several of his plays. But as you can guess from the title, this one takes place in small town America, not rural Ireland. Whether McDonagh succeeded in his self-imposed challenge of setting with "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" still splits audiences.

Mildred Hayes (Frances McDormand, who won Best Actress for the performance) is a woman grieving the still-unsolved rape and murder of her daughter, Angela (Kathryn Newton). To apply some pressure to police chief Bill Willoughby (Woody Harrelson), she puts up three billboards outside the town that read, in succession: "Raped While Dying." "And Still No Arrests?" "How Come, Chief Willoughby?" Mildred turns her grief into a spectacle the town can't look away from.

Upon wide release, "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" attracted a vocal backlash alongside its accolades. The main lightning rod was the character Jason Dixon (Sam Rockwell), a racist police officer accused of torturing a Black suspect, who attempts a soulful redemption arc. Many found that approach in poor taste; Dixon doesn't repent his bigotry, but the film insists he has a heart in spite of it.

McDonagh has said he did not intend "Three Billboards" as a message movie about American politics, and he's definitely not the type of writer who uses his characters to deliver moralistic lectures. The easy answer is that McDonagh was a little careless about adding local color to the kind of story he's written about Irish villages before. Mixed with his predilection for asking audiences to sympathize with immoral people, that approach landed the wrong way for many. McDonagh's settings usually feel whimsical, like black comedy fairy tales, and that doesn't quite mesh with politically potent themes.

Two of McDonagh's most frequent leading men are Colin Farrell and Sam Rockwell, but he's only used them together in one movie: his third film, and second feature, "Seven Psychopaths," which is a much stranger, more contemplative movie than its violent-sounding title suggests. McDonagh's most structurally ambitious movie, "Seven Psychopaths" is Spike Jonze and Charlie Kaufman's "Adaptation" by way of Quentin Tarantino.

Farrell plays Marty, a writer's block-afflicted screenwriter working on his new script "Seven Psychopaths." He's also best friends with a criminal, Billy (Rockwell), who gets himself in hot water after kidnapping mob boss Charlie Costello's (Woody Harrelson) dog and sleeping with Costello's girlfriend, Angela (Olga Kurylenko).

As Marty, Billy, and Billy's partner-in-crime Hans (Christopher Walken) drive away fleeing the gangsters, the movie tips its hand. Marty suggests that, in his "Seven Psychopaths" script, "the first hour should be like a perfect set-up for an out-and-out revenge flick." But then the leads should "walk away" and just go out to the dessert and talk like real people. Billy is dumbfounded ("No shootouts?!"), but lo and behold, that's what the actual "Seven Psychopaths" you're watching does.

The movie's meta approach lets McDonagh engage in some amusing self-criticism. "Your women characters are awful," Hans tells Marty. Marty, not even trying to deny it, just answers that "it's a hard world for women." There are also layered interludes demonstrating Marty's ideas for his screenplay, like a former Viet Cong soldier (Long Nguyen) on a vengeance quest.

Your mileage with "Seven Psychopaths" will depend heavily on your tolerance for metafiction. But if you can get on its wavelength, it's a very funny movie with three excellently played leads.

As a filmmaker settles into their career, there's always the risk they'll start going through the motions, i.e. making films that only echo what they've said or accomplished in previous, better films. I mention this because McDonagh's latest film "Wild Horse Nine" has the exact same essential premise as "In Bruges" — two professional murderers on holiday where one has been tasked with killing the other.

In 1973, Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) are CIA agents working in Santiago, Chile to undermine the country's democracy and bring dictator Augusto Pinochet to power. They take a vacation to Easter Island; Chris is dying of cancer, and he wants Lee to kill him in a peaceful place. Their boss, MJ (Steve Buscemi), is worried because Chris is talking about penning memoirs and sharing the CIA's darkest secrets.

This is both Malkovich and Buscemi's first time working with McDonagh, and both actors take to his dialogue easily. Malkovich is perfectly cast as the airy and impish Chris, just as Buscemi brings his tightly wound Mr. Pink from "Reservoir Dogs" energy to MJ. "Old killer haunted by his past" is nothing new, but Chris isn't broody and self-flagellating even though he is suffering Catholic guilt. He's more like the eccentric grandfather who says what's on his mind because he's aged past caring about consequences.

The first chunk of "Wild Horse Nine" is a little uneventful, as Lee and Chris tour Easter Island and bicker. But the same could be said of "In Bruges," so I should've trusted the process. The movie's emotional arcs and its mysteries come together beautifully in the second half. It's also politically sharper, or at least angrier, than "Three Billboards." If you want to hear how America supposedly "protects democracy" across the world, watch something else.

"Breaking up" with a longtime friend can be just as painful as ending a romantic relationship. Don't believe me? Then live a little, but before that, also go and watch "The Banshees of Inisherin," the definitive and brutal friend breakup movie.

In 1994, McDonagh tried to write a play titled "The Banshees of Inisheer," but couldn't crack it. He hung onto the title, and years later he found a story for which to use it (albeit tweaked to reflect the change from the real Irish island Inisheer to the fictional Inisherin). Set in the 1920s, "Banshees" follows two former lifelong friends, farmer Pádraic (Colin Farrell) and fiddle player Colm (Brendan Gleeson).

Colm decides one day he doesn't want to be friends anymore. Unlike your typical movie feud, there's no real inciting incident. Pádraic is a nice guy, but boring, and so Colm — who's in a midlife crisis and wants to write a musical composition that history will remember — doesn't want to speak to him any more. You can tell they've been friends because of convenience first: It's a small island and they have little else in their lives. Since Pádraic didn't do anything wrong, there's no real way to repair their friendship, and attempts at reconciliation eventually beget revenge.

Farrell and Gleeson's casting carries extra weight considering they starred together in McDonagh's "In Bruges." That film was about their characters' saving each other through their friendship, whereas this one is about them hurting each other as a friendship dissolves. Farrell's puppy dog face is perfect for the spurned and confused Pádraic, while Gleeson's turns his usual jovial presence as cold as Inisherin's ocean winds. The virtual third player is Kerry Condon as Pádraic's sister Siobhán, the exasperated straight woman of Inisherin.

"In Bruges" holds a special place in my film-loving heart. I saw it when I was about 14 years old, and, as a Catholic school alum just beginning to love Quentin Tarantino, I was perfectly primed for it to floor me. I still remember it as a pivotal moment in my journey as a cinephile and it holds up as McDonagh's most effective, perfectly-executed movie.

Ray (Colin Farrell) and his mentor Ken (Brendan Gleeson) are two British-Irish hitmen sent to hide out in a Belgian city, Bruges, and await instruction from their boss Harry (Ralph Fiennes). Ken loves the town's old-fashioned charm and the sight-seeing, but Ray is irritable and makes it clear Bruges is the last place he wants to be.

What seems like a buddy comedy reveals itself as a devastating drama when we find out why the pair are in Bruges. During their previous job (Ray's first), a little boy died as collateral damage. It was an accident, yes, but it still only happened because Ray shot up a priest (Ciarán Hinds) by ambushing him in a confessional. So, yeah, can't imagine the good Lord will be looking too kindly on that! Ray has to rediscover the will to live, and Ken — who'd been assigned by Harry to kill Ray as punishment for killing the kid — is his unlikely guardian angel.

From the character arcs to the tone (which remains frequently funny even after we get the devastating truth), "In Bruges" is a writing masterclass elevated even higher by three perfectly in-tune performances. Ray's redemption was echoed off-screen, too. Colin Farrell taking on such a complex and morally compromised but still empathetic character let him prove what a great actor he is after a rough few years prior.

Godzilla Minus Zero Ruled The Weekend Box Office And Hit A Monstrous Milestone

I Don't Think We're Going To Get A Street Fighter II, And Here's Why I'm Okay With That
