When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Honestly, I didn't think any Godzilla movie could ever top Godzilla Minus One since it quickly became my favorite Godzilla movie of all time, but I was wrong. Dead wrong. Its sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero, is my NEW favorite Godzilla film.

I know what you're probably thinking: Oh, you must not be a real Godzilla fan. You probably got into the character with the MonsterVerse. But no, pump the brakes, buddy, since I've been a Godzilla fan since before I can remember. I've watched every Godzilla movie from every era (yes, even the animated ones), and I've even called Godzilla the greatest character in cinematic history! So, yeah. I'm a guy who loves his Godzilla.

So, when I say that Godzilla Minus Zero is the greatest Godzilla movie I've ever seen, I mean it! Here's why.

I think anybody who loved Godzilla Minus One will tell you that the reason that movie was so successful was that it focused on the human characters and made Godzilla more of a background character. Minus Zero doubles down on that (Some might even say to the film’s detriment, but not me!).

This time around, Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and Noriko (Minami Hamabe) are married, and they’ve taken Akiko (Sae Nagatani) in as their adopted daughter. Noriko currently helps out in an orphanage for children who have lost their parents to Godzilla and the war, and a lot of the children there resent Akiko for having parents. Heavy stuff!

We also get a new character in Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who has survivor’s guilt due to the death of his family in the bombing of Hiroshima, as well as a returning Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), who is now the director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau. Another new character is Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who links kaiju appearances to the weather. Both she and Noda also have a great deal of guilt, which seems to be a theme of both of these Minus films - what do you do with your guilt? Do you let it sink you, or do you use it to push you forward to help others?

All of this is to say that even though this is a movie that ALSO has Godzilla fighting King Ghidorah to the death, the human characters still take center stage, and the movie is all the better for it.

I know there are a lot of movies that tout that they were made specifically with IMAX in mind (And I’ll definitely be checking out The Prestige now that it’s coming back in that format), but honestly, I can’t name a single movie where IMAX was just as instrumental to the film as, say, 3D was for Avatar. Until now, that is, because Godzilla Minus Zero is SUCH an amazing movie in IMAX that I honestly couldn’t think of seeing it in any other format.

In fact, I’ve now seen the movie twice - once by myself, and once with my nine-year-old son (I HAD to see it twice since it’s rated R and I needed to know if it was appropriate for him…don’t get me started on that one), and both times, I was blown away by how LOUD the movie can get, and also by just how enormous the kaiju are on the big screen, most notably with Ghidorah.

There’s even one scene in particular involving Ghidorah chasing after planes that really, genuinely put me on the edge of my seat, and a lot of it was due to the sights and sounds on such a massive screen. My son said that scene made his legs shake, and I don’t blame him. I was genuinely on edge myself.

This also goes for the final fight, which really does feel like one big battlefield on such a large screen. As I said up top, I’ve seen every Godzilla movie, but this is the first that really made me feel like I was witnessing an actual disaster. I guess that’s the power of IMAX.

Oh, man. I know I initially wanted Hedorah to be Godzilla’s main antagonist in this movie, but I take that back a million times over, since King Ghidorah was just the bee’s knees. I’m talking out of sight, Jack (Okay, I’ll stop now). A major complaint I’ve seen online is that Godzilla isn’t in this movie nearly enough, but I couldn’t disagree more. When Godzilla arrives, he takes ALL of your attention, and his battle at the end with King Ghidorah is by far my favorite Godzilla battle ever.

First off, I love the close-up of Godzilla’s eyes when he sees Ghidorah. I have never seen Godzilla more pissed off in my life (Well, besides in Godzilla, Mothra, and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack). And then, the battle itself is so intense. Ghidorah starts ripping Godzilla apart, and he even picks him up and drops him.

As often happens, Godzilla gets his butt whooped at first, but then rallies to victory. But this time, the human characters are directly connected to his success, which again, makes the human story so closely tied to the battle. The best part, though, was Godzilla doing ultra MEGA atomic breath. With the soaring soundtrack, it was just heaven.

So, yeah, even though I kind of didn’t want Godzilla to face off against another foe initially, I now think this is the best and most interesting Godzilla movie yet, and this final kaiju battle - which Minus One was lacking - definitely helped.

Lastly, even though I loved Minus One with my full heart and soul, I still didn’t get so emotionally invested in it that I cried while watching it. However, there were several moments in Minus Zero where I genuinely cried.

Now, the first time was with the aforementioned scene where Ghidorah was chasing airplanes. I’ve loved Godzilla my entire life, but I’ve never felt genuine dread watching a kaiju as I did with King Ghidorah in that scene. It was so glorious that I had tears in my eyes by the end of it, and was smiling from ear to ear. Another moment was when Kanji Murakami was banging his head over and over again in his lab over the guilt of his family. I know Japanese Godzilla films are often allegories for the destruction of the atomic bomb, but this one spelled it out even more clearly. Such a powerful scene.

It was at the end, though, when Akiko’s parents came back to the orphanage just to say that they were leaving, that the waterworks really came for me. In fact, I’m lucky the movie was so loud because people would have heard me sniffing if it wasn’t. When she called them liars, but then wished them safe travels, thinking that she would never see them again, I just couldn’t take it. I cried, dammit. I cried!

It’s for that reason and more that I genuinely don’t think I’ll see a better film this year. Godzilla Minus One was my favorite movie of 2023, and I’m pretty sure Minus Zero will be my favorite movie of 2026. I can’t see anything else beating it. It was just that damn good! Best. Godzilla movie. Ever!

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3592. Superman Sequel Will Officially Introduce the DCU’s Wonder Woman, Report Says

Man of Tomorrow is reportedly bringing in another Justice League hero

On Monday, James Gunn and Peter Safran stepped down from their leadership roles at DC Studios. Skydance — which recently finalized its acquisition of DC parent company Warner Bros. Discovery — tapped Jeremy Latcham to lead DC. He used to work at Marvel Studios, and coincidentally was a producer on Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy.

When sharing his story about the news, The Wall Street Journal's Ben Fritz seemingly confirmed details about Gunn's next movie, 2027's Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow. In a post on X, he wrote that Gunn and Safran will debut Wonder Woman in next summer's blockbuster.

Fans have long speculated that Princess Diana of Themyscira would appear in Man of Tomorrow. Adria Arjona (Andor) was cast in the Superman sequel in April, with some reports pegging her as playing the relatively unknown character Maxima while Gunn remained tight-lipped about her role. Arjona hasn't confirmed who her character is either, but her training regimen for this fall's Onslaught and Man of Tomorrow has led fans to think she's Wonder Woman. Some outlets, like Cosmic News, have definitively stated that she will be Wonder Woman, which seems more plausible after Fritz's post. He doesn't specifically say Arjona will be Wonder Woman, but no one else in the cast fits the bill.

Wonder Woman's alleged appearance in Man of Tomorrow isn't the only notable part of Fritz's post. He also wrote that The Brave and the Bold is slated to come out in 2028. This film would introduce the DCU's Batman in live action. While we've known DC Studios has been planning The Brave and the Bold, the film has been without a release window.

Fritz also said that Gunn and Safran were "aiming for Gunn-directed Superman sequels" in 2029 and 2031. Apparently, those sequels "low-key evolved into Justice League" movies at some point. While Gunn recently confirmed he was working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, he hasn't officially announced what that film will be.

For now, it's unclear what the future of the DC Universe will look like with Latcham stepping in to lead the charge.

Man of Tomorrow will see David Corenswet and Nicholas Hoult reprise their roles as Superman and Lex Luthor, respectively. Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane, Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Isabela Merced as Hawkgirl, Milly Alcock as Supergirl, Lars Eidinger as Brainiac, and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart/Green Lantern will all appear as well. It will hit theaters July 9, 2027.

#3591. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Will Have Some Unexpected Main Characters [Exclusive]

Don't let the title fool you: "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" may suggest that this Prime Video series is all about the origins of Sauron (played by Charlie Vickers), but the truth is much more complicated than that. In the very first scene of Season 1, we see the events of the saga told through the eyes of Galadriel (Morfyyd Clark), positioning her as our de facto main protagonist. In the time since, an ensemble of characters have risen up to take the reins of this story. There's Robert Aramayo's Elrond, the Dwarf king Durin (Owain Arthur), our lovable clan of Harfoots, and so many more spread out over the vast expanse of Middle-earth. But, if you ask the show's creative team, Season 3 takes this versatile approach to even greater heights.

In fact, I did ask them exactly that. At the recent press junket for "The Rings of Power," I spoke to co-showrunner Patrick McKay about whether he sees these three seasons as a Sauron-centric narrative or something that extends far beyond our favorite Dark Lord. According to McKay, it's a tricky balance:

"Sauron is going to be the center of gravity in many ways, but it's an ensemble show, and we love the idea that from episode to episode, sequence to sequence, someone might surprise you [...] We love that we can do that."

McKay actually singled out one particular character by name who takes the lead at one point in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, but we'll save that (very minor) reveal for below. Needless to say, it's a perfect example of the series' writers staying light on their feet. With such a talented cast, the show might as well use them to its advantage.

Without spoiling any specifics, one of the more memorable instances of this comes in the early episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3. While Sauron's ongoing conquest of Middle-earth puts the pressure on the forces of good, the sequestered island nation of Númenor is dealing with its own troubles closer to home. Caught in the middle of this turmoil, the family made up of Isildur (Maxim Baldry), his sister Eärien (Ema Horvath), and their father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) are hard-pressed to keep up a united front. This subplot may not be the most obvious favorite for many viewers of the show, but Season 3 goes out of its way to shine a brighter spotlight on one secondary character in particular.

According to Patrick McKay, fans ought to be on the lookout for what Episode 2 has in store. "The second episode this season, arguably the protagonist is Ema Horvath's character Eärien over in Númenor — who you abstractly would never think that the sister of the [character] over in that particular story would take that kind of prominence," he explained. It's a calculated gamble, but one that speaks to his and co-showrunner J.D. Payne's new mentality. McKay added:

"We're just looking [for] ways to shake it up and surprise you, and we know what Ema can do. And we were very excited to give her that chance."

The storylines revolving around Galadriel, Sauron, and Jamie Campbell Bower's newly-introduced Celeborn will likely make most of the headlines this year, but don't sleep on the supporting characters populating this world. You never know which one might surprise you. "The Rings of Power" Season 3 premieres November 11, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3590. Report: Apple and Samsung outperform rivals as smartphone chip shipments tumble 21%

According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details.

At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors.

Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series.

Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn.

That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market.

According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%.

MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%).

After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%.

Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter.

Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said:

“We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.”

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year.

During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters.

#3588. Before Euphoria, Sydney Sweeney Starred In An Overlooked Psychological Thriller That's Streaming For Free

2019 was a big year for Sydney Sweeney, marking her debut as Cassie Howard in HBO's "Euphoria." That proved to be her breakout role, but it wasn't her only memorable performance of 2019. That same year appeared in "Clementine" as Lana, a mysterious and beguiling figure who enters into a complicated relationship with another woman trying to reckon with a recently-ended love affair. Like Sweeney's character, the movie is hard to pin down. As Variety's Lisa Kennedy noted in her review, you're never quite sure whether this is "a coming-of-age meditation or a psychosexual thriller," a "breakup drama or simmering horror flick," making it a compelling watch throughout. All of which makes it a shame this one got lost in the shuffle — a result of having been overshadowed by Sweeney's "Euphoria" debut and the global pandemic of 2020. Thankfully, "Clementine" is now available to watch for free over on one of the best streaming services available, Tubi.

Sweeney hasn't always had the easiest time outside of "Euphoria." Thanks to the $100 million box office smash hit "Anyone But You" and her lead performance in Paul Feig's excellent, wicked drama "The Housemaid," the actor has managed to remain relevant. But Sweeney's 2025 film "Americana" was ignored at the box office and "Madame Web" speaks for itself.

That said, Sweeney has always subverted expectations and will no doubt continue to see success in the coming years. Heck, she has already overcome perceptions of her as an attractive young actor with little else to offer via excellent performances in a range of projects, many of which simply haven't been given the attention they deserve. "Clementine" is just one example.

/Film's list of the best Sydney Sweeney movies is a testament to the actor's versatility, with everything from romantic comedies to the intense, nerve wracking portrait of United States Air Force veteran Reality Winner that was "Reality." 2019's "Clementine" is harder to define but just as worthy of your attention.

The film is written and directed by Lara Jean Gallagher, and represents the Pennsylvania-native's debut narrative feature following a series of short films and commercials. It tells the story of 30-year-old Karen (Otmara Marrero), who, having broken up with her older girlfriend, D (Sonya Walger), travels to her ex's lake house to take stock of the relationship. There, she meets 19-year-old Lana (Sweeney), who's first seen sunbathing by the lake and very quickly captures Karen's attention. As the pair grow closer, Karen suddenly finds herself in a similar situation to D in her former relationship. Wary of developing feelings for someone significantly younger, yet hopelessly drawn to Lana, Karen has to navigate a delicate relationship.

Gallagher told Movablefest that with "Clementine" she wanted to interrogate the often contradictory nature of female relationships. "I was just really just interested in exploring female relationships," she said, "and how it can feel like a sister dynamic or like rivals, or like a mother/daughter at times or even sexual in nature all at the same time." That can be seen in the often confounding connection between Karen and Lana, which  makes for a movie that's at once tense and touching, hazy yet sharp.

Prior to her "Euphoria" debut, Sydney Sweeney was making a name for herself with roles in Netflix series "Everything Sucks!" and HBO's "Sharp Objects," in which she played a psychiatric patient Alice alongside Amy Adams' Camille Preaker. Sweeney also played Eden Spencer in Season 2 of "The Handmaid's Tale" and her star was clearly on the rise. It's a shame, then, that "Clementine" flew under the radar in the way that it did, as it boasts an enigmatic yet darkly enchanting performance from Sweeney that surely would have helped boost her profile had the film received more attention.

"Clementine" premiered at the 2019 Tribeca Film Festival ahead of distributor Oscilloscope Pictures releasing the film on virtual screens in May 2020 — a late pivot that came in the wake of the global pandemic. It managed a perfectly respectable 62% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, and while that may seem slightly underwhelming, certain critics were all in on Lara Gallagher's psychological thriller.

The aforementioned Lisa Kennedy praised Sweeney for "deftly shape-shift[ing] from late teen to younger — too young? — often within the same scene," while Slant's Jake Cole was convinced that Gallagher is "every bit as adept as Josephine Decker and the Safdie brothers are at wringing unease from the most mundane of scenarios." David Ehrlich of IndieWire might have felt the film was "too prone to navel-gazing to leave a strong impression" but Nell Minow of RogerEbert.com seemed to enjoy what she described as an "exploration of the shifting power in relationships with striking images and overtones of duality." So, if you're looking for a good psychological thriller, "Clementine" is arguably one of the best movies on Tubi right now.

Bari Weiss has been the editor-in-chief of CBS News for over a year now, and her tenure has been quite eventful. For months, media analysts have weighed in on Weiss’ direction of the company and, while she’s received praise in some circles, she’s also received backlash. Of course, running a media corporation is no small feat and, just recently, Weiss was asked about what it’s really been like for her to hold down the big job. With that, the veteran journalist shared some candid thoughts about the inner workings of the brand.

For the most part, it’s rare that Weiss sits down to discuss her role at CBS in depth, and she did just that during a recent discussion held by The Information at the WTF Summit. Weiss discussed a number of topics amid the conversation (which can be seen on YouTube), including concerns about 60 Minutes’ low ratings and the notion of her running CNN someday. Host Jessica Lessin asked Weiss about the practicalities of running a news outlet, leading the E-I-C to make some quick jokes:

I don't work out. I don't sleep. I don't have any friends left. I mean, that would be one answer to that question.

After sharing those quips, though, Weiss got serious quite quickly, saying the experience had been “consuming.” Lessin went on to make note of CBS News’ position within the pantheon of legacy news outlets and how old-school principles may work against Weiss’ vision for the brand. While Weiss mentioned that there had been success within the company, she also spoke to some of the challenges facing it:

I would say on the inside, it's been tremendously successful. The disparity — I mean, I'm sure you all work at places that are covered and scrutinized. You know that the gap between the stories that are being told and the actual experience of it in the case of CBS, it's like a chasm. If I spent all of my time being concerned about trying to tell a different story, I would not be able to run the actual news organization.

One Of Bari Weiss’ New 60 Minutes Stars Has Blunt Advice For CBS News Staffers Amid Backlash

One of the key points of discussion that has surrounded Bari Weiss since David Ellison hired her involves her editorial prowess. Some of her choices have come under fire, including her last-minute decision to cut a 60 Minutes story about the Terrorism Confinement Center in El Salvador almost a year ago. At the time, Weiss concluded that more research needed to be done before the story could go to air. Weiss has still, however, been accused of initiating “journalistic interference,” and journalists like Dan Rather and Scott Pelley have criticized her leadership abilities, particularly due to her lack of broadcast journalism experience prior to CBS.

However, CBS Evening News anchor Tony Dokoupil spoke positively about Weiss’ vision and said he hadn’t witnessed any news bias. Newly hired correspondent Sir Trevor Phillips also defended Weiss and her approach to putting together a team of journalists. Regardless of praise or criticism, though, Weiss emphasized during the interview that she had been aiming to tune out noise. She now seems to be looking ahead to the future, and she explained her intention to create change in an ever-evolving media landscape:

This is one of the most storied important news organizations in the world. It was built for a time where there were three news channels that you could choose from on the television. We now live in a world of infinite information, choice and possibility. By necessity, that means it has to change. Every single legacy news organization has to change, because we're in — the attention, whatever you want to call it, we are in a a fierce competition to get people to command people's attention to make sure that [what] we are offering them is something that matters.

Bari Weiss went on to say “the change that's required is painful as it would be in any organization that has to change the way it does business.” It is indeed true that the industry has been experiencing growing pains as of late as the overall media model undergoes alterations. While we can’t say just how CBS News will fit into that framework moving forward, Weiss seems keen on running the brand in a way that’s fluid and viable.

Mean Girls is arguably one of the best movies of the 2000s, and it’s no surprise fans continue to support the film that launched a mini franchise with a sequel, a musical reboot released in 2024, and a Tony-nominated musical. The talented movie cast has gone on to do amazing things, which has kept them mostly apart until now. For the first time in a long time, Lindsay Lohan reunited with some of her Mean Girls cast on the set of her newest film, Return to You, and I’m not the only one obsessed with the photos.

Lohan, who famously played Cady Heron in the 2004 flick, has been filming an upcoming Netflix film alongside Mean Girls director Mark Waters. Last month, Waters revealed the film was filming at an iconic Mean Girls location, and now it seems they’ve tapped some of the cast to join them in this walk down memory lane. Waters once again took to his Instagram to share the photos of the mini reunion with Sharron Matthews, Stefanie Drummond, and Daniel DeSanto:

A post shared by Mark Waters (@mark_s_waters)

For those who might need a refresher, Waters also included photos of Matthews, Drummond, and DeSanto as their Mean Girls characters Joan (a teacher), Bethany (a fellow high school student), and Jason (Gretchen’s on-again, off-again boyfriend). It’s so heartwarming seeing them reunite, and I’m not the only one who thinks so. Fellow Mean Girls actor Jonathan Bennett, who played Aaron Samuels, was quick to comment on the post, writing:

As much as I would love to see the Freakier Friday actress reunite with “The Plastics” in another movie, I’m obsessed with the fact that Waters and Lohan, who is also producing the project, chose to include some of the iconic but lesser-known actors from the film. It also makes sense since Return to You is set to take place in the noughties, 2008 to be exact.

Lohan will play a lonely attorney who has been accidentally sent an emotional DVD from a dying woman addressed to the woman’s husband (played by Henry Golding). While it’s unclear what role the trio will play in the Netflix rom-com, the photos do give us some clues. DeSanto is definitely going to be a lawyer of some sort; whether that be a coworker or an enemy remains to be seen. Matthews can be seen in an office setting, which makes me think she could be a potential client. Drummond looks like she’s in a home, so maybe she plays a sister or mother of the dying woman.

Of course, all of this is purely speculation at this point. With production of the romance film just starting, it’s going to be a while before Return to You is available for those with a Netflix subscription, but that also means that there’s time for even more Mean Girls references and cameos to make an appearance in the film. Until then, fans can stream Mean Girls with an active Paramount+ subscription.

#3584. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Secret Weapon Is A Member Of J.R.R. Tolkien's Family [Exclusive]

It takes a village to make a gargantuan, big-budget fantasy series on the level of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power." No, scratch that. It takes a veritable army of hard-working artists and technical wizards and production heads, all pulling in the same direction to bring the vision of co-showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay to life. On top of that, add the unique pressures of crafting a new story set in the world of J.R.R. Tolkien's beloved Middle-earth and, needless to say, the creative team is all too happy to get as much help as humanly possible.

One name in particular, highlighted in the end credits throughout this season, will practically jump off the screen to diehard fans. Despite any online grumbling about changes made to the Prime Video series, there is a clear vetting process that Payne and McKay go through before bringing the written word of their scripts to the small screen. One small but crucial aspect of that includes Simon Tolkien, grandson of the famous author and the official "Creative Consultant" on "The Rings of Power" since the first season.

During a recent press junket prior to the release of the Season 3 premiere (you can check out the Season 3 trailer here), I asked McKay about Simon's role and what sort of input Tolkien's grandson may have had on the direction of these upcoming episodes. After cautioning that he has to remain "slightly cagey" and avoid going into specifics, McKay responded:

"I would say that we have the benefit of working with great people who know Tolkien and the lore and the literature, in addition to all these amazing craftspeople in the film world. And Simon's one of those people who, it's like phone a friend. We are in a constant dialogue with him. He'll push on things, we'll push back [...] we're very lucky to work with Simon. He's a real asset to the show."

Patrick McKay's characterization of a give-and-take, back-and-forth dialogue with Simon Tolkien will almost certainly raise eyebrows among fans. It's worth noting that, for a series built entirely upon select passages from J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Lord of the Rings" books and a series of appendices that mostly amount to Cliff's Notes (summarizing eons of lore from the First and Second Ages of Middle-earth), "The Rings of Power" was always going to step outside the text in order to fill in storytelling gaps. This includes introducing wholly original characters like the Elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), compressing the sprawling timeline to fit the needs of a television show, and plenty more.

But, while the response to adaptation choices in "The Rings of Power" has been immediate and vocal, it's fair to say it's been quite disproportionate, as well. After all, Peter Jackson's acclaimed "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy (along with his much more divisive "The Hobbit" movies) did the exact same thing. The prologue of "The Fellowship of the Ring," depicting events that "The Rings of Power" will eventually catch up to, took almost a decade of in-world history and smashed it into a single epic battle. Elsewhere, entire characters were made up, other established fan-favorites were rendered almost unrecognizable compared to their book counterparts, and each subsequent movie strayed further and further from the source material.

Naturally, Season 3 will introduce yet more changes (including an explanation behind everyone's favorite MIA hero, Jamie Campbell Bower's Celeborn). But, remember, the ever-protective Tolkien Estate signed off on this series and, well, Tolkien's books are right there. "The Rings of Power" Season 3 debuts November 11, 2026 on Prime Video, and so far, critics are united in their reactions.

#3583. Benito Skinner’s ‘Overcompensating’ Returns for Season 2: More Laughs, More Sex, More Gay

It’s been a year and a half since the first season of Benito Skinner’s Prime Video comedy series, Overcompensating, debuted, and a lot has changed for him in that time. For one, Skinner—also known as Benny Drama, his online alter ego—is blond now. It’s a change he says may be permanent or perhaps semipermanent. “It’s how I see myself—as a blond,” he tells me over Zoom. “So we’re going to keep going with it for a sec.”

But Skinner has transformed in much less superficial ways since the launch of his hit Amazon series, which is based on his experiences coming out as gay as a Georgetown undergrad. Equal parts raunchy and heartwarming, the first season follows Benny (Skinner), a closeted former high school football player who attempts to navigate the chaos of college, where he forms an unlikely bond with a fellow student named Carmen (Wally Baram).

Skinner shares that making the second installment of the series was “way more fluid, way less stressed.” As it should have been. The first season was a popular hit for the streamer (it has a 93% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes), hard-launching Skinner as an exciting new voice plucked from the internet and ready for prime time.

Benny and Carmen begin the season as enemies.

The second season, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on February 17, 2027, expands the world he created with new storylines for the supporting characters—and bigger stakes for Benny as he comes into his own with his sexuality. Benny navigates not only coming out to his sister, Grace (Mary Beth Barone), and his parents (Connie Britton and Kyle MacLachlan), but also his own sexual exploration—and all the awkwardness that comes with it.

So much of what made the first season a hit—the awkward comedy, the silly themed parties, the talking Megan Fox poster—returns, but this time many of the characters grapple with deeper issues. Yet Skinner felt lighter making the show this time around. “I think in season one, Benny is that stressed, so that kind of worked,” he says. “But in this one, we’re having more fun. He has some joy, so we can loosen up a little bit.”

Connie Britton, center, reprises her role as Benny's mom.

After Overcompensating premiered, Skinner was approached, he says, by “a few gays” who told him, “I thought it’d be gayer, the show.” He promises that the second season delivers just that: “We’re creeping out of the closet,” says Skinner.

In the first season, Benny is trying to find his place on campus while constantly living in fear that the people around him will discover he’s gay. He falls for a dashing British classmate named Miles (Rish Shah), only to find out he is straight and has kissed Carmen. The season ends with Carmen revealing that she has also slept with Grace’s boyfriend, Peter (Adam DiMarco), and in the final moments, Carmen accidentally lets slip in front of Grace that Benny is gay.

Skinner and Lukas Gage reunite in season two.

In the upcoming season, Benny heads back home with his sister for the start of Christmas break, struggling because he hasn’t yet come out to his family. “If season one was about friends, I think this season is about family, and trying to reintroduce yourself to your parents after starting to become yourself,” says Skinner. The way his father finds out about it makes for an especially tense moment, and Benny goes to great lengths (like joining the crew team) to mend that bond with his dad. “That relationship between gay men and father, I think, is always fraught and confusing,” he says. “I just wanted to make it as honest as possible.”

At the start of the new season, Benny and Carmen are at odds; Grace and her boyfriend, Peter, have broken up; and many of the characters are exploring those feelings of loneliness that can crop up in college. A handful of exciting new faces also join this season. Australian actor Aisha Dee (The Bold Type) plays a new student who becomes an instant It girl on campus. AnnaSophia Robb (The Carrie Diaries) joins as an intense coxswain (the one who does the yelling) on the crew team. And Tony-nominated stage actor Tom Francis (Sunset Boulevard) plays the captain of the team, serving as Benny’s newest love interest.

Peter (Adam DiMarco) is looking for his path forward.

For Skinner, the second season is about capturing the ups and downs of coming out. It’s not just one reveal and then you’re out of the closet and everything is better. “I get to be even more specific about coming out and also tell a story that I think I haven’t seen yet done in this way, which is the complication of coming out—how you can take 10 steps forward, a hundred steps back,” he says.

Benny joins the crew team, where he meets a new love interest (Tom Francis).

There’s also a lot more sex. “There are a couple scenes that are definitely going to be off-limits for the family,” Skinner says. But of course, in Overcompensating, the sex scenes aren’t always smooth sailing. “I think our show is about trying to be sexy and then it going wrong, or feeling like you start to come into yourself but you get made a fool,” he says.

Skinner adds the title of executive music producer to his résumé this season. “It feels like a return to my radio-DJ roots, and that feels right,” he says. There’s more Britney Spears and Charli xcx (who appeared in a cameo last season), and he wanted the show’s music to remain an important part of the world. He even wrote a letter to Coldplay when he wanted to use the band’s song “Fix You” in this new season. “I love doing the letters to these guys because I’m like, So is Chris Martin reading this? Is this sent by owl? What’s the vibe?” he says with a smile.

Overcompensating’s return will come almost two years after its debut, and Skinner, who says he always plans to keep this story set in the characters’ college years, wants to make the wait a little shorter next time. “I apologize to everyone that it took a while,” he says. “TV takes a long time, so I’m trying to go faster, but daddy has to write it.”

“I don’t want any of these characters to feel like we’re pandering to maybe what we think the internet will want,” says Skinner of crafting the second installment after a hit first season.

“What I wanted to do is surprise people with where we took it,” says Skinner of the new season, “and have them be like, ‘Oh, this isn’t what I asked for, but it is something kind of delicious and new.’”

#3582. The Best New Video Games of 2026 (So Far)

One last look at the year's best before GOTY deliberations begin

It's hard to believe, but 2026 is winding down. Well, maybe that's easy to believe if you remember that Code Vein 2 and Highguard kicked off the year in January, and both now feel like ancient history. We're getting closer to putting together our year-end game of the year come December, but there's still a long road until then. We're still catching up on a busy year of games, from big-budget hits to indie hidden gems. Oh, and there's still this little game called Grand Theft Auto 6 to consider.

While you'll have to wait for our final list to see where recent releases like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Phantom Blade Zero will land on our final list, as we're still digesting them, these are just some of the games that are on our mind heading into the home stretch. Mind that this list is not ranked. It is ordered reverse-chronologically.

How we pick the best games of 2026. For consideration, a game has to be out for at least three weeks, so we know it's not just a flash in the pan. We also select games that are beloved not just by their reviewer but also widely across the team. We'll update this article periodically throughout 2026.

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

It's 2026 and pod racing is cool again thanks to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Fuse Games' impressive debut is the second coming of Burnout, sending you racing across the galaxy in junky vehicles that are ready to explode at a moment's notice. That makes for fast, thrilling races filled with glorious slo-mo explosions. Oli Welsh, Polygon's resident racing game aficionado, called it the "most original and exciting racing game in a generation" in his review, which is very high praise. All of that gives us enough reason to love it even before factoring in the game's breakout star, Biddy Blas.

For a certain kind of RPG sicko, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave might be the most impressive game Nintendo has ever made. The sprawling tactics game, which takes well over 100 hours to complete, ties four wild storylines together into one wartime epic. Though it requires a lot of patience from players, those who click with it have discovered an excellent RPG filled with the series' most weird and wonderful characters to date. "Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is dazzling as much for the scope of its ambition as for how adroitly developer Intelligent Systems executes that vision," Josh Broadwell wrote in his glowing review. "It's a gigantic turn-based tactics game that, despite a few missteps, carries itself with grace and purpose."

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

There's a world where The Blood of Dawnwalker was little more than a pale imitation of The Witcher. Thankfully, we don't live in that timeline. Instead, Rebel Wolves' debut RPG is a bold riff on CD Projekt Red's formula, drenching it in blood and innovation. The star of the show is its controversial timer, which forces you to spend time wisely as you prepare to save Coen's family from vampires. While it's stressing some players out, Polygon's Marloes Valentina Stella praised the system for pushing players to use their time meaningfully. "Usually, when I play an open-world RPG, I follow the main story for an hour at most, and then I forget all about it while I'm off doing a bazillion other things," she wrote in her review. "But in Dawnwalker, I've met Coen's family, I've felt his despair, and I've only got 30 days to save them. Knowing every time segment brings me closer to their moment of doom, every action I take must bring me closer to victory."

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Star Wars: Zero Company was a bit of a shocker when it launched in August as one of the best reviewed Star Wars games of all time. In retrospect, that response should have been obvious from the outset. Created by veterans of the XCOM series, Zero Company took everything that made Firaxis' genre-defining tactics game great and combined that with the rich lore of the Star Wars universe. It was a match made in heaven, something that Polygon's Elijah Gonzalez praised in his review. "On top of delivering the XCOM-lite thrills of playing as a field commander, it nails the specifics of this particular time in the Star Wars mythos," he wrote. "Unlike the halcyon image of a 'more civilized age' promised by Ben Kenobi, we see the Republic as the messy, flawed institution it was to the average person not living in a Jedi temple on Coruscant."

Big Walk is unforgettable. Untitled Goose Game developer House House evokes the puzzle-solving exploration of Myst in a brilliant co-op adventure that's all about hanging out with your best pals. It looks silly, what with its goofball characters, but Big Walk's trick is that it's a surprisingly emotional journey built to sharpen your communication skills with the people you love. It all pays off in an astounding ending sequence that you have to experience to truly understand. If you can't find a crew to play with but want to know more, you can read Polygon's journal-like review that chronicles our playthrough from three perspectives.

Where to play: PS5, Switch 2, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

There was never any doubt that Denshattack! would be a special game. Right from its debut trailer, the indie about a kickflipping train felt like a jolt of Dreamcast energy. What's so impressive about the final game, though, is that it's not just a one-trick gimmick. Developer Undercoders went all out to build a varied platformer that combines the best elements of Sonic the Hedgehog, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, and Jet Set Radio. As I wrote in my review: "Denshattack! remembers that reinvention is what made games of the time so radical, and it isn’t afraid to totally jump the shark in creating an over-the-top variation of an old extreme sports formula that’s just ridiculous enough to work."

Where to play: PS5, Switch, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Mina the Hollower, Yacht Club Games’ ode to the top-down Zelda era, pulls off something remarkable. Rather than settling for easy Game Boy nostalgia, it reinvents a retro adventure format in so many notable ways. Its perfectly-implemented Bloodborne inspiration, for instance, could have felt forced and frustrating in less capable hands, but Yacht Club pulls it off with finesse by understanding where 40 years of video game history naturally intersects. “FromSoftware’s games draw on foundational game design principles that powered ‘80s adventure games,” I wrote in my review. “Mina the Hollower is just the link between worlds.”

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

It’s been a long time since we’ve gotten a great James Bond video game, but IO Interactive has ended a long drought in spectacular fashion. 007 First Light nails the assignment, combining the cinematic highs of Uncharted with Hitman’s immersive sim brilliance. That’s all anchored by Patrick Gibson’s strong take on a young Bond that sells First Light’s origin story premise. “He's exactly as you'd expect a younger, bright-eyed, bushy-tailed Bond to be,” Ford James wrote in his review. “Far more talkative than his jaded, older self, but with the perfect amount of defiance for authority, back-chat, and quick-wittedness, alongside enviable levels of suavity.”

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Zero Parades: For Dead Spies is the kind of game you need a little distance from to appreciate. Haunted by the drama surrounding its developer, Disco Elysium studio ZA/UM, it was initially too easy to write off the spy RPG as a hollow copy. In actuality, Zero Parades tells a remarkable story about a career screw-up embarking on an apology tour. "You have to go through the work of earnestly apologizing to an old crewmate, knowing the entire time that Cascade’s end goal is roping them into another suicide mission that she can’t get a handle on," I wrote in my review this spring. "Forgiveness is always just out of reach, because you’re ultimately in a line of work that forces you to backstab your colleagues to survive."

The Forza Horizon series is about as reliable as it gets in gaming. Playground Games' open-world racing games never cease to impress, even if they're not trying to do anything particularly new. That's true for Forza Horizon 6, which doesn't mess with an excellent formula. "Forza Horizon 6 is excellent, because of course it is," Oli Welsh wrote in his review. "It's polished, welcoming, huge, sensible, gorgeous, flexible, intense, relaxing, lavish, detailed, tasteful, dorky, glamorous, and upbeat, because of course it is." Even if it's more of the same, the gorgeous Japanese scenery and some much-needed progression tweaks make Forza Horizon 6 another victory for a series that's all gas, no brakes.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3581. 10 Best Horror Movie Remakes Of The 21st Century, Ranked

While some folks may still understandably bristle at the idea of horror movies getting the remake treatment, there have been undeniably great ones in recent history. Following celebrated 20th century horror remakes like "Invasion of the Body Snatchers" and "The Thing," the 21st century has its own fair share of memorable chillers. Whether it's Americanized takes on foreign films or updates of longstanding fan-favorites, some of the best horror movies of the 21st century are remakes. With that in mind, we're taking a look at some of the entertaining scary movie remakes released in 2000 and beyond.

A few caveats to keep in mind for this particular list is that remakes that reuse a title but feature a vastly different story, like 2020's excellent "The Invisible Man," are omitted. Other notably enjoyable movies not included here are 2017's "It" and 2013's "Evil Dead," which we would normally recommend but not for the purposes of this list. "It" was previously adapted as a television miniseries, not as a movie, while "Evil Dead" offers a broad retelling, but its post-credits scene suggests it's in the same universe.

All right, here are the 10 best horror movie remakes of the 21st century ranked, each providing a fresh take on an established classic.

There is a surprising number of horror movies set around Valentine's Day, and one of the best horror movies featuring the amorous holiday is the 1981 slasher flick "My Bloody Valentine." This was then remade in 2009 to take advantage of the latest resurgence in 3D filmmaking for American audiences with "My Bloody Valentine 3D." The movie features a small-town community terrorized by a serial killer dressed as a miner linked to a mining tragedy over a decade prior. At the center of this mounting murder mystery is Sheriff Axel Palmer (Kerr Smith) and his old friend Tom Hanniger (Jensen Ackles).

3D gimmickry aside, or maybe partially because of it, "My Bloody Valentine 3D" is a lot of fun. Like its '80s source material, the movie leans into the inherent viciousness of its premise, loading its kills with gratuitous gore and imbuing the character dynamics with heightened melodrama. But the movie also subverts expectations on how this particular version of the story is going to unfold, right down to its climactic confrontation. A deliberately trashy slasher thriller ride, "My Bloody Valentine 3D" hits all the right notes as it retells its tale of small-town carnage.

The 1980 slasher movie "Maniac" is a nasty piece of work, following the perspective of its killer Frank Zito, played by Joe Spinell, who also co-wrote the film. Elijah Wood revisited this concept over 30 years later for the 2012 remake of the same name, starring as Zito. Relocating the gruesome spectacle to Los Angeles, compared to the original's New York City, the remake also unfolds from a first-person perspective. This iteration of Zito also scalps women that encounters, befriending a woman named Anna, played by Nora Arnezeder in the remake, which affects his murderous habit.

With its inventively immersive perspective, the 2012 "Maniac" is one of the most stylishly shot movies on this list. Even with this modern update, the movie doesn't avoid just how sadistic the stakes truly are, with the kills still unrelentingly brutal. Wood really holds the whole thing together, with his wide-eyed performance keeping the audience captivated as he turns lethal on a dime. Bringing a truly twisted take on its already cruel source material, "Maniac" takes slasher bloodletting into an arthouse direction.

This may be a divisive inclusion, given how far it deviates from the original, but some would contend that the 2018 "Suspiria" is the best horror remake ever made. Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino takes the broad premise of the 1977 classic by Dario Argento, with American student Susie Bannion (Dakota Johnson) enrolling in a West German dance academy. As increasingly disturbing and violent phenomena occur around the school, it's revealed that the academy is a front for a coven of witches. This sinister ensemble is headed by Mother Helena Markos (Tilda Swinton), who targets Susie for a fiendish ritual in the inner bowels of the school.

While some argue that the 2018 "Suspiria" remake is better than the original, I won't personally go that far. What I do appreciate is that Guadagnino's version looks and feels markedly different from Argento's film, going with a bleaker color palette and Cold War tension. The movie also does a great job in subverting expectations for those familiar with the original movie, particularly with its sanguine climax. Bringing its own kind of dreary atmosphere rather than Argento's vibrant vision, the 2018 "Suspiria" offers a distinctly entertaining thrill.

Before reimaginings of "Halloween" or "Friday the 13th," it was 2003's "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" that ushered in the slasher remake craze. Directed by Marcus Nispel and produced by Michael Bay, the movie is set in 1973, reflecting its 1974 source material, and it maintains the same basic premise. Protagonist Erin Hardesty (Jessica Biel) is part of a friend group driving through Texas that has a horrific encounter with a hitchhiker. This leads them to the Hewitt family, a cannibalistic clan that includes the masked chainsaw-wielding madman Leatherface (Andrew Bryniarski).

The 2003 "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" brings a slightly more stylish approach to its story, while retaining how mean and nasty the whole thing is. The scariest scenes capitalize on how stealthy Leatherface is, and the remake doubles down on the gore that was only implied in the original. Of all the horror properties remade by Bay's Platinum Dunes, it stands clearly as the best, keeping things hot, tense, and dark as it proceeds. After slashers saw a resurgence with "Scream," "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre" reminded audiences how vicious the genre could be and was all the better for it.

It may have seemed too early to remake the 2022 Dutch-Danish thriller "Speak No Evil" a mere two years later, but the 2024 version quelled all doubts about its efficacy. Written and directed by James Watkins, the remake follows an American family vacationing in Europe who befriend a British family. Accepting an invitation to stay at their remote English home, the Americans grow increasingly uncomfortable with their hosts' behavior. As the ensemble realizes the truth about their devious hosts, they try to escape from their ordeal in one piece.

"Speak No Evil" is an Americanized horror remake that actually works, in contrast to forgettable fare like "Pulse" or "The Uninvited." A big part of that success is Watkins not slavishly sticking to the source material, while staying true to the spirit of the original version. James McAvoy, playing the duplicitous host masterminding this getaway from hell is in fine form as always, having previously proved his horror bonafides in "Split." Considerably less bleak than the original version, the "Speak No Evil" remake doesn't compromise its brutal stakes as it offers its own take on the story.

Looking back, Zack Snyder's best film is his 2004 "Dawn of the Dead" remake, and it's not even close. Whereas the 1978 original by George A. Romero took place with the zombie apocalypse underway, the remake opens with the start of undead ravenously rising. This brutally intense beginning sets the tone for the rest of the movie, complete with zombies that chase down their prey at a full sprint. Like the original, the movie centers on a small group of survivors who take shelter in a shopping mall, barricading themselves from the undead amassing outside.

The 2004 "Dawn of the Dead" takes its scares seriously, though it does offer its own moments of dark humor with a larger ensemble of main characters. Snyder brings a saturated cinematography to the action, giving the movie a striking visual style that sets it apart from the original and reflects its contemporary aesthetics. But this all takes a backseat to how pulse-poundingly intense the whole ride is, starting and ending particularly strong. The "Dawn of the Dead" remake feels tougher and meaner than Romero's original, setting the stage for "The Walking Dead" to unleash a resurgence in zombie fiction.

Before "The Lost Boys," there was "Fright Night" as a classic '80s teen vampire flick that gave audiences a bloody good time. The 1985 movie received a remake by Disney, of all studios, in 2011, retelling the story of geeky teenager Charley Brewster (Anton Yelchin) getting a vampire as a nextdoor neighbor. This charming bloodsucker, Jerry (Colin Farrell), realizes Charley has learned his secret and targets the teen as he turns more and more members of the community into his undead ranks. Desperate, Charley recruits Las Vegas magician Peter Vincent (David Tennant) to help him vanquish the vampire and save his victims.

While it doesn't have the same campy charm as the 1985 original, the 2011 "Fright Night" is a surprisingly good remake. A lot of this comes from the strength of its main cast, including Yelchin, Tennant, and Imogen Poots as Charley's love interest Amy Peterson. But the real standout is Colin Farrell as an all-time great horror villain, both smolderingly sexy and bringing plenty of monstrous menace. Smartly constructed and repurposed to appeal to modern audiences, the "Fright Night" remake is a solidly sanguine take on the story.

The 1998 Japanese horror movie "Ringu" was remade for American audiences as "The Ring" in 2002 by a pre "Pirates of the Caribbean" Gore Verbinski. The movie follows journalist Rachel Keller (Naomi Watts) who learns about a cursed video tape that mysteriously kills anyone who watches it seven days after a viewing. When both Rachel and her young son Aidan (David Dorfman) watch the tape, they have to find a way to be spared of the curse before it's too late. This leads Rachel to launch an exhaustive investigation into the history of the tape and the haunting figure who appears in its footage.

Over 20 years after debut, "The Ring" has evolved into a horror masterpiece that's arguably better than its Japanese source material. Verbinski's American version handles its dramatic scenes more effectively, and Watts is phenomenal in her lead performance. The 2002 movie also provides its own terrifying scares and explores the moral consequences of escaping the central curse on a deeper level than Hideo Nakata's original. Starting a wave of American remakes of Japanese horror movies, none did this cultural transposition better than "The Ring."

Before he helmed "The Batman," filmmaker Matt Reeves crafted his own version of the Swedish horror movie "Let the Right One In." Retitled "Let Me In," the 2010 movie offers its own retelling of Owen (Kodi Smit-McPhee), an ostracized boy in 1983 New Mexico, befriending a vampire. After meeting Abby (Chloë Grace Moretz), Owen realizes that she's a vampire, but he quickly forges a friendship with her that develops into something more. This young romance is challenged by the community discovering Abby's growing body count, while Owen's bullies escalate their harassment.

Though it retains the narrative broad strokes, Matt Reeves avoids making a copy-paste remake with "Let Me In." To really distinguish his version, Reeves leans into the aesthetics and sensibilities of Reagan-era America, complete with a memorable television broadcast by Reagan himself. That added cultural context goes a long way in imbuing the 2010 movie with its own personality, while still bringing plenty of vampiric action. Punctuating its coming-of-age romance with gruesome scares, "Let Me In" respects its source material while making its tale distinctly American.

In remaking the 1922 silent film masterpiece "Nosferatu," filmmaker Robert Eggers dug up his lifelong love of vampires for his 2024 version. The movie reframes Ellen Hutter (Lily-Rose Depp) as someone targeted by the vampiric Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård) since she was a little girl in 19th century Germany. Years later, Ellen's husband Thomas (Nicholas Hoult) meets Orlok at his Transylvanian home to sell him property in his hometown before learning his client is a vampire. Orlok brings death and pestilence with him to Germany, prompting Ellen to resort to desperate means to save her community from this undead terror.

Robert Eggers resurrects "Nosferatu" as a scary fever dream, significantly dialing up the sensual themes to the story. This approach is underscored and elevated by Eggers' penchant for striking art design, with the 2024 remake being his most visually sumptuous production to date. While everyone in the cast does a stellar job, including Depp and Skarsgård, it's Eggers' usual collaborator Willem Dafoe who steals every scene that he's in. Remaking "Nosferatu" is always a tall order, but Eggers proved himself more than ready for the task, while including his usual themes into this retelling.

Robert Downey Jr. has a habit of stealing the spotlight, and apparently, he has also stolen a Marvel Cinematic Universe record from one of his oldest co-stars. With Avengers: Doomsday hitting the 2026 movie calendar and bringing the former Iron Man actor back as Doctor Doom, Paul Bettany has lost something he briefly had all to himself. Judging by his reaction, he's taking it about as well as you'd expect from the man who used to live inside Tony Stark's computers.

Bettany, who is back playing Vision in the series VisionQuest, streaming with a Disney+ subscription, was recently asked about Downey's return during an interview with BBC Radio 1's Ali Plumb, who posted a clip of his interview to his Instagram. The actor pointed out that after Downey's exit in Avengers: Endgame, he could claim to be the MCU's longest-serving performer. Then Marvel decided to bring back his old boss. As Bettany joked in the video below, he said his former Avengers pal was stealing his “legacy.”

I love that he's treating this like yet another indignity Tony Stark has inflicted on him. Honestly, if you've spent nearly two decades working within the MCU, you deserve at least a little time to enjoy being the franchise's longest-serving employee. Unfortunately, Downey has apparently returned to collect his old parking space, too. As he hilariously put it:

He stole my legacy, as he has stolen so many other things from me. Maybe I still outlast him. We'll see.

The funny thing is that Bettany was there from the beginning. When 2008's Iron Man kicked off the MCU, the British actor voiced J.A.R.V.I.S., the artificially intelligent assistant helping Tony build suits, monitor threats and occasionally deliver a perfectly timed sarcastic comment. He didn't even have to show his face to become one of the franchise's most familiar performers.

Then, in 2015, Avengers: Age of Ultron gave him an actual body as Vision. Since then, Bettany has played the synthezoid across several Marvel movies as well as the TV show WandaVision and its aforementioned spinoff series, VisionQuest. That's an impressive career for someone who originally signed up to record a disembodied computer voice.

Downey, of course, was also there in 2008. He headlined Iron Man and helped turn Marvel into a box-office juggernaut before Tony's death in 2019's Endgame. Bettany kept appearing in new MCU projects after that, which gave him a brief moment atop the seniority chart. But with Downey officially playing Victor von Doom in December's Doomsday, the two actors will once again share a franchise history stretching back to the same first movie. So I wouldn't exactly call this a formal record being smashed. It's Bettany's wonderfully petty description of losing an exclusive bragging right.

And I hope their friendly rivalry continues. Bettany has previously spoken about how meaningful Vision has become to fans, especially those who identify with the character's struggle to belong. The actor's own MCU future remains open after VisionQuest, and he hasn't been officially confirmed for Doomsday. So, for the moment, his next opportunity to outlast Downey is still anybody's guess.

As for Downey, I'm curious to see how Marvel handles the actor who helped establish its cinematic universe now playing one of its most dangerous villains. Doomsday arrives on December 18 as part of the slate of upcoming new superhero movies, with Avengers: Secret Wars scheduled for the 2027 release calendar.

I'm rooting for Bettany to reclaim his title eventually, if only because I want to hear how he delivers the news. After all these years as J.A.R.V.I.S. and Vision, surely the man deserves to win one argument with Tony Stark.

#3578. Before Batman: The Killing Joke, Legendary Comic Writer Alan Moore Wrote A Clayface Story

Ah, the 1980s, when a not-yet-broken-by-the-comics-industry Alan Moore would still write as work for hire on superhero comics. In 1986, Moore wrote "Whatever Happened To The Man of Tomorrow?" and imagined a hypothetical ending for the Superman mythos.

The previous year, Moore contributed three Richard Corben-drawn pages to the exquisite corpse comic "Heroes for Hope: Starring the X-Men." Moore depicts the then-reformed Magneto experiencing a bleak fantasy of a ruined world where his Brotherhood of Evil Mutants stands triumphant, albeit on a mountain of corpses.

Then there's 1988's "The Killing Joke," the infamous origin (maybe) for the Joker. It's one of the most famous and influential Batman stories ever. "Batman" and "Batman Returns" director Tim Burton has said, "['The Killing Joke' is] the first comic I've ever loved." But many hate it for a pivotal sequence where the Joker shoots, strips, and disables Barbara Gordon.

Moore has praised Brian Bolland's artwork but has voiced regrets about writing the comic. "I think ['The Killing Joke'] put far too much melodramatic weight upon a character that was never designed to carry it. It was too nasty, it was too physically violent," Moore has said, feeling it spawned the "regrettable trend" of "grimness and psychosis" in superhero comics.

Previously, in 1987, Moore wrote a story about a different Batman villain: Clayface. "Mortal Clay," drawn by artist George Freeman, was published in "Batman Annual" #11. The issue (advertised as "Villains In Love!") includes two stories: "Love Bird," a backup by Max Allan Collins and Norm Breyfogle, about the Penguin attempting to reform, and "Mortal Clay," about Clayface's obsessive romance with ... a department store mannequin. It's got the flowery prose and super-villainous psychological depth of "The Killing Joke" without the "nastiness" that makes that story a classic in most people's eyes (but not Moore's).

"Mortal Clay" is not about Matt Hagen, the character featured in the DC Universe's "Clayface" movie (played by Tom Rhys Harries). In the "Batman" comics, there have been many Clayfaces. "Mortal Clay" is about the third one, Preston Payne, who's distinguished by his wearing a glass helmet containment suit.

Clayface III debuted in "Detective Comics" #478-479 by Len Wein and Marshall Rogers. Preston Payne had the hormone disorder acromegaly. To cure his condition, he stole a sample of Matt Hagen's blood, hoping Clayface's shapeshifting would transfer over to him. Instead, he not only became a mud monster like Hagen but one with a touch that dissolves living flesh (hence his containment suit).

Payne is also delusional. He dotes on his girlfriend, Helena, even rushing back into his burning hideout to save her. Except "Helena" is actually a wax museum figurine, because Payne can only touch inanimate matter. During these issues, Batman is reeling from his girlfriend Silver St. Cloud leaving him, so a romantic villain makes for a compelling foil.

Clayface's dark romantic spirit carries over into "Mortal Clay." Searching Gotham City, Clayface rediscovers "Helena" (really, a department store mannequin). He embraces her like a lover and hides himself in the mall so at night, he and Helena can "live" as man and wife.

"Mortal Clay" is narrated entirely by Preston, with a clear dissonance between what his warped mind claims and what the more objective images of the comic show. Later in his narration, he claims men close their eyes when they kiss because they're afraid they won't see love in their partner's eyes staring back. Maybe that's one reason why men like Preston prefer a "woman" who is literally just a pretty object, incapable of speech or thought.

"Mortal Clay" explores the loneliness that Clayface's poisonous touch brings. Payne embraces his delusions because that's the only "love" possible for him. The way Clayface anthropomorphizes Helena, though, leads to jealousy and ruin. He thinks Helena is "cheating" on him when she's used as a lingerie standee, or when a night guard steals a scarf off her display for his own wife — cue Clayface melting him. Once Batman shows up to investigate the murder, Payne concludes the Dark Knight is Helena's gentleman caller. Batman, for his part, recognizes what's happening and pleads: "Preston ... let me help."

"Mortal Clay" ends with Clayface sitting in Arkham Asylum with Helena. Payne drinks beer, watches TV, and resents his "wife" — a portrait of a marriage. In a closing line of beautiful dramatic irony, Payne smirks and narrates: "One day I shall be free [of Helena]. After all, she can't live forever."

"The Killing Joke" also ends with Batman extending his hand and offering to help a nemesis. The Joker rejects it, not spitefully but earnestly, because "The Killing Joke" demonstrates Alan Moore's belief there has to be something human that drives the Joker. ("Dark Knight Returns" author Frank Miller, who feels the Joker is "evil incarnate," claims he and Moore once had an hours-long disagreement about that.)

The best companion piece for "Mortal Clay," though, is Moore and Rick Veitch's "Swamp Thing" #56, or "My Blue Heaven." Stranded on an alien world, Swamp Thing uses his powers to remake a simulacrum of his life on Earth, including a plant puppet of his wife Abby. But Swamp Thing knows he's fooling himself, whereas Clayface deludes himself into genuinely believing Helena is a real person. As "Mortal Clay" shows, not even that ignorance has brought him bliss.

A rainy day, a fireplace, a great book, and 300 pages to go.

Which historical figure do you most identify with?

What is the trait you most deplore in others?

Seven parties in seven days for Maya Angelou’s 70th birthday.

What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery?

If you could change one thing about yourself, what would it be?

To be less judgmental and more confrontational.

Not taking a year off after ending The Oprah Show and jumping right into runninga network.

All-time? Filming The Color Purple in 1985, hosting the Legends Ball for African American She-roes, and Christmas Kindness 2002, where we surprised thousands of kids throughout South Africa with gifts.

What Glinda the Good Witch said: “You’ve always had the power.”

What do you dislike most about your appearance?

What or who is the greatest love of your life?

The Oprah Show, and all 21 dogs I’ve had throughout my life, who’ve taught me so much about living and dying.

Chewing gum—and people who chew with their mouths open, showing the gum. Ugh!

Creating spaces where people could see themselves more clearly and recognize the best of who they are.

If you were to die and come back as a person or thing, what do you think it would be?

My first-edition Pulitzer Prize books, dating back to 1918; slave rosters with the names and ages of each enslaved person in the household; and six charcoal drawings Nelson Mandela drew from prison. He called me into his office and gave them to me by hand.

Ordinary folks who do extraordinary things: what author Dacher Keltner calls acts of moral beauty.

#3576. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

As of late, 90 Day Fiancé's Sarper Güven has been dipping his toes into the world of stand-up comedy. That venture is apparently proving to be fruitful as well, as he's allegedly making bank, if these latest court filings are to be believed. As Sarper and Shekinah continue to navigate the divorce process following their time on The Last Resort, it's being alleged that he has cleared over six figures from touring over the past year.

The latest news comes from TMZ, which reports that Shekinah is seeking thousands in monthly spousal support. It's a steep sum, even with both coming off the 2026 TV schedule where they netted pay for appearances within the TLC franchise. If these numbers are accurate, however, I'm shocked to say it might be justified.

Per a post on TMZ's Threads account, Shekinah wants $6,189 a month in spousal support, as well as reimbursement for $35,000 in legal fees. She went on to claim in court documents that Sarper's stand-up comedy netted $280,000 on their joint tax returns, with a $180,000 net profit.

I find that number more jaw-dropping than Sarper's body count. Sure, I'd previously written about him selling out comedy shows, but 90 Day Fiancé fans have witnessed a lot of his comedy already. I personally hadn't seen anything on TV that convinced me his stand-up was worth the price of admission, but it would seem some people do!

Shekinah also alleged in the court documents that her own business suffered a net loss of $55,000 due to her closing down the business temporarily to support Sarper on tour. The only thing I can think of is how ironic it is that Sarper might not be on the line for any of this had he signed the prenuptial agreement like she originally requested.

While none have ever presented a full pay stub to see, the general consensus amongst 90 Day stars is that they don't make a ton of money doing the show. To that point, Stephanie Matto alleged she only made a couple thousand dollars per episode. Also, while it's true that not all cast members are paid the same, many of them keep their day jobs in addition to doing the show.

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way Just Hit On Andi And Nigel's Biggest Issue, And I Don't See Them Getting Over It

All this to say, while some reality shows allow their stars enough money that they can live off that alone, that doesn't seem to be the case for 90 Day stars. That makes it even wilder that Sarper has reportedly made so much money from his stand-up comedy work alone, especially when he's playing relatively small venues.

As these divorce proceedings continue, it'll be interesting to see what information may come out as a result. Shekinah and Sarper were on 90 Day Fiancé for many seasons, and I'd be curious to see what, if anything, comes out about the show as they make filings.

Neither of the two is currently on 90 Day Fiancé, but Sarper is rumored to be returning in a future season of The Single Life. As for Shekinah, she's allegedly done appearing on TLC, but we'll see if she follows through on that promise.
