#3560. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: A lot more than touch

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display last week, and it brings some of the biggest changes to the Mac in years. There’s a tandem OLED screen, a significantly lighter design, and the long-awaited addition of touch. Oh, and the Apple logo glows again.

Here’s what it’s like actually using the new MacBook Pro.

In 2016, Apple unveiled an all-new MacBook Pro design that prioritized thinness and portability above almost everything else, kickstarting what proved to be a rocky period for Apple laptops. The thinner, lighter MacBook Pro was marred by the butterfly keyboard, poor thermals, and an overall focus on form over function.

In 2021, Apple righted the ship. It unveiled a completely redesigned MacBook Pro that reversed many of those controversial decisions, bringing back ports, replacing the Touch Bar with a physical function row, and dramatically improving performance with Apple Silicon.

There was a trade-off, though: the MacBook Pro got bigger and noticeably heavier. The smaller model grew from 13 inches and 3.1 pounds to 14 inches and 3.5 pounds, while the 16-inch model went from 4.3 pounds to 4.7 pounds.

At the time, we were all willing to make that compromise. Now, with the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, Apple is once again making its pro laptops lighter — but without sacrificing what made the 2021 redesign so great.

The 14-inch model has dropped from 3.5 pounds to just 3.0 pounds, while the 16-inch model has gone from 4.7 pounds to 4.0 pounds. In fact, both new MacBook Pro models weigh essentially the same as their 2016 counterparts, despite having larger displays, significantly more powerful hardware, and none of the compromises that defined that generation.

Both models are also slightly thinner than before, with the 14-inch model measuring 0.59 inches thick (down from 0.61 inches) and the 16-inch measuring 0.63 inches (down from 0.66 inches).

How did Apple pull this off? The biggest change is the switch from mini-LED to OLED. Because OLED doesn’t require a separate backlight, Apple could make the display assembly significantly thinner and lighter. The company is also using custom on-cell touch technology to integrate touch sensing into the display panel, instead of adding multiple separate layers.

But while the new display technology played a major role, the weight reduction also came from countless other smaller engineering optimizations throughout the machine.

You notice the lighter weight of the new MacBook Pro immediately when you pick it up. My review unit is the 16-inch MacBook Pro, and I’m genuinely surprised at how nice it feels. It’s not light, but it feels less like a tank.

I’ve always used the smaller of the two MacBook Pro models for portability, most recently a 14-inch M4 Pro. The weight of the new 16-inch MacBook Pro has me reconsidering that preference, though. It feels remarkably nice for a laptop with such a large display, and I’ve really enjoyed having the extra screen space without feeling like I’m sacrificing too much portability.

The new MacBook Pro also features slimmer bezels around the display. Apple has eliminated the thicker bottom bezel, and for the first time, all four corners of the display are rounded. It’s a relatively small change, but I think it gives the MacBook Pro a cleaner, more symmetrical look.

And finally: the glowing Apple logo is back. Unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.

The logo’s brightness is still tied to the display brightness, just like it was a decade ago. The higher your display brightness, the brighter the Apple logo on the back. It also factors in your environment’s ambient brightness.

When the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign. Open it up, and it glows. It’s unnecessary, but I’m so thrilled it’s back.

The display is what Apple is most proud of on this new MacBook Pro. After all, the full marketing name is apparently “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.” It doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue, but I think it shows what Apple sees as the big differentiator compared to other MacBook Pro models it still sells.

And rightfully so. The PROLED XDR Display is stunning. It’s a major upgrade over the mini-LED display that Apple debuted in the MacBook Pro back in 2021 (which was no slouch, to be clear). The OLED panel’s color saturation, contrast, and deep blacks are miles better than any other laptop I’ve seen, including Windows PCs with high-end OLED displays.

The viewing angles are also noticeably better, with colors and brightness staying remarkably consistent even when you look at the display from the side.

One downside of the MacBook Pro with mini-LED is blooming. Because the mini-LED display used local dimming zones, there was a subtle halo around bright objects against dark backgrounds. With the OLED display on these new MacBook Pros, every pixel is independently illuminated, so that blooming effect is gone.

If you’re worried about burn-in, Apple says the new MacBook Pros have a revamped display engine that continuously monitors pixel usage, temperature, and other factors. It compensates individual pixels in real time to mitigate burn-in and maintain brightness. We’ll have to wait and see whether this holds true over time, but anecdotally I haven’t noticed any burn-in on my OLED iPad Pro after more than two years.

The improvements on the new MacBook Pro’s display go well beyond simply being OLED. Brightness is another area Apple emphasizes.

In direct sunlight by a window or on the patio, the display gets more than bright enough to remain easily readable. I rarely find myself needing to crank the brightness all the way up.

Those brightness improvements dovetail nicely with another area of emphasis on the new MacBook Pro: reflectivity. The new MacBook Pro’s glossy display has just 1% reflectance, which Apple says is due to two things. First, the OLED panel itself is designed to minimize reflections. It also has a custom antireflective coating that reduces reflections from the cover glass.

My review unit has a standard glossy display, and my previous MacBook Pro was a 14-inch model with nano-texture, so I’ve been paying especially close attention to the differences in reflectivity.

As I write this review, I’m sitting next to a large window that gets a lot of direct light. I’m very impressed with how well this glossy 16-inch MacBook Pro display handles reflections. It’s not, of course, as antireflective as my 14-inch MacBook Pro with nano-texture. But it’s much closer than I expected, and significantly better than my glossy MacBook Air.

I haven’t had a chance to try the nano-texture on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, but Apple says the nano-texture is now “precisely etched into the cover glass,” so it should be even better than before.

All told, the PROLED XDR Display is impressive by every metric, both on paper and in the real world. Whether it’s the core improvements of an OLED panel, improved reflectivity, or higher brightness, you’ll notice the better display from the moment you turn the MacBook Pro on.

There’s something uncanny about using the new touchscreen MacBook Pro for the first time. This is still unmistakably macOS, with the same interface and software controls that we’ve known for years. Except now, you can reach out and touch the screen … and it actually responds.

Apple famously resisted adding touch to the Mac until now. Steve Jobs called the idea of a touchscreen Mac “ergonomically terrible” in 2010.

When Apple announced these touchscreen MacBooks, that clip of Jobs went viral. As usual, Jobs’ comments have more nuance than last week’s social media reaction suggests.

“Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” Jobs said at the time. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.”

A lot has changed since those comments from Jobs, but I don’t think adding touch to the MacBook Pro proves him wrong. The ergonomics of using a touchscreen as the primary input method on a laptop-style device are, in fact, terrible. Your arm does get tired.

The good news, however, is that Apple is very intentionally not trying to make touch the primary interaction method on these new MacBook Pros. It’s clear from both using this touchscreen MacBook Pro and Apple’s own messaging that touch is intended to be a secondary input method. It’s there when you need it or want it, but you can also ignore it completely and never feel like you’re missing out.

So, with that out of the way: what’s it like using a touchscreen MacBook Pro?

Apple has made a variety of small tweaks throughout macOS to accommodate touch input. For example, when macOS detects touch input, items in contextual menus are spaced further apart.

When you long-press on something like an app icon in the Dock, it enlarges and shows you a more spaced-out list of contextual menu items. If you long-press an item in Finder, it lifts up under your finger, and you can drag it or drop it anywhere else.

The classic traffic light window controls also expand after you tap them. The first tap expands the controls without actually activating any of them. Then, tap a second time on the specific control you’re trying to activate. It’s a bit awkward having to tap the same spot twice in a row like that.

These tweaks are all about making macOS dynamically adapt to the fact that your finger is less precise than a pointer. Rather than redesigning macOS around touch, Apple has made the existing interface accommodate it when needed.

You also get all the typical touch gestures. You can pinch to zoom, swipe with four fingers to switch between Spaces or Mission Control, and swipe up to reveal the dock. You can pull to refresh in Safari, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and flick a window to the side to tile it.

Apple has also added automatic video stabilization that compensates for screen movement when you tap the display during a video call. This helps keep your camera feed steady, even when the screen itself wobbles slightly. It seems to work as advertised in my testing.

So far, I’ve found the touchscreen on MacBook Pro to be a “nice-to-have” addition, but not a reinvention of how I use the Mac. I catch myself idly reaching up to scroll a webpage instead of using the trackpad, tapping on the occasional Dock icon, and using pinch-to-zoom in the Photos app.

Touch input is also legitimately useful in places like iPhone Mirroring and the Xcode simulator. I can imagine people who regularly use rendering apps like Blender will find the touchscreen more useful than I do, since my primary job is manipulating text.

One reason I think touch might be less useful, or less important, on a Mac than on a Windows PC is that Apple’s trackpads are simply too good. There’s little reason for me to bother reaching up and using four fingers to swipe between Spaces when I can do it on the beautiful, big, glass trackpad. On a Windows PC with a crappy plastic trackpad? I bet multi-touch interaction is much more appealing on the touchscreen.

There have been a few instances where I just forget this MacBook Pro has a touchscreen until I reach up to flick a piece of lint or dog hair off the screen, and accidentally tap on something.

But I think that’s exactly how it should be. Using the touchscreen is a conscious choice, not a requirement. You can buy this computer and literally never touch the screen, or turn it off entirely via Accessibility in System Settings. For some Mac users, this is probably the most important thing. Apple hasn’t compromised the traditional macOS experience to accommodate touch.

The one thing that hasn’t changed with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is performance. Much like the standard MacBook Pro models unveiled earlier this year, the new PROLED models are available with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned thermal system optimized for the new design, while also maintaining the same performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max we’ve come to expect.

My review unit is the 16-inch M5 Pro configuration with an 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, and 48GB of unified memory. In GeekBench testing, the new MacBook Pro performs virtually the same as the models introduced earlier this year.

In my day-to-day use, I haven’t noticed any differences in performance or thermal behavior compared to my previous MacBook Pro. Admittedly, my workflow of writing, researching, editing photos, and dozens of Safari tabs doesn’t come close to pushing the M5 Pro to its limits. But the new MacBook Pro handles all of that effortlessly, without noticeable heat or fan noise. In fact, I haven’t heard the fans kick in once.

That’s not a definitive test of Apple’s claims about sustained performance, but it’s reassuring that the thinner and lighter design hasn’t introduced any noticeable compromises in my everyday use or in benchmarks.

This makes for an interesting predicament for MacBook Pro shoppers. Rumors say that Apple believes the M7 generation will offer such a dramatic improvement in performance, particularly around AI, that it’s skipping the higher-end M6 chips altogether.

The first M7 chips are expected sometime next year, likely late in the year for the high-end MacBook Pro. This means that if you buy an M5-equipped MacBook Pro right now, you’re buying a computer with a chip that will effectively be two generations behind in less than a year.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are plenty fast, and these MacBook Pros also come with OLED, touch, and other changes mentioned throughout this review. Still, there’s something a little strange about Apple pairing its biggest MacBook Pro redesign in five years with chips that debuted eight months ago, particularly with the next major leap in Apple silicon reportedly on the horizon.

The Dynamic Island comes to the Mac for the first time with the new MacBook Pro. It never made sense to me that Apple added the notch to the MacBook Pro with so little software accommodation. The Dynamic Island finally addresses that, bringing a familiar iPhone experience to the Mac.

Live Activities now show up in the Dynamic Island, along with Now Playing info from apps like Music and Podcasts. For example, clicking (or tapping) the Dynamic Island while Music is playing brings up the mini player for easy access to controls. From the mini player, you can click again to open the full Music app. Live Activities from your iPhone also show up in the Dynamic Island on MacBook Pro, rather than in your menu bar like on other Macs. Spotlight on Mac bounces out of the Dynamic Island.

I’ve very much enjoyed having the Dynamic Island on the Mac. It’s one of my favorite iPhone features, especially for Live Activities. The implementation on the Mac is a great continuation of that experience.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned six-speaker system that delivers 50% deeper bass. The speakers do indeed sound fantastic. Apple also specifically calls out improved speaker tuning when using the MacBook Pro with its lid closed and connected to an external display. In my testing, the difference is noticeable. The speakers sound less muffled and significantly louder.

Apple says battery life is unchanged on the new MacBook Pro models compared to the non-OLED variants.

I haven’t done any scientific battery testing, but anecdotally, my 16-inch M5 Pro model seems on track to match Apple’s claim of up to 17 hours of wireless web browsing.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a fascinating product. It’s both a major evolution of the MacBook Pro and a better version of the same laptop we’ve come to love since its Apple Silicon reinvigoration in 2021.

The addition of touch is getting all the attention, but I think the lighter design is actually the more significant change in day-to-day use. I never expected a 16-inch MacBook Pro to have me reconsidering my longstanding preference for the 14-inch model.

Touch hasn’t fundamentally changed how I use the Mac, but it’s a welcome addition that feels overdue. People reasonably expect to touch their laptop screen and have it respond. Some people will undoubtedly find it more useful than I have, and Apple has done an excellent job integrating it into macOS without compromising the traditional experience.

With or without touch, the PROLED XDR display is a spectacular upgrade, with improvements in brightness, contrast, and reflectivity that you’ll notice every time you open the lid.

These new OLED MacBook Pro models command a $400 premium over the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models Apple is still selling. Those machines are also heavier, lack touchscreens, and miss some of the bells and whistles of the pricier models. Presumably, these two product lines will eventually converge, but right now the MacBook Pro lineup is a little awkward. The 14-inch PROLED model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399.

But that awkward positioning doesn’t take away from the product. This is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve come to love over the last five years. Apple has taken an already excellent laptop and made meaningful improvements to nearly every aspect of the experience. And it just so happens to have a touchscreen now, too.

#3559. Elon Musk’s Cybertruck Is Dumb, Ugly, and Mercifully Dead

In March 2024, a Tesla Cybertruck speeding down Sunset Boulevard slammed head-on into the Beverly Hills Hotel’s iconic entrance sign just before midnight. Passersby winding through the Flats slowed down to watch as Elon Musk’s statue to his own insecurities—the stainless steel embodiment of nuance-free American ego—demolished in front of Hollywood’s unofficial canteen.

Every decade gets the iconography it deserves. At just about the midpoint of the 2020s, ours had arrived, fully formed.

And now the Cybertruck is dead, which is wonderful news. Musk, who’s having a historically bad November, announced late last week that Tesla will be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck around mid-2027, putting an end to the most hated car in America. I was going to call it the most polarizing car in America, but honestly, no one likes this thing. And it’s not entirely due to anti-Elon sentiment: Tesla’s general sales have been relatively steady, going down a bit as Musk went full DOGE mode in 2025 before rebounding in 2026. People like Elon’s cars. They just do not like the Cybertruck.

True, its death has been mourned by some—especially the self-selecting devotees who installed bulletproof glass in their Cybertrucks before shooting them with rifles. These people exist. But mostly, the news has been greeted with a rush of enthusiasm, relief, and, more than anything else, blue-pilled schadenfreude.

Now would be the right moment in the news cycle for an art writer such as myself to make a contrarian argument: that the Cybertruck was secretly a design masterpiece—some kind of neo-Donald Judd breakthrough unleashed ahead of its time.

I am not going to make that argument, because that is not true. Not even close. No one in the future will look back on the Cybertruck as an unheralded art object. It’s The Jetsons for meatheads, a Batmobile for people who secretly root for the Joker. It looks like a birdhouse designed by Zaha Hadid, which I would love to have as a vessel for feeding hungry birds at my (sadly hypothetical) Zaha Hadid house. But I would not want it as a vehicle to park in a driveway. It is a bad car.

And yet, that crashed Cybertruck in front of the Beverly Hills Hotel is seared into my brain, playing on repeat like the most un-subtle Lana Del Rey song ever written. Even beyond that crash, the Cybertruck is the ultimate symbol of this surreal and cruel decade, one that started with a global pandemic and a government suggesting the possibility of a bleach injection as treatment. It’s a decade that wound through four years of a former president denying the lawful election of a current president, only to see that former president return to power. Through it all, we’ve sunk deeper into our collective psychosis—one that’s forced us into rooms with our devices, addicted to social media and artificial intelligence, consuming half-real information and spewing it back out into the world.

It’s a perfect world for the Tesla Cybertruck to define.

The Cybertruck arrived right at the dawn of the decade, in what we can now see as a completely different timeline.

Musk unveiled the car in November 2019 at Tesla’s design studio. Head designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demonstrate the vehicle’s shatterproof glass by hurtling a metal ball at a window at full speed. The window shattered. Great omen! It was also pretty weird that Musk was introduced by a hologram of someone called “Cybergirl,” who people speculated was actually a hologram of Grimes, the pop star Musk was dating at the time.

Plenty of design press fawned over the shiny new thing—“Long live the Cybertruck. See you in the Thunderdome,” wrote Dwell. But Wired wisely asked the opinion of an actual expert: Raphael Zammit, who chairs automobile design at Motor City’s own College for Creative Studies.

“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness! What did Tesla do? What did they do?” he said. “It literally breaks every rule we tell to our students. It’s what we tell them not to do.”

Regardless, the Cybertruck started to infiltrate the cultural atmosphere. It was lampooned on The Simpsons. There were countless memes. It was embraced, very early, by rappers. Weeks after the unveiling, Travis Scott used his personal connections to the Tesla CEO (they did Christmas together with the Kardashian-Jenners) to snag a Cybertruck for his video for “Gang Gang,” a posse cut with the Cactus Jack crew.

Three years later, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, and Tyler, the Creator featured the Cybertruck in their video for “Cash In, Cash Out”—rendered in Claymation. Offset’s video for “Swing My Way” has Anok Yai sitting atop a Cybertruck. Bad Bunny said, “Me monté en la Cybertruck y me acordé de la Montero de los viejos tiempo.” Meek Mill said, “They was doing cyber attacks, so I bought a Cybertruck.”

The cars fascinated artists too. Julia Wachtel’s CyberChrist, on view at Todd Von Ammon’s DC gallery, von ammon co, earlier this year, pictures Jesus Christ pulling an elongated Cybertruck behind him. I recall with great happiness the perverse thrill of Frieda Toranzo Jaeger’s Cybertruck, a painting in her 2022 show at MoMA PS1. These artists were certainly taking a critical eye toward the Cybertruck, but for some art collectors, there was nothing ironic about it. At least, a specific kind of collector. When I arrived at the convention center for Art Basel Miami Beach in 2024, the first full year of Cybertruck distribution, there was a line of Cybertrucks wrapped around the block.

But that’s the thing about the Cybertruck: There was always more supply than demand. Musk initially hoped to sell 250,000 units per year. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, Tesla moved nearly 39,000 of them in 2024, a decent start. In 2025, sales dropped, then dropped again in 2026.

Perhaps the Cybertruck could have endured the ridicule of design experts, car enthusiasts, and aesthetes with even just a whiff of good taste if it weren’t for the massive backlash that accompanied Musk’s move into radical right-wing politics, and his full-throated support of Donald Trump. After his efforts at DOGE resulted in the gutting of USAID and other agencies, along with unprecedented and remorseless mass firings, Cybertrucks started getting vandalized around the country. Some owners tried to protect their weird boxy investments with mea culpa stickers—“I bought this before Elon went crazy,” etc.—but no one believed that, or really cared. The cars got defaced. No one stepped in to intervene. The Cybertrucks deserved it.

There was also a bleaker incident that parallels the Cybertruck at the Beverly Hills Hotel: the dystopian hellscape of the Cybertruck that exploded on the Las Vegas Strip, in front of the Trump International Hotel & Casino. The man responsible for that explosion served in the US Army, and authorities believe he suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound just before the vehicle detonated. The Beverly Hills crash was an accident in which no one was harmed—but the charred, deadly remains of the truck in Las Vegas seemed downright terrifying, a vision of American capitalism and greed that had met its grisly moment.

Perhaps now, with a new era of Washington poised to define the final years of this most delirious of decades, we’ll eventually look back at the Cybertruck with at least some nostalgia for its silliness, its boxy stupidity, its pop culture ubiquity. If it does linger in the annals of history, maybe we’ll think of the Cybertruck as a roadbound folly of the world’s first trillionaire, and a footnote in Musk’s legacy, for better or for worse.

Put it this way: By the time Hollywood studio heads arrived at the Polo Lounge for their Monday power lunches, the mess of the Cybertruck that had crashed at the Beverly Hills Hotel the night before was gone. Almost as if it never happened at all.

#3558. 5 Reasons Why Godzilla Minus Zero Ruled The Box Office

The King of the Monsters is back on top of the box office. Director Takashhi Yamazaki's "Godzilla Minus Zero" stomped into theaters over the weekend and it made quite the impact. Given that "Godzilla Minus One" was officially the first movie in the franchise to win an Oscar, the pressure was on for the sequel. It's safe to say that Yamazaki delivered.

Released by Toho and GKIDS, "Godzilla Minus Zero" opened to $30.5 million domestically to go with $31.4 million internationally for a $61.9 million global debut. That's the biggest opening weekend ever for a live-action foreign-language movie in North America, topping Jet Li's "Hero" ($17.8 million). It's also the biggest global opening for a Japanese "Godzilla" movie. Since we're talking about a 72-year-old franchise, that's pretty darn good.

For context, "Minus One" opened to $11.4 million en route to $114 million worldwide. The fact that the sequel opened nearly three times higher is staggering. Yes, this movie carries a bigger budget, but bigger is relative. It's still believed to be in the $20 million range, which is hard to believe but makes this instantly profitable for all involved.

So, what went right here? How did Toho manage to turn this into a massive breakout sequel? How did Yamazaki manage to live up to such high expectations? We're going to look at the biggest reasons why "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office on its opening weekend. Let's get into it.

Having critics on a movie's side certainly never hurts. Having critics and audiences on a movie's side? That's when good things can really start to happen. And much like "Minus One" before it, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has proved to be a real crowd-pleaser through and through.

The sequel currently holds a stellar 90% critical approval rating to go with an outstanding 96% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. It also earned an A CinemaScore, which bodes very well for word of mouth in the coming weeks. A big opening weekend is one thing, but "Godzilla Minus One" became fall 2023's unexpected box office hero thanks to excellent legs driven by real-world buzz from moviegoers. It looks like something similar is in store this time around, only much bigger.

Takashi Yamazaki's follow-up takes place two years after the events of "Minus One," bringing back much of the same human cast. A new threat in the form of King Ghidorah emerges, plunging Japan into chaos once more, leading to an epic monster bash with Godzilla himself.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai said "Godzilla Minus Zero" is "bigger" and "badder" but "not quite better" in his review. Whether or not one necessarily thinks the sequel is better than its predecessor is a conversation for another time, but it at the very least appears to be satisfying the intended audience. Almost nobody seems to be leaving theaters disappointed. That matters more for the moment than how we, as a society, may ultimately rank these movies in the future.

"Godzilla" has been around as a franchise for more than 70 years. The big lizard is a truly enduring cinematic icon unlike any other. The past few years, in particular though, have been shockingly fruitful. We're truly living in the golden age of "Godzilla." This recent surge in the character's popularity has also brought a lot of new fans on board. In particular, the Japanese movies in the series have been opened up to a much wider audience thanks almost exclusively to "Godzilla Minus One."

This franchise contains multitudes. A lot of people grew up engaging with the Toho movies passively, perhaps seeing something like "Godzilla vs. Mothra" on TV. But "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever because it was, quite frankly, one of the greatest movies in the history of this cherished series. It was too good to be ignored and people who only passively engaged with the previous movies discovered something to love.

"Minus One" opened Western audiences up to Japanese "Godzilla" movies more than ever before. Yes, the MonsterVerse movies like "Godzilla vs. Kong" have been very successful in North America, but engagement with these Japanese-language entries is now happening on another, much larger level. The fact that "Godzilla Minus Zero" made nearly three times what its predecessor did on opening weekend speaks to that.

Come what may in the weeks andmonths ahead, there's no question that this movie's breakout success is a direct result of "Minus One" opening up this corner of the franchise to a much wider audience globally.

IMAX has proved that it's more important to the box office than ever before time and time again in recent years. Hollywood studios literally plan their biggest releases around the availability of those premium format screens because those higher ticket prices add a lot to the bottom line. Movies like Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and "Top Gun: Maverick," among many others, made a great deal of extra cash thanks to IMAX. The same can now be said for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

According to a press release, the sequel opened to $21.3 million worldwide on IMAX screens, representing the biggest IMAX global opening ever for a Japanese film. Even more impressive? IMAX screens delivered around 34% of the movie's global opening on less than 1% of total screens. Toho benefited greatly from those screens this time around.

But that's only part of the equation. "Minus Zero" earned the "must-see in theaters" label, becoming a true cinematic event. IMAX isn't the only game in town as far as premium formats go; 4DX, Cinemark XD, and Dolby Cinema screens were also packed out across North America and the rest of the world. Comparing Dolby Cinema to IMAX and how these formats differ isn't important to this conversation. All of these formats warrant higher ticket prices, which audiences were clearly happy to pay in this particular case. That played a big role in driving the record-breaking opening.

"Godzilla Minus One" benefited greatly from an early November release date, and "Godzilla Minus Zero" has arrived three years later in a similar spot on the calendar. GKIDS and Toho went with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" line of thinking with the scheduling, and it's tough to argue with the results. This was the absolute perfect spot on the calendar for this movie.

There is often a bit of a lull at the box office in early November. There's the post-Halloween horror hangover and studios are generally holding back their biggest, best stuff for the Thanksgiving corridor. "Minus Zero" opened against "The Cat in the Hat," which flopped with $20.5 million, and Angel's "Drummer Boy," which was non-threatening at $9.3 million. Looking ahead, "Ebenezer" may top the box office this upcoming weekend, but it's also going for a very different audience.

A big threat doesn't emerge until "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" on November 20, when "Godzilla" will already be three weekends in. Sure, once Thanksgiving arrives with "Focker In-Law" and Disney's "Hexed" both opening, competition will be more fierce but it's easy to see an R-rated monster movie still serving as solid counterprogramming throughout the entire month.

"Godzilla" has been broadly popular as a franchise ever since its inception. Like any long running franchise though, it's had some peaks and valleys. Right now? It's at an unquestioned peak. So much so that it's easy to make the argument that Godzilla is one of our most important modern movie stars. That may sound silly, but it's no less true.

In the 2020s, few real-life movie stars can compete with the King of the Monsters. Even in 2021 when theaters were on life support, "Godzilla vs. Kong" battled the pandemic and won, proving that blockbuster cinema could still exist. It's arguably one of the most important hits in recent history. That's just the tip of the iceberg though.

We've already mentioned that "Godzilla Minus One" became the biggest Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever, serving as a real shock at the time. Then, just a handful of months later, "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, pulling in more than $570 million worldwide.

"Godzilla x Kong" pushed the MonsterVerse past the $2 billion mark globally as well. We certainly have to give King Kong his flowers, but Godzilla has been remarkably consistent in the 2020s. Even the re-release of "Shin Godzilla" last year outperformed the movie's original 2016 release in North America. The character is more popular on a global scale than he's ever been seven decades after his inception. That can't be denied and it's beyond impressive.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3556. Instagram launches Edits for Mac with multi-track video editing and 4K exports

Instagram users can now download a Mac version of Edits, the company’s free video editing app, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, direct publishing to Instagram, and 4K exports. Here are the details.

Instagram is launching Edits on desktop today, bringing its free video editing app to Mac with a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts that can match those of other video editors.

Like Edits on mobile, Instagram says its desktop counterpart will receive weekly updates and is asking users for feedback to help shape future improvements.

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.

One particularly interesting feature of the new desktop app is the ability to publish videos directly to Instagram, with support for native features such as tagging, location, and trial reels.

Instagram adds that it is expanding Edits to support “multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.”

As for the actual editing tools, Edits for desktop makes basic operations like splitting, cutting, and trimming videos easier, while also offering a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, precise audio waveforms, and advanced color grading tools such as color wheels, curves, and log conversions.

Users can also import their own LUTs and fonts, customize keyboard shortcuts, and access Instagram’s licensed audio library.

Instagram says saved audio and text styles from the mobile app are already available on desktop. However, the ability to seamlessly edit the same project across Mac and mobile is still in development.

Instagram’s desktop Edits app also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages, as well as hundreds of sound and video effects, all for free.

Pixar movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, especially the Toy Story franchise. We were treated to another adventure with everyone's favorite toys when Toy Story 5 hit theaters earlier this year, with the project now streaming with a Disney+ subscription. I've been wondering why that army of Buzz Lightyears spent so much of the film wandering around the woods, and now we finally have some answers behind that narrative choice.

Toy Story 5 reviews were positive, and plenty of folks liked the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears roaming around the woods together. During an interview with Gold Derby, director/writer Andrew Stanton got real about why the squad of Buzz toys spent so much time in the wilderness. As he explained:

We wanted them in the woods because then they wouldn't be constantly bumping into humans. And we just needed a nondescript shortcut to get wherever they're going. But then somebody in my story group drew a Buzz Lightyear petting a bunny, and it was like watching an actor choose something that was instinctual. We all knew that deep down under that tough exterior that Buzz has such a soft heart. And animals can sense when you're kind. And it just made sense that they would get along with cute woodland creatures.

Honestly, this makes a great deal of sense. We all know that toys in the animated franchise play dead whenever humans encounter them, hiding the secret that they're actually alive. So when Toy Story 5 brought in an entire group of new Buzz Lightyears, they had to be put in a setting that allowed the action figures to continue guarding that secret.

Toy Story 5 made fans appreciate Jessie, but the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears was a delightful side plot during the movie's 102-minute runtime. It was heartwarming to see the toys connecting with various animals in the woods, which also served as an A+ reference to Bambi. As the filmmaker went on to share:

And there's something meta about woodland creatures and animation and Bambi, and it just felt like all these roads met at the same time to the degree that when we were putting the scene together and it was cracking us up privately by putting Bambi's ['Love Is a Song'] in there. I said we should look into getting the rights because it's the one time I would be willing to go off script composer-wise, much to Randy Newman's chagrin. But to really sell the joke and to sell the moment, it's just this kind of animation history.

The Toy Story franchise is known for including easter eggs to other Disney projects, so the fact that the fifth movie went full Bambi shouldn't have come as much of surprise. Still, I'm glad that we got some answers about why the Buzz squad was kept in the woods for the majority of the movie.

Toy Story 5 is streaming now on Disney+ as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the House of Mouse moves forward with a sixth installment of the beloved property.

#3554. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Exit Exposes A Bigger Hollywood Problem

James Gunn and Peter Safran are officially out as DC Studios co-heads in what is a major shock to both the industry and fans expecting much more from their still burgeoning DC Universe. The pair were announced as the shepherds of DC's cinematic enterprise back in November 2022. But four years later, their journey has come to a premature end. What comes next is anyone's guess. All we know for sure is that former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham is taking over and that Gunn will still release his "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow."

In fairness, Gunn and Safran's approach seemed ill-advised from the outset. The now shuttered DC Extended Universe, or "Snyderverse" as it was known, went out in 2023 with a string of flops that proved audiences were tired of what Warner Bros. and DC were providing. Instead of starting from scratch, though, Gunn and Safran rebooted the franchise with a few caveats, retaining elements of the previous cinematic universe while jettisoning most of the major characters and storylines. At a time when superhero movies were already starting to lose their box office appeal, it seemed like an odd approach, at the very least.

On the plus side, Gunn was allowed to take big swings by green-lighting projects based on little-known DC characters. That, at a time when popular IP is being mined for all its worth, was refreshing, if risky. Now that he and his DC Studios co-head are gone, however, we'll almost certainly see much less of that and a lot more focus on well-known characters with proven box office appeal. It's a complex and nuanced situation that ultimately leaves DC in a precarious position ... and audiences even more confused and frustrated than they already were.

The Warner Bros. Discovery/Paramount merger became official in October 2026, after which it looked as though James Gunn and Peter Safran were relatively safe in their roles as DC Studios co-heads. David Ellison, CEO of the newly-christened Skydance,  previously seemed to support the pair's vision for the DCU going forward. He even flew to the "Man of Tomorrow" set prior to the merger becoming official, in what appeared to be tacit approval of Gunn's DC roadmap. Alas, it seems Ellison had other plans all along.

At this point, we don't know the details of Gunn and Safran's departure. As we await further information about what Jeremy Latcham has in-store, it seems almost certain he won't be green-lighting shows such as "Creature Commandos," the animated series that Gunn used to kick off his DC Universe, or movies such as the box office flop "Supergirl." Instead, we're likely to see DC double down on its marquee characters: Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman.

On the one hand, that is a real shame, as it reinforces Hollywood's fixation on established IP and suggests filmmakers with more interesting creative visions will be sidelined. On the other, you have to wonder what Gunn and Safran were thinking with these projects based on characters of whom mass audiences had little to no awareness. By all means, make an animated "Creature Commandos" show and talk up your movie based on the "Authority" comics. But maybe save them for after we've gotten over the whole superhero fatigue issue and restored DC's cinematic fortunes?

Ironically enough, former Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav, who appointed James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios co-heads, couldn't get enough of IP. In his first investor conference, he told shareholders that Warner Bros. was "the greatest treasure of global IP," prior to approving a Harry Potter reboot series that surely stands as the most conspicuous symbol of Hollywood's obsession with IP and nostalgia. When Gunn laid out his vision for the DC Universe, he wisely touted "Superman" as the centerpiece of his plans. But he also spoke enthusiastically about projects based on characters nobody outside of comic book fandom had heard of.

Since then, he's overseen some hits: the aforementioned "Superman," the HBO series "Lanterns," and the most recent DC Studios movie, "Clayface." But at the same time, he's overseen "Supergirl" flopping in spectacular fashion, and his animated series "Creature Commandos" didn't make the kind of splash that the DCU needed (despite being well-received by those who watched it). What's more, we've been getting podcasts in which he discusses whether his 2021 film "The Suicide Squad" is canon to the DCU or not. I think this is the sort of stuff that, viewed in hindsight, will seem so obviously misguided.

Meanwhile, the threat of a DC cinematic universe populated by bland, big-budget movies designed to capitalize on audiences' awareness of IP looms. Viewed from any perspective, this is a pretty dire situation that will do nothing to help bring superhero movies back to prominence, and it may even actively hasten their decline. And to think, all we needed was a full DC reset in 2022.

#3553. Avedon Director Ron Howard On Richard Avedon’s “Creative Courage,” and His Favorite Images From 'In the American West'

In his new documentary Avedon, director Ron Howard traces the vivid legacy of the influential photographer Richard Avedon, which premieres November 11 on Netflix. “The subjects he worked with on the commercial side of his career were dazzling and beautiful, and he was so entertaining and expressive in the way that he would shoot them. But I really had no idea how he applied his status, his influence, his access to tell this other kind of story about human beings that was honest, insightful, and more journalistic,” Howard tells Vanity Fair.

The glamorous heights of Avedon’s career were what first caught Howard’s attention. “I became aware of him really in the ’80s. Then it was even his TV commercials, like Brooke Shields [in Calvin Klein ads],” Howard said. Later, he realized a few of his favorite portraits were taken by Avedon. One of these was a portrait of a young Kareem Abdul-Jabbar at a playground in New York holding a basketball “and kind of casually standing there looking straight into the camera. It’s not against a white background…” notes Howard. “I know Kareem a little bit. It so captured the foundational strength of character and intelligence that Kareem carried with him along with his basketball talent.”

Initially, Howard, who spent three years making the film, thought it was going to be more focused on the fashion and celebrity worlds that Avedon inhabited. However, his fascination with photographs like “sad Marilyn” (Avedon’s 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe) grew into a respect for the full breadth of Avedon’s career, and his “creative courage as an artist.”

In the film, footage of Avedon and new interviews with Lauren Hutton, Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Joel Meyerowitz, Larry Gagosian, and Avedon’s son John, among others, paint a picture of a driven, curious, and sometimes mercurial artist. In the 1950s, Avedon’s career took off when he began shooting for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and Vanity Fair. He injected a sense of play and prewar European glamour into his images by drawing inspiration from the films of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. Eventually, he ventured into documentary assignments and more political subjects, including Nothing Personal (1964), a photobook with text by James Baldwin that captured the tensions of the Civil Rights era alongside a broader look at American life, a three panel portrait of anti-war protesters the Chicago Seven, and members of America’s political and financial elite at the time of the country’s bicentennial (“The Family”) for Rolling Stone. At the height of his career, he seemingly shifted quite easily from photographing celebrities to documenting anti-war protests and the counterculture of the 1960s, even when his work was met with mixed reactions.

Dovima with elephants, evening dress by Dior, Cirque d’Hiver, Paris, August 1955.

James Baldwin, New York, January 9, 1963.

Avedon (left) with Gloria Vanderbilt and Sidney Lumet at a party for the movie premiere of East of Eden (dir. Elia Kazan), 1955.

“We tried to reflect the risks he took and the transitions he made with his art and his career,” Howard shares. Had Howard made the documentary in Avedon’s lifetime, he would have liked to have asked him directly about the turning points in his career. “In all the interviews, he just kind of made it seem like it was a natural step. But to me, it's not a natural step to stop getting thousands and thousands of dollars an hour to shoot commercials and shoot for the world's most read magazines, and go to Vietnam where no one was really. He wasn’t on assignment initially… he just committed.”

In 1979, the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas, commissioned Avedon to capture a portrait of the West. He worked on this ambitious portfolio periodically through 1984, traveling across 17 states like California, Colorado, Iowa, North Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, with assistants and a researcher, Laura Wilson, who helped Avedon arrange 752 portrait sittings. (Wilson also documented the making of the project in her own remarkable photographs and writing.) In total, Avedon printed 124 photographs (some as large as four feet tall) and exhibited them at the museum in 1985. The result was In the American West—a turning point in Avedon’s career. Prior to the project’s completion, in 1983, Vanity Fair ran five photographs from the eventual series, showing coal miners covered in dust and one lone oil worker alongside a feature on Wagner’s operas and an excerpt of Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold.

“One of the reasons I was drawn to [In the American West] is because my family roots are in the Midwest,” Howard says. “I see a lot of truth in these images.”

Avedon conducting a portrait session for In the American West beside his 8x10 camera.

In a similar fashion to August Sander’s massive undertaking People of the 20th Century, Avedon went looking for “men and women who work at hard, uncelebrated jobs, the people who are often ignored or overlooked,” Wilson wrote. In doing so he joined a whole legion of photographers whose images have come to define broad swaths of middle and western America. But unlike common readings of Sander’s project at the time, Avedon was clear that his version of the West was totally subjective, more of a cinematic panorama than an objective record. He was emphatic that all photographs are filtered through the photographer’s eye, and become their interpretation. Through Wilson, he declared, “This is a fictional West. I don’t think the West of these portraits is any more conclusive than the West of John Wayne.”

Below, Howard reflects on five of his favorite photographs from Avedon’s In the American West.

“I asked if that was makeup, and I was assured that none of it was. [Avedon] set up, and just as workers were coming off their shift, he was getting them in front of the camera. I mean, wow, this is what these workers look like. This is what was in their lungs and their pores. I have cousins and uncles who worked in the oil fields. I never had any idea that they had their days looking like they’d been through what this guy has been through on his shift.”

“The boy with the rattlesnake was the first photo that [Avedon] took where he knew he was going to get at something deeper... He felt like this was almost religious iconography in a way, or mythic. [The subject] was a teenager. As Avedon says, he's a boy turning into a man, and here he's doing this kind of work, so it speaks to a transformation. It also speaks of that region as a very pragmatic region. My own dad, to try to get some spending money [in the ’30s], was hunting and trapping raccoons to sell skins to the junk dealer or possums they could eat. Absolutely just a pragmatic way of life there. So that image always resonated with me. It is also featured in the documentary because it was the proof in [Avedon’s] mind that he was going to be able to identify moments and individuals that would be arresting and mean a lot on an artistic level.”

“The beekeeper is, of course, a stunning image–one that doesn't have that much to do with the American West. I think [Avedon] could have found somebody like that in almost any corner of the planet, but it certainly is fascinating and a tribute to the research team that was working with him to help find him.”

“The maintenance worker who’s dressed up in a really flashy suit, suit jacket, tie and hat, that just looks very familiar to me. I mean, the jacket and all the embroidery on it, the flowers, I never saw anything like that with my family. They didn’t have that kind of flourish. This guy looks like he could be a country western singer or could be trying to be a country western star. But the hat, the tie, the gaze, the posture looks very, very familiar to me. That looks like a hardworking guy getting dressed up on the weekend.”

“This young girl is beautiful, and yet you feel she’s a little haunted. She’s at a point in her life where I think the real world is really coming into focus. You can feel that in a very specific way in the region that [Avedon] was covering. I think that also speaks about her generation: young Americans beginning to see the country that they live in; the world that they’re meant to function in and try to thrive in.”

Since Sir Patrick Stewart’s passing, I have spent a great deal of time reading stories from his co-stars about his work and impact. It’s lovely to see tributes continue to pour in, but the sentiments that have truly hit me in my feels have come from Ian McKellen, Stewart's longtime best friend (and sometimes on-screen nemesis). While Sir McKellen broke his silence weeks ago, he just shared additional thoughts on his late comrade, and I may or may not need a tissue.

While Stewart and McKellen battled on the big screen as X-Men's Professor X and Magneto, respectively, the two seem inseparable in real life. They were actually so close that McKellen even officiated Stewart’s wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. So, when the actor stopped by Entertainment Tonight to promote his movie, Ebenezer, he got a chance to reflect on his friendship with Stewart, and his comments are just too sweet:

Well, what I thought about Sir Patrick of late is because he did his own version of Christmas Carol. He was a one-man show. He played all the characters. He did it on Broadway and did it on London’s West End a number of times. I think he toured with it. It’s a big part of his life. I just remember his friendship and his - A good man. Serious-minded. And always looking to make the world a better place, and he achieved that.

I think everyone would be better off having a friend who speaks about them as lovingly as McKellen discusses Stewart. To put it simply, the two were the definition of friendship goals, and the seasoned actors elevated everyone around them. I can't imagine it's easy for McKellen not having his good friend around, but I love that he's choosing to remember him in such a positive way.

Of course, given McKellen’s role in Ebezener as Jacob Marley, it makes sense that his friend would be on his mind. Stewart's take on A Christmas Carol still serves as a high point in his career and a benchmark for stage acting in general. It seems I'm not the only one who is feeling a a way about this tribute either based on the comments of the Instagram video. I think toriyikes sums it best: “Making me cry in the afternoon!” Fans may agree after watch ingthe video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Shortly after Patrick Stewart's death was reported, Ian McKellen took to X to share a sentimental message. In it, the star reflected on his and Stewart's time serving at the Royal Shakespeare Company and discussed their subsequent work and endearing friendship.

While Stewart was greatly known for his work as an actor, McKellen’s words were a a sweet reminder that he was so much more. Yes, he was “serious-minded,” but he was also always up for a laugh and even gave his own eulogy back in 2015 at a Just for Laughs gala. There's a reason his roles as Professor X and Jean-Luc Picard are still iconic, and it's because the compassion that he put into the world. Just as McKellen said, he made it a little better, and that's something we should all remember.

Of course, it should be noted that we will the two X-Men alums together one more time when Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 schedule on December 18. The movie will now mark Stewart's final on-screen performance following his death at 86 due to Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Trailers have already teased that Stewart's Professor X and McKellen's Magneto will share the screen again, and I'm not sure I'm prepared for that reunion.

I'm confident that Patrick Stewart's final turn as the X-Men's leader will be satisfying and that his body of work as a whole will stand the test of time. More than that, though, if the comments from Ian McKellen and so many others are anything to go by, Stewart's kind spirit won't be forgotten either.

#3551. David Carradine Faced Off Against An Action Legend In A Forgotten 1983 Neo-Western

David Carradine came to prominence playing a martial arts master so it was only right that he eventually found himself in a duel with the great Chuck Norris. As Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine in "Kung Fu," Carradine traveled the Old West facing down all manner of challenger. But he never reckoned with the might of a solitary Texas Ranger with a deadly aim — that is, until 1983's "Lone Wolf McQuade," which saw Carradine and Norris do battle in what was one of the better projects of the 1980s for both actors.

By 1983, Carradine had come a long way from his TV debut in the short-lived Western series "Shane." Having become a household name thanks to "Kung Fu," the actor tried to subvert audience expectations by appearing in a number of exploitation flicks and B-movies. More well-known 1970s examples include "Cannonball," "Death Race 2000," and "Deathsport." In the 1980s, however, Carradine was basically churning out direct-to-video fare, and in "Lone Wolf McQuade" he came face to face with the king of schlocky DTV actioners, Chuck Norris.

The neo-western was directed by Steve Carver, who'd worked at Roger Corman's New World Pictures at the same time Carradine had fronted several of the studio's features in the 1970s. With "Lone Wolf McQuade," Carver paid homage to the Spaghetti Westerns that had helped move the Western genre into its revisionist era. As such, there was a self-aware aspect to the movie, which knew exactly what it was and wasn't about to apologize for it. The final showdown between its two stars was emblematic of its excess and was, it turns out, a lot more real than you might imagine. In fact, Carradine and Norris seemingly gave everything they had to their climactic battle and ended up injuring themselves.

"Lone Wolf McQuade" isn't the type of '80s actioner that gets mentioned alongside such legendary features as "First Blood" or "Die Hard." But it's also not the kind of movie that should be lumped in with the worst examples of the decades' bombastic nonsense. In fact, it's easily one of the best Chuck Norris movies, and in its unapologetic embrace of the uber macho ethos of the era and its reverence for the great Spaghetti Westerns, manages to turn it into a sort of paean to both the golden age of action cinema the influential films that preceded it.

That's not to say the film is some sort of artistic masterwork. This is, at the end of the day, a film in which Norris and David Carradine beat each other senseless for our entertainment. "Lone Wolf McQuade" stars the former as Texas Ranger Jim "J.J." McQuade, an ex-Marine who is the epitome of the '80s action stereotype: a lone wolf lawman who routinely flouts the rules and lives a solitary existence in the wake of his divorce. Oh, and he also literally has a pet wolf.

The film follows McQuade as he tangles with David Carradine's Rawley Wilkes, an arms dealer who also happens to be a martial arts expert. It seems Carradine's Kung Fu specialist is selling weapons to terrorists, and J.J. isn't about to let that go unpunished. When Wilkes captures his daughter, Sally McQuade (Dana Kimmell), he all but guarantees a confrontation with J.J., which is exactly what we get in the film's climactic moments. That particular battle is a protracted slog in which Norris and Carradine go all out.

In a 1990 issue of Psychotronic Video (via archive.org), David Carradine recalled his showdown with Chuck Norris in "Lone Wolf McQuade." Neither actor opted to use a stunt double, making for what sounds like a brutal on-set experience. "We worked on that fight for four days," he said. "We shot it for four days. And we were little old men by the end of it. All our old injuries came back, we got new injuries, and we were stumbling around like little old men."

According to the actor, he and his co-star needed canes and crutches by the end of shooting their fight, which in Carradine's recollection was the result of Norris wanting to outdo his famous showdown with Bruce Lee in 1972's "The Way of the Dragon." "We were actually trying to go beyond that," continued Carradine. "I think we did. I think photographically we didn't. But as far as the fight was concerned, the combination of the two styles, you know, because I was very flowing and loose, and he was very solid and hard, I think we accomplished what we set out to do."

I'm fairly confident in saying that Jim "J.J." McQuade vs. Rawley Wilkes was not, in fact, quite as memorable as Tang Lung vs. Colt. But it was an impressive ending to one of Norris' best films and reminder of the physical talent that had made Carradine a star a decade prior.

#3550. WhatsApp adds shareable event invites and a new Events hub

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

When you create an event, you can add a cover photo and share the invite link by text or email. WhatsApp also gives you the option to share a QR code.

WhatsApp says your phone number is hidden from guests you don’t know, and “guests without a WhatsApp account will only see the event address after they RSVP.”

You could already create events in WhatsApp group chats and one-on-one conversations.

With this update, WhatsApp is adding a dedicated Events section in Settings where you can create invites, manage RSVPs, and see past and upcoming events you’ve organized or been invited to.

You can also set custom reminders and give guests the option to bring a plus-one.

WhatsApp says the updated Events feature will roll out to everyone over the next few weeks.

#3549. Game Awards 2026: All Game of the Year Front-Runners and Predictions

What’s in pole position for gaming’s top prize? Let’s make some predictions

With only a month to go until the 13th Game Awards, set for Dec. 10, every key competitor but one (the big one) has been released. The likelihood of anything emerging to stop Grand Theft Auto 6 from sweeping the night looks increasingly slim in what is turning out to be a much weaker year than it looked on paper.

At this point, we have a clear idea of what games will be favored by The Game Awards' voting body: A high Metacritic rating (preferably over 90) is a must; role-playing games and action-adventures are strongly favored, as are games with strong narrative elements; indie and multiplayer games struggle harder for recognition than AAA single-player adventures. We used these metrics to correctly predict last year's winner, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, and the 2024 winner, Astro Bot. In 2025, we also predicted all six GOTY nominees and correctly called 20 other categories.

Below, you'll find our predictions for the most likely nominees, of which there are six each year, for Game of the Year 2026 — taken only from games that have already been released (or made available for review). We'll update these rankings throughout the year as new games are released. We'll also list some likely upcoming contenders and some of the 2026 GOTY race's dark horses, too.

Update (Nov. 9): The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has emerged as the highest-rated game of the year to date, and critical acclaim has been followed by a huge wave of social love as players share their rediscovery of the classic adventure. Ocarina's status as a dead-cert for a GOTY nomination is only matched by the seeming impossibility of a remake of a 28-year-old game winning Game of the Year. That said, it looks stronger than much of the competition, most of which is struggling to maintain momentum in one way or another; the most recent entry, Phantom Blade Zero, seems to have failed to capture the conversation.

Why it could win: Resident Evil is a reliable contender at The Game Awards, with three GOTY nominations since 2019, and many more in other categories. Requiem combines the fan appeal of the remakes with the freshness of a new entry, and blends their gameplay successfully, too. It's slickly produced, digestible, thrilling, with both global appeal and a serious side: a perfect Game Awards GOTY contender.

Weaknesses: Requiem's critical reception was very good overall, but perhaps a tiny bit soft to be a true GOTY contender — it sits in the high 80s on Metacritic and OpenCritic. How well it fares in the long run will depend on the strength of the competition, but for now, it's in the lead.

Momentum (holding steady): Potential challengers to Requiem's status as pack leader just keep falling by the wayside. Nothing else released this year combines critical acclaim with a perfect Game Awards genre profile so effectively, and nothing else will until GTA 6 comes out. It's a lock for a nomination.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Resident Evil Requiem.

Why it could win: A beloved classic, with a reputation as the best game ever made, lavishly remade by a team at the top of their game, and showered in critical plaudits like no other game this year. It may be just a remake, but Nintendo has mustered a huge sense of event around Ocarina, from its dramatic visual reinvention to its bold positioning against GTA 6 in the calendar.

Weaknesses: After all, though, it's still a remake of an old game, and a very faithful one. The jury will want to recognize Nintendo's achievement here (as it has done for the likes of Resident Evil 4 and Final Fantasy 7 Remake in the past), but a Game of the Year win seems inconceivable for such a well known quantity.

Momentum (new entry): Shortly after launch, Ocarina fever is at an all-time high and shows little sign of abating. And while the art direction initially seemed divisive, players and press alike seem united in their praise.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Why it could win: House House's co-op puzzle adventure has a fantastic critical reputation — it currently sits at 91 on Metacritic, higher than any other game on this list. The developer has pedigree: Untitled Goose Game was a dark horse GOTY contender in 2019, and even won the overall award at DICE. It's a refined design in a currently voguish genre. Co-op games go down well at The Game Awards (It Takes Two won in 2021). And there's a good chance jury members have had a good time playing it together.

Weaknesses: As an online multiplayer game, best experienced with a group of friends, Big Walk requires time and social organization to experience properly, which may be tricky for many jury members.

Momentum (📈 from No. 4): Big Walk is now fully confirmed as the top indie title of 2026, and while it doesn't look like a traditional GOTY contender, that could be to its advantage amid a field of underachieving AAA games.

Read Giovanni Colantonio, Julia Lee, and Johnny Yu's full review of Big Walk.

Why it could win: Reviews are very strong, at 89 on Metacritic. Critics love that Fortune's Weave has united strong storytelling with refined combat in a Fire Emblem game for the first time in a long time, and it helps that it's done so on an epic canvas. There's growing recognition at the TGAs for deep and authentic Japanese-developed RPGs like Metaphor: ReFantazio, and there's big fan support too: Fire Emblem: Three Houses was an unlikely winner of the Player's Voice award.

Weaknesses: Fortune's Weave is a tactics RPG, but the Game Awards jury always nominates Fire Emblem games in the Sim/Strategy category, which never overlaps with Game of the Year. If it is nominated, it will be the first strategy game ever to break into GOTY consideration. And as a Nintendo release, it may be eclipsed by the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

Momentum (📉 from No. 3): Fortune's Weave still looks like the best-positioned RPG (or RPG-adjaccent game) of 2026. But it hasn't quite managed to break containment and reach beyond series and genre fans, while some aspects of the game are proving more divisive than they seemed at first.

Read Josh Broadwell's full review of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave.

Why it could win: Phantom Blade Zero is this year's Black Myth: Wukong, a visually spectacular action game from an exciting new Chinese studio that muscled its way into the GOTY race. Unlike Black Myth, and unlike this year's Korean competitor Crimson Desert, it's got strong reviews (88 on Metacritic, 90 on OpenCritic).

Weaknesses: While it has reviewed well, Phantom Blade hasn't quite pulled away from a crowded action-adventure field that will be competing for the last couple of nominations, including Control Resonant and 007 First Light.

Momentum (📉 from No. 2): Phantom Blade Zero had a colossal launch on Steam (presumably powered by its Chinese fans) but has notably failed to inspire any conversation at all in critical circles, which doesn't bode well for its status with the jury.

Read Paulo Kawanishi's full review of Phantom Blade Zero.

Why it could win: IO Interactive's debut James Bond game has made a confident splash with critics, earning a decent 87 Metascore. This kind of slick, cinematic action-adventure usually goes down well with the jury, while the inclusion of some of Hitman developer IO's trademark "social stealth" gameplay lends it additional gamer cred.

Weaknesses: Licensed games very rarely get nominated for Game of the Year, and First Light's critical reception is a little soft, with some reviewers unimpressed by IO's shift in a more commercial direction.

Momentum (holding steady): Like Crimson Desert before it (only better), 007 refuses to be dislodged from this list. Until GTA comes along, it stands as the best-executed classical AAA adventure of the year, which stands it in good stead for GOTY.

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

The Blood of Dawnwalker: This vampire RPG from key talent behind The Witcher 3 underwhelmed a little on release, and lives deep in its big brother's shadow, but it's going to be a Best Narrative contender and is a perfect Game Awards game in many ways.

Star Wars Zero Company: It would be unprecedented for one strategy game to breach the GOTY field, never mind two, but jury members who have stuck with Bit Reactor's tactics game have universally fallen in love with it, and will be strong advocates for it.

Pragmata: Capcom's endearingly old-school sci-fi action game has some strong sentiment behind it, and gameplay that's innovative enough to register.

Pokémon Pokopia: On review sentiment alone, Pokopia would be a lock for a nomination, but as a life sim and a Pokémon game, it isn't what we usually think of as GOTY material. Nevertheless, it remains in the conversation.

Crimson Desert: Pearl Abyss' much-hyped everything game never gathered the critical support necessary to compete, and yet it remains on the fringes of the competition through sheer tenacity.

Control Resonant: Never rule out Remedy Entertainment at The Game Awards, although Resonant's reception is perhaps not what the developer was hoping for.

Grand Theft Auto 6: The presumptive Game of the Year looks like a dead cert… as long as it makes its release date, which is only days before The Game Awards' eligibility deadline.

#3548. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.
