#3547. 5 Possible Reasons Behind James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit

The hierarchy of power in the DC Universe is about to change. The Paramount/Warner Bros. Discovery merger was recently made official, with a new mega-corporation, Skydance, emerging on the other side. As a result, major changes are being made at all of the companies under the corporation's umbrella, and those changes have come for DC Studios.

In a surprise move, James Gunn and Peter Safran are exiting as co-heads of DC Studios, with former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham taking over. What this means for the future of the DC Universe that Gunn and Safran have been building together since 2022 remains to be seen, but this is one of the bigger shake-ups in the realm of superheroes and comic book happenings in a long time.

For now, we have more questions than answers, and the biggest question on everyone's minds right now is what, exactly, prompted the divorce between Gunn, Safran, and DC Studios. While we don't have a definitive answer yet, there are some strong possible reasons for the man behind Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" trilogy and his trusted producing pal to exit the company.

We're going to look at some of those reasons as we try to make sense of what just happened and what might come next. Let's get into it.

In early 2023, when James Gunn announced the first chapter of the new DC Universe and called it "Gods and Monsters," it was clear the idea was for DC Studios to focus on characters other than Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman. Yes, Gunn was going to direct "Superman," but projects like "Swamp Thing" and "The Authority" were also in the mix. Many of the projects have yet to come to fruition, but others, such as "Clayface," have. They've delivered mixed results.

Gunn and Safran weren't focusing all that much on A-list DC characters at the time. A new Batman is due to debut in "The Brave and the Bold," but that movie doesn't even have a release date, and Gunn has confirmed that Robert Pattinson's Batman won't join the new DCU. It admittedly complicates matters with "The Batman Part II" now in production. All the same, the new DCU absolutely needs a Batman. It needs a Wonder Woman. It needs A-listers.

Skydance is now a mega-corporation that is tens of billions of dollars in debt. On paper, it might be good to have a movie like "Clayface" make well over $100 million on a $44 million budget. But that's relatively small potatoes compared to what a "Batman" movie can make. Skydance wants to focus more on those A-list characters. Right or wrong, the company is likely eager to get a new Wonder Woman on screen and a new Batman cast to exist alongside David Corenswet's Superman.

There may well be room for movies like "Swamp Thing" or "The Authority," but not before the A-listers get sorted out. Again, this is speculative, but since IP is still king in Hollywood, there's good reason to believe the brass is looking at DC with more urgency in this regard.

We can have creative discussions all day, and undoubtedly, people will be sharing a lot of opinions on what James Gunn and Peter Safran have produced during their time as the heads of DC Studios. However, at the end of the day, Hollywood is a business, and from a business perspective, the box office returns just haven't been good enough. In particular, "Supergirl" is a glaring issue that needed to be addressed.

Gunn's "Superman" was the biggest comic book movie of 2025 at the box office with $618 million, but that was still less than Zack Snyder's "Man of Steel" ($670 million) did 13 years earlier, unadjusted for inflation. It was a promising enough start, but not a resoundingly great one. Superhero movies are no longer automatically successful in theaters like they were in the 2010s, which certainly doesn't make things any easier. All the same, results are not just expected, but needed to justify the sky-high budgets for these blockbusters.

"Supergirl" flopped at the box office earlier this year, taking in just $126 million worldwide on a $170 million budget against mixed reviews. While Supergirl isn't quite an A-list character, she's a heck of a lot bigger than Clayface or Peacemaker. The fact that the movie bombed in such high-profile fashion was not a good look for DC Studios. Ultimately, it reflects back on Gunn and Safran, even though Craig Gillespie was in the director's chair.

In truth, DC is in the midst of one of the biggest box office bad streaks ever. The misses far outweigh the hits. Not all of that can be placed on Gunn and Safran, but something needs to change. Relatively modest hits like "Clayface" aren't going to cut it forever.

James Gunn worked as a smaller filmmaker for years before he ascended to Hollywood's A-list. When "Guardians of the Galaxy" became Marvel's most unlikely box office smash hit, everything changed. That eventually led to him becoming a studio head, but occupying an executive suite was never his ambition. He wanted to be a director. Put simply, it sounds very much like Gunn didn't want to be a Hollywood executive anymore.

After the news about his exit broke, Gunn explained his departure as DC Studios' co-head and his statement made it seem like the job was very taxing on his personal life, as well as his creative life. "DC Studios has been trying, to say the least," he said. "I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job."

Gunn also noted that he had a tough time "dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

Not to say that there weren't other factors involved, but if we take Gunn at his word, the last four years have been pretty difficult for him. He wasn't just making giant movies like "Superman" and next year's "Man of Tomorrow," but he's been creatively managing all of the output at DC Studios. It's not terribly hard to see why he might want to go back to just being a writer and director.

There's no telling what has been going on behind closed doors at Skydance ever since the merger went through. CEO David Ellison has his own ideas of how he wants the company, and its various divisions, to run. Ellison isn't the guy who launched DC Studios when James Gunn and Peter Safran's new division started at Warner Bros. It's entirely possible there was a bit of a culture clash.

It's certainly interesting to note that Both Gunn and Safran were announced as part of the executive structure at Skydance after the Warner Bros./Paramount merger was made official. That was just a few weeks ago. Would Ellison have announced them as part of the new company if the plan was to move on and have Jeremy Latcham take over? It's hard to imagine. That implies that something may have happened in recent weeks that prompted the exit.

What could that be? There are a lot of moving parts. Ellison, as well as his new film chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, undoubtedly had their own ideas about how to handle things at DC Studios. If Gunn and/or Safran bumped up against them in ways they didn't with the previous regime, it's not hard to imagine the camel's back breaking under the weight of one too many straws.

Without aimlessly speculating as to what they all could have disagreed about, it seems probable that if all sides got along and shared a vision for the future, they could have figured something out.

DC Studios was under the Warner Bros. umbrella, but it seemed like James Gunn and Peter Safran were granted a great deal of creative freedom to shape this new DC Universe as they saw fit. There's virtually no question that Skydance, David Ellison, and the rest of the new brass at the studio have their own ideas about what to do with the treasure trove of IP that is the DC Comics library. It's not hard to surmise that Skydance's ideas didn't align with Gunn and Safran's intended plans.

James Gunn's DC Universe plans shifted after Warner Bros.' initial announcement, but that never meant that Gunn and Safran lost control of the ship. They were steering. They were making sure things were lining up for eventual, future plans. Those plans haven't fully revealed themselves (and we may never know the full scope of what they wanted to do), but it's clear there was an ultimate plan in place.

If Skydance has different ideas (and it feels safe to assume they do), that would complicate matters. If Gunn and Safran spent years building out this slate only to have to bend to what the new leadership wants, that would be frustrating. Without putting words in anyone's mouth, it could even be taken as an insult.

Again, I'm not here to recklessly speculate, but these two guys had a vision that Warner Bros. bought into. If Skydance doesn't share that vision, or something close to it, Gunn and Safran making their way to the exit door makes a lot of sense.

We can all agree that the Olaf animatronic walking itself around Disneyland Paris is adorable, all on its own. Now it's even cuter, with his own magical sleigh to help transport him around the Kingdom of Arendelle as he makes his way to a stage where the Arendelle Carolers perform for the holidays.

One of the biggest drawbacks that came with introducing a “living” animatronic Olaf to guests in Disney’s European theme park is the fact that it can’t walk very far very quickly. I mean, he is a snowman after all. So now, and just in time for the holiday celebration, the adorable snowman who just wants to live his best summer is taking on winter in style with his own magical sleigh. Check out the short clip of a cast member steering Olaf around as he waves to the adoring masses gathered around:

A post shared by EveryCharacter.com (@everycharacter)

The holidays are in full swing in the Disney theme parks around the world, and no one embodies the winter season better than Olaf the snowman from Frozen, one of Walt Disney Animation Studios’ most popular franchises of all time. As a result, I’m happy to see that the beloved character has his own mode of transportation, especially after a few incidents of Olaf failing, freezing, and falling over. It’s a frightening sight when it happens, though Josh Gad has kept a sense of humor about it all, as the actor who is responsible for the snowman's lovable personality.

Getting to meet beloved Disney characters is a longtime tradition, where animated characters become live-action characters in the parks. While we knew that Disney Parks had been working on robots for a few years, it wasn’t until we actually got to see Olaf in action that I realized just how remarkable the achievement was. I’m also thankful that they’re continuing to build on that by creating this sleigh, which seems to have a purpose bigger than just transporting the character around the World of Frozen in Disneyland Paris.

In the video clip, you can see that Olaf’s sleigh, while too freaking cute just on its own, has the dual purpose of also working as a bridge to get him onto the stage at the foot of North Mountain so that he can join the Arendelle carolers for a 15-minute musical performance where he leads the choir. The sleigh transforms into a short platform that Olaf can shuffle across to the back of the stage where he can do his part in the show, avoiding the need for someone to have to physically lift him up and get him on the stage some other way.

While more Frozen films are in the works, we won’t see Frozen 3 until November 24, 2027. Until then, I’m hoping we’ll get more Olaf fun in and around the Disney theme parks, as he’s a character that would be a welcome addition to the U.S. locations as well.

#3545. Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models [U: Now available]

Apple Creator Studio updates were announced late last month, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.

At the time, Apple didn’t give a specific availability date beyond sometime in November, but the updates are rolling out today …

Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.

Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.

Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.

Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.

The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.

Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.

Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.

A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.

In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.

New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3543. George Lucas Expected Star Wars To Be Compared To A Sci-Fi Movie He Says Is Even Better

It's easy to underplay just how monumental "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope" was at the time of its original theatrical release in 1977. George Lucas' decision to keep the licensing and merchandising rights for the film resulted in a multi-billion-dollar lesson for every studio in Hollywood, while the special effects pioneered by the movie paved the way for the VFX industry we have today. It's also, quite simply, a very good film that combines an eclectic collection of influences to deliver a hugely entertaining space opera with the flair of Westerns and samurai flicks.

Still, while "Star Wars" is typically counted amongst the best sci-fi movies of all time (including by us here at /Film!), Lucas doesn't entirely consider it a sci-fi film. In a 1977 interview with Rolling Stone, he even described the movie as being closer to a Western than, specifically, Stanley Kubrick's classic 1968 sci-fi saga "2001: A Space Odyssey." As Lucas put it:

"I am fairly pleased that they haven't compared it that much to '2001.' Actually, it is being compared more to Westerns than '2001,' which is really what it should be. On a technical level, it can be compared, but personally, I think that '2001' is far superior."

But Lucas wasn't merely being coy about his admiration for Kubrick's movie, he was being practical about the stark differences between the two films. "You know, it had 10 times more money and time, and obviously, it came out better. In special effects, one of the key elements is time and money," he continued. "Most of those special effects in 'Star Wars' were first-time special effects — we shot them, we composited them, and they're in the movie."

It's neither news nor a surprise that George Lucas has always admired Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssey." After all, Lucas originally went to Douglas Trumbull, who had done the visual effects for Kubrick's film, to work on "Star Wars." However, it was only after Trumbull passed on the project that he recommended John Dykstra instead. This resulted in a collaboration that changed the special effects industry forever, as Dykstra pioneered a motion control camera that allowed Lucas to pull off the climactic Death Star trench run in "Star Wars."

But it wasn't just Trumbull that he tried to recruit from the crew behind Kubrick's film. In fact, Lucas' first choice of cinematographer for "Star Wars" was "2001" director of photography Geoffrey Unsworth, who seemed like an ideal pick to capture the documentary feel that Lucas wanted while at the same time being able to handle the movie's visual effects demands. And when Unsworth declined the offer, Lucas ended up going with a different Kubrick cinematographer in the form of Gilbert Taylor (who had worked on "Dr. Strangelove").

Yet again, this creative decision proved essential to making "Star Wars" as unique and effective as it is. Indeed, Taylor managed to ground the movie's operatic spectacle, at times creating a fly-on-the-wall visual sensibility. It makes it seem as though you're not just watching some grand fairy tale set in space but real events that happened a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away.

An era in superhero-related media is officially coming to an end, as James Gunn and Peter Safran are officially stepping down from their posts as the co-CEOs of DC Studios. This surprising news arrives only a few weeks after the finalization of the Paramount/Warner Bros. merger. At this point, the news is still very fresh and, based on social media, the responses to this major development vary tremendously. Interestingly enough, amid all that, one fan brought up a wild fact regarding Gunn’s tenure, and I’m feeling so many emotions.

Gunn and Safran joined DC Studios in 2022 and, from there, they began to construct their DCU continuity, which was to span movies, TV and video games. The pair eventually developed a ten-year plan and, up to this point, that strategy has yielded films like Superman and Supergirl as well as shows like Creature Commandos and Lanterns. The wild comment that was recently shared by an X user had nothing to do with any projects like that, though. Instead, they marked the end of this chapter by naming a long-gestating flick:

Very funny/sad that the entire Gunn era took place between THE BATMAN and THE BATMAN PART 2.

I’m honestly at a loss for words here, as this fact is absolutely correct. Matt Reeves’ The Batman was released in March 2022 months before Safran and Gunn were hired. The sequel was announced in April of that year and, since then, the movie has seen a variety of delays and is currently set to hit theaters in early 2028. On the one hand, it’s understandable that someone would chuckle over the fact that this sequel’s development will have outlasted the Gunn/Safran era. But, on the other hand, I’m actually a bit sad.

James Gunn Doesn’t Hold Back About Rumors Swirling Around Man Of Tomorrow And More DC Projects

As someone who has been interested in the DCU thus far, I’m a bit disappointed over the possibility of another reboot. However, what really makes me sad about the fact pointed out in the social media is that it’s a reminder of just how long The Batman: Part II’s development has taken. Of course, I do understand the reasons, though, as the Hollywood strikes played a key role in that. Also, more recently, Reeves had to take a step back from the film to handle a personal matter, and Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to complete principal photography. Reeves isn’t leaving the movie entirely, though, as he'll remain in touch with Soderbergh during the shoot and completely retake the reins during post-production.

It was just weeks ago that Reeves’ situation was announced and it was mentioned that he had support from Safran and Gunn. That’s just one detail that makes the news of their departure all the more surreal to me. Gunn posted about his exit on his Instagram and reflected on the highs of working for DC. Additionally, the filmmaker praised the various collaborators he had the chance to work with. Overall, Gunn – a longtime fan of DC Comics – seems to have a lot of gratitude for his time serving as co-CEO of the studio.

While James Gunn and Peter Safran will vacate their positions ahead of Jeremy Latcham’s arrival by December 1, their work within the DCU isn’t done just yet as, at the very least, he’s still in post-production on his Superman follow-up, Man of Tomorrow, which is set to be released amid the 2027 movie schedule. Also, Gunn and Safran are still credited as producers on The Batman’s sequel. I’m not sure what lies ahead for DC but, for now, I’m going to be glued to my screen to see if any other fans drop any other wild facts.

Man of Tomorrow soars into theaters on July 9, 2027, while The Batman: Part II opens on February 18, 2028.

#3541. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3540. iPhone Duo durability tested on unfolding livestream, now over 260,000 folds

CNET built a ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that’s been constantly folding and unfolding iPhone Duo for over a week to test durability, while livestreaming daily. Here’s how it’s going.

How durable is the iPhone Duo’s hinge and folding display? Several early reviews tried to answer that question, including in some cases by building machines that constantly folded and unfolded the device.

CNET built a custom ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that has been folding and unfolding the iPhone Duo 24 hours per day, 7 days a week for over a week now.

When the livestream wrapped up yesterday, iPhone Duo had hit just over 260,000 folds.

#3539. How To Watch Brad Pitt's Heart Of The Beast At Home

David Ayer's "Heart of the Beast" wasn't really a sleeper hit, given that it stars Brad Pitt, but the harrowing survival film turned out to be a surprisingly leggy box office performer thanks to solid word of mouth. Now it's about to find a wider audience as it moves to streaming on November 10 (as the opening of Pitt's kinda-sorta anticipated "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" nears).

The film caught on with moviegoers due to its deeply affecting narrative about a retired Army veteran (Pitt) and his combat dog struggling to survive in the Alaskan wilderness after their seaplane crashes. The crash is caused by Pitt's character having a heart attack, but he's not down for the count — not yet. He and his dog are uniquely equipped to hoof it 58 miles back to civilization, but this terrain is every bit as treacherous as a battle zone. Along the way, they encounter wolves (dredging up memories of Joe Carnahan's "The Grey"), a grizzly bear and other obstacles that test their resolve. Each challenge leaves them a little (or a lot) worse for the wear, but they are determined to emerge from this ordeal as they've done so often in their war-torn past.

Again, "Heart of the Beast" will begin streaming via Premium VOD on November 10, and consumers will get a few extras to go along with their purchase.

According to a press release issued by Paramount today, the PVOD "Heart of the Beast" will include a behind-the-scenes featurette titled "One Last Mission," which is said to be a "love letter to the land, the people, and most of all the dogs who made this film shine." (Their names are Uber, Seeka and Ryker.) Because you can never get enough good-dog footage, there's also "Uber & Brad: A Soulful Bond." Not sure why Seeka and Ryker were denied a mention here, but I guess I'll find out when I watch it. Finally, there are deleted scenes that promise to "play tug of war with your heart strings," so get ready to weep some more once you've finished the film (and you will weep).

While it would've been nice if this visually stunning film remained in theaters for a little while longer, it was clear from jump that its destiny was to become a dad movie classic. It'll be streaming for years and years to come, forcing grown men to complain about their dusty living rooms/man caves. And if you're one of those people who needs to know the fate of the pooch ahead of time, /Film's got you covered.

#3538. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

I can barely remember a time when Carson Daly wasn’t hosting something on my TV screen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Carson Daly has been a host and a constant presence in my life since the ‘90s. I first became aware of him with his spot as a nighttime host on L.A.’s influential and highly rated alternative rock station KROQ-FM. So, by the time he became a presence on MTV with Total Request Live when the show debuted in 1998, he was already a trusted voice in music and pop culture for me.

Before YouTube and social media, MTV was the place to go if you wanted to be exposed to music you might not have already been aware of yet, and TRL brought heightened awareness to the pop princesses and boy bands of the era. You could catch the hottest music videos of the time while also seeing celebrities drop by to chat with Carson Daly about projects they were promoting.

He always had an ease and comfort with the talent but could also engage with the very passionate viewers as they agreed and disagreed with him. And there’s something comforting about seeing him officially step into the gig as co-host of Saturday Today, all these years later. The Voice host expressed his gratitude to People when reflecting on his latest gig:

I started many years ago at MTV and I feel like I’ve been really lucky. I’ve sort of grown up with an audience. So, if you were 18 and came to TRL, you might be 38 now and have a couple of kids and come to the Plaza. And so, I’ve just been lucky generationally to continue to work in TV, have new opportunities and people have been there with me.

While I never went to TRL in person, and likely won’t make it to the Plaza where they shoot Today, I did tune in often, especially when the likes of Britney Spears or any other popular pop stars were performing, so that I could teach myself the dance steps, to varying degrees of success. I am part of that audience that has grown up with Carson Daly, and I continue to watch him across a variety of projects to this day. And although I do miss the glimpse Total Request Live gave viewers into the lives of the biggest music stars of that era, the most recent attempt at a revival and the decline of MTV in general have made that impossible to recapture.

As someone who has had the successful host on my own TV screen over the decades, I found it particularly touching that when he officially added the Saturday Today co-anchor job in New York City to his already busy schedule that includes shooting The Voice in Los Angeles, he immediately thought of his mother watching the Today Show in their kitchen while he was getting ready for school. He clearly knows how proud his mother would have been to see her son become a part of something that was so important to her own life. Daly explained:

Well, I thought about my mom. My mom, God rest her soul, was the biggest ‘Today Show’ fan of all time. When I was growing up – elementary, junior high and high school – every morning I went in the kitchen, the ‘Today Show’ was on a tiny little TV. And when I got this job, just being here, she was here.

Admitting he teared up over how his mother would feel about his latest hosting gig made me tear up in the process, knowing firsthand how hard it is not to share such a big accomplishment with the one person you know it would mean the most to. He also joked that the other bonus of being gone on Saturday mornings is that it gets him out of making breakfast for his kids, but that they better not DoorDash as a replacement since that’s just too expensive.

There are still rumors that Carson Daly will be leaving The Voice after Season 30 wraps on the 2026 TV schedule, which likely won’t die down anytime soon, especially with Keke Palmer stepping in as host for Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity. But until we know for sure, the former TRL host can be seen doing his thing on Saturday Today as well as guiding the The Voice singers through the return of the Live Shows as they get closer to announcing a winner in December.

#3536. iOS 27.3 gives Apple One’s high-end tier a compelling upgrade

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.

#3535. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3534. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Gives Its Best Boy the Happy Ending He Deserved Decades Ago

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a mostly faithful remake, true, but there's a generous handful of tweaks and expansions that fill out this version of Hyrule beautifully. Most of those changes are grim. This game is sad — if speaking to the Kokiri after clearing The Great Deku Tree dungeon didn't clue you in on that, just chat to people with the Mask of Truth on — and it wants you to be sad too. One of these changes flies in the face of misery and is defiantly happy, though, and it involves the game's bestest boy: Richard.

Richard is a dog, a very good dog. You might even say the best dog. Though even if you didn't, his owner, Mamamu Yan, certainly would. She lives in Castle Town at the start of the game, and her favorite things to do are watch Richard play and talk about how much she loves Richard. It's cute! Less cute when she's rude about the town's other dogs, but no pup can choose their owner, I guess. It's not Richard's fault. He's a blameless angel.

And in the 2011 Nintendo 3DS version of Ocarina of Time, he's a literal angel. After young Link spends seven years in the Sacred Realm, Castle Town is in ruins thanks to Ganondorf and an army of ReDead, the Zelda series' version of zombies. Navi doesn't say it when you get her to tattle on the monsters, but given how much of a horror show the rest of the game is, it seems pretty likely these creatures used to be the denizens of Castle Town. Not all of the town's weird and wonderful folks died, though. Some of them escaped to Kakariko Village, including Mamamu Yan. In the 3DS version, she speaks of Richard in the past tense. He was the best dog, a famous one, even. Mamamu Yan doesn't seem particularly distressed about Richard's death, but I certainly was when I played.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

In the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake, Richard lives! He's alive and well, frolicking happily around Kakariko Village during the daytime and remaining decidedly un-lost at night. Little guy obviously learned his lesson back in Castle Town. Anyway, I originally thought maybe Mamamu Yan was one of those people who names every pet the same thing. Maybe this was Richard the Third or something. But no, it's the same wonderful little fuzzball from before. Mamamu Yan waxes at length about the virtues and splendor of her Richard, with no mention of ancestors or dead Richards or anything of that kind.

It's a sweet little bright spot and a welcome one after stumbling into the village following the horrors of Future Castle Town. Good boy, Richard. May you live forever.

#3533. Christopher Nolan's Batman Begins Borrowed Part Of Its Plot From A Beloved Animated Series Episode

In each of the three "Dark Knight" trilogy films, the villains make an attempt to destroy Gotham City from within. In "Batman Begins," one of those villains is Doctor Jonathan Crane/The Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy). The head of Gotham's Arkham Asylum, Crane is obsessed with fear. With ingredients provided by the League of Shadows, he's manufactured a "fear toxin" that can drive anyone exposed to it to terror. Using Arkham inmates, Crane has been dumping the toxin into Gotham's water supply via the asylum's pipe systems.

"Scarecrow tries to infect Gotham City with fear toxin" has become a stock "Batman" plot, like in the 2015 video game "Batman: Arkham Knight" or the 2021 comic crossover "Fear State." Look back, though, and you'll find it before "Batman Begins" — specifically, in "Batman: The Animated Series" episode "Dreams in Darkness," written by Judith and Garfield Reeves-Stevens. Batman, exposed to the Scarecrow's fear toxin and suffering hallucinations, is judged insane and locked inside Arkham as a patient.

Under his doctors' noses, Scarecrow plots to dump his toxin into an underground river that flows into Gotham's reservoirs, infecting the city and sparking a mass frenzy of fear. Crane isn't doing it for ransom or a statement; a former academic, he's running a mass experiment in studying the psychological effects of fear.

Still, it's hard to write off the similarities between "Dreams in Darkness" and "Batman Begins" as coincidental. The scene of Batman (Christian Bale) defeating Crane is even taken from a different "Batman: The Animated Series" episode: Scarecrow's debut, "Nothing to Fear." Batman poisons Scarecrow with "his own medicine," causing Crane to hallucinate Batman as not merely a man in a bat costume but a demonic, man-sized bat creature.

Whereas in "Dreams in Darkness" Crane is moving in and out of his cell, "Batman Begins" put him in control of Arkham (reimagining Crane's original backstory as a college professor). "Dark Knight" trilogy co-writer David S. Goyer has said he convinced Christopher Nolan that Scarecrow needed to wear his mask, and they devised a practical reason: The mask is a gas mask that keeps Crane from ingesting his fear toxin and scaring his victims who do. That is not the case in "Dreams in Darkness," where Crane is exposed to the toxin while in costume and ends the episode back in his cell as a hysterical mess.

Goyer has said the selection of Scarecrow as the villain of "Batman Begins" came out of the movie's theme of confronting fear. If you're going to steal, steal from the best, because "Dreams in Darkness" is a masterclass at showing Scarecrow getting under Batman's skin. It's the most frightening Scarecrow episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" and the only one that actually comes close to being a horror story, thanks to Batman's repeated and menacing hallucinations.

The first fright is a jump scare; Batman sees the Joker walking towards him reflected on the Batcomputer's screen, only to turn around and find it was Alfred. The terror doesn't let up, and once Batman makes it to Arkham, there's also the dash of psychological horror. Batman is locked in the same asylum as his greatest foes, where no one believes his pleas, and their doubt could cost a city's worth of lives. Granted, the doctors' refusal to believe Batman does border on incompetence. Scarecrow wanting to poison the city is just another night in Gotham, but Arkham's staff treat Batman like he's raving mad.

Many of the best "Batman: The Animated Series" episodes feel like 22-minute film noirs, and "Dreams in Darkness" is no exception. The episode begins in media res at Arkham, with the opening twist that the "new patient" the doctors are talking about is Batman. Batman gets a voiceover narration — a noir staple — as flashbacks explain how he ended up in a straitjacket.

The hallucinations get worse before they get better. Batman's cell door swings wide open, bathing him in a hellish red light. His parents walk into a dark tunnel, disappearing as that tunnel becomes the barrel of a giant handgun. Once Batman escapes and makes it to the caverns where Scarecrow dwells, he imagines a rat taking on the Joker's face. Imagined villains then keep gruesomely metamorphosing into others. As Batman imagines himself falling into an abyss, the darkness becomes a spiral shape with Scarecrow's face in the center.

It's beautifully animated and genuinely creepy stuff; the central image of Batman falling looks right out of Alfred Hitchcock's "Vertigo."

As for the straw-man of the hour, Scarecrow doesn't appear much. He only shows up onscreen halfway through and spends his time waiting on a countdown for his experiment. But "Dreams in Darkness" is Scarecrow voice actor Henry Polic II's best, and most subtle, performance in the role. His baritone is soft, almost mellifluous, which only makes moments like Scarecrow's cruel snicker at how he's left Batman "much, much worse" off than death more unnerving. Polic's time as Scarecrow can be overshadowed by Jeffrey Combs' later, superior performance on "The New Batman Adventures," but "Dreams in Darkness" shows he could be as great a Scarecrow as Combs — or, indeed, Cillian Murphy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before the Arrowverse existed, fans had a Superman show without Superman called Smallville, and that series defined my childhood. Now, it’s celebrating it’s 25th anniversary (and making me feel old). The series focuses squarely on Clark Kent, and it makes some interesting choices regarding the DC mythos. Interestingly, the show never saw Tom Welling's Clark fully suited up as the Man of Steel, and the actor himself shared some BTS details about why that was the case.

Just to refresh fans' memories, Clark never wore the classic red-and-blue suit, and barely hit the skies. However, the final moment gave a little wink at who this fan-favorite Clark Kent had become by showing him running across the rooftop of the Daily Planet and ripping open his shirt to reveal the classic S on the chest. This was the closest fans came to seeing the actor in the hero tights.

When Welling and his co-star, Michael Rosenbaum, (who played Lex Luther) spoke with Variety, he revealed the reason behind the lack of a super suit:

We got to set that day, and they had given me just a T-shirt with no sleeves to wear underneath the shirt. Because they didn’t have the money to put the suit on, and they weren’t going to see it anyway.

The absence of a full suit wasn’t a major surprise, given creators Alfred Gough and Miles Millar initiated a “no flights, no tights” rule when they started the show. Only one of those was ever broken. While Welling admits that they “toed the line a few times” when it came to the suit, they never did get the actor in a pair of tights. The reason for that was pretty simple. They weren’t able to do so unless Welling gave the “all right,” and to this day, this iteration of Clark has not suited up.

Funny enough, the closest we came to seeing Clark in a hero costume was when he wore the Green Arrow suit for an episode. Years later, along with Erica Durance (who played Lois Lane), Welling did reprise his role as Clark for a scene in the Arrowverse's "Crisis on Infinite Earths” crossover event, though even by that point, the character had given up his powers and retired as a hero. Despite Kent not taking to the skies in the final shot, Welling enjoyed the series, and he had this to say about his character's status:

We can’t go with him. But he’s out there.

This is technically true, and there have also been plenty of Supermen before and after Smallville. Yet fans have remained dedicated to the series. That's partially thanks to Welling, Rosenbaum, and several cast members reuniting conventions around the country. Plus, Rosenbaum and Welling host the re-watch podcast “Talkville,” which is currently recapping Season 9. With that, fans continue to hear BTS stories and re-live their favorite moments.

While there have been other Supes shows, the former WB/CW series still stands as the only series to solely focus on Clark and not his alter ego. But this could change if Welling and Rosenbaum succeed in reviving the series. The duo have been reportedly attempting to bring back Smallville via an animated sequel, and this could potentially mean (finally) seeing Clark in the suit.

I'd still actually like to see Tom Welling don the costume in a live-action production, though, even if the chances of that happening seem slim to none. At the very least, fans can enjoy Clark's entire journey by streaming all 10 seasons of Smallville with a Hulu subscription.

#3531. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.

#3530. This Classic Marvel Villain Could Reshape The MCU — And Introduce Nova

With heavy-hitting villains like Loki, Thanos, the Red Skull, Galactus, and now Doctor Doom already featured — and in most cases, thoroughly defeated — in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, it's easy to wonder who might be next in line to pose a threat to the Avengers. It is, after all, pretty difficult to raise the stakes higher than the death and resurrection of half the universe in "Infinity War" and "Endgame," even when there's an entire multiverse out there just waiting to be put in danger. There is, however, one major Marvel Comics villain who has yet to step into the spotlight in the movies, with a track record as one of the deadliest enemies not just to a single team of heroes, but to the entire cosmos.

Annihilus, the insectoid ruler of the Negative Zone, has over 60 years of comics history and has proven himself to be every bit as deadly as Thanos, but without the veneer of nobility that came with the goal of seeking some kind of cosmic balance. Annihilus has no noble goals or grand designs, just a massive army of mindless drones hellbent on consuming everything in its path, and if he's introduced into the MCU, he has the potential to not only wreak havoc across the entire universe, but also pave the way to finally introduce the fan-favorite hero Nova to the big screen.

Originally introduced in 1968's "Fantastic Four Annual" #6 with the ominously over-the-top nickname of "The Living Death That Walks," Annihilus was at one point considered by director James Gunn to be the villain of "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," and with good reason. While he's been a perennial foe for the Fantastic Four, Annihilus' most prominent and destructive moments came in the 2006 crossover "Annihilation," which saw him unleash billions of locust-like drones across the galaxy in an "Annihilation Wave" that toppled long-established star-spanning empires and still has lasting effects on the Marvel Universe two real-time decades later.

Perhaps most importantly, "Annihilation" paved the way for the introduction of the modern Guardians of the Galaxy. Rather than the original Guardians concept of a team of sci-fi heroes in the distant future of the 30th century, Annihilation and its sequel, "Annihilation Conquest," rebooted them as space-faring hard-luck heroes led by Star-Lord, which led directly to the version that made it to the MCU. As a result, Annihilus is a natural fit to face off against the Guardians in some form, so it makes sense that he'd be considered for the third film, even if the decision was ultimately made to focus more on Rocket's origin and pit the heroes against the High Evolutionary instead.

Despite not making it into "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," Annihilus remains one of the biggest comic book supervillains who hasn't been tapped for a role in the movies, providing the MCU with an opportunity — although not necessarily one that fans might expect. After "Annihilation," Annihilus wasn't just tied to the Fantastic Four, but found a new arch-enemy: Nova.

The Nova Corps were introduced to the MCU back in the first "Guardians" movie as an organization of galactic peacekeepers, but Earth's representative, Richard Rider, has been floating around for years as a potential addition to the franchise. We haven't seen him yet, but if the films continue to draw on the events of "Annihilation," the fact that the Corps is already established makes it possible for the films to recreate one of the comic's biggest moments. As the opening shot in his war against the rest of the galaxy, Annihilus, well, annihilates the Nova Corps on the planet Xandar, leaving Rider as the sole survivor. Rich does eventually get his revenge, literally punching down Annihilus' throat and tearing out his guts in one of the most truly badass moments in Marvel Comics history, and one that plenty of fans would love to see recreated in the films.

Of course, insectoid space dictators and comic books being what they are, Annihilus did eventually make his way back from the dead, but that could be very beneficial considering that unlike the comics, the movies have a tendency to kill off their villains. Giving them the ability to return and rise again allows their characters to develop over time alongside the heroes, even if some of them definitely deserve their fate.

#3528. All 5 Finalists For The Next James Bond, Ranked

Now that Amazon has paid an exorbitant price for the James Bond franchise and made us all wait what seems like an eternity to find out who will play the new 007, it's almost time for an official announcement. At this point, plenty of names have been bandied about and auditions have been ongoing for some time. Now, however, it looks as though Amazon is preparing to crown a successor to Daniel Craig.

Producers have reportedly whittled prospective James Bond actors down to five finalists, including "Disclosure Day" and "Wake Up Dead Man" star Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner of "Fantastic Beasts" and "Eternity" fame, and Jack Lowden, who plays River Cartwright on the best spy show on TV, "Slow Horses." The trio are said to have carried out screen tests alongside Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult, though at this point it remains unclear who will actually don the tux and embark on yet another mission for King and country.

But that just means we have time for a bit more speculation ahead of an official announcement. Bearing in mind Craig's "Casino Royale" casting prompted a major backlash in the early 2000s, before he delivered the greatest James Bond movie ever made, all of this should be taken with a pinch of salt. Nobody can say for sure how well suited an actor is to a role, and whoever is cast will no doubt put their all into bringing England's greatest spy to life. But Amazon MGM Studios sure are taking their sweet time announcing the next Bond, so in the meantime we might as well rank the frontrunners.

Thus far, Nicholas Hoult has missed out on playing both Batman and Superman, losing the former to fellow Bond contender Robert Pattinson. As talented an actor as he is, if we're considering him alongside these other candidates, he should probably miss out on Bond, too.

That's not to say he wouldn't do a decent job in the role. Hoult has proven himself a versatile performer, delivering memorable turns as villains in both the critically-acclaimed 2024 crime thriller "The Order" and "Superman," in which he played an intensely odious tech bro Lex Luthor. But there's just something a bit too boyish about Hoult, and it's not just the fact he came to prominence as a child actor.

It all depends on what sort of story director Denis Villeneuve has planned for his Bond movie. Perhaps Hoult has exactly what the "Dune" filmmaker is looking for. But in a general sense, not only does the British star seem to lack a bit of the grit required to play a decent 007, he's also already a well known actor. The best Bonds have all been relative newcomers with a bit of a darkness to them. I'm sure Hoult could manage it, but compared to the other frontrunners, I just don't see it.

Callum Turner isn't the most recognizable face among the five Bond finalists, but I think that's a good thing. What's more, while he's yet to deliver a definitive performance and might be seen as perhaps a tad forgettable based on his performances in the "Fantastic Beasts" films, I get the sense that, with 007, Turner could prove the naysayers wrong.

As Idles frontman Joseph Talbot once sang, "I don't care about the next James Bond / He kills for country, Queen and God / We don't need another murderous toff." But what about a murderous spy with a working class background? The best James Bond, Sean Connery, took the long road to acting, having grown up in the working class area of Edinburgh known as Fountainbridge before dropping out of school at 13 and considering a career as a professional soccer player. When he debuted as 007, he was still a little rough around the edges and that served him well in the role.

Turner similarly grew up on a council estate and, oddly enough, was also committed to a soccer career. As such, there's an authenticity and an edge to the British actor. If Villeneuve can help him capitalize on that, and Turner can find a fresh way to work it into his performance (Connery, Timothy Dalton, and Daniel Craig have all brought a similar roughness to their Bond portrayals) then he could make a great Craig replacement.

At first, Robert Pattinson seems like a bit of a safe choice for Bond. A well-spoken London boy with a middle class upbringing and a string of well-received performances — if Denis Villeneuve and the Amazon MGM producers wanted to play it safe, Pattinson seems like the man. But this is an actor who, over the past decade especially, has consistently proven his ability to completely disappear into a role.

Since giving his most Pattinsonian performance in the Safdie Brothers' "Good Time," the actor has shown a particular affinity for playing creepy little weirdos, such as the lascivious Rev. Preston Teagardin in "The Devil All the Time." But he's also delivered a compelling, understated turn as the Dark Knight in "The Batman" and an uncanny rendition of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson in "Primetime." At this point, Pattinson is easily one of the most talented and chameleonic actors working today.

With that in mind, it's impossible to imagine him dropping the ball with Bond. Pattinson always makes interesting choices and that hasn't failed him yet. As safe as he might seem on the surface, he could prove to be the biggest wild card of the bunch, and unlike Nicholas Hoult, is much more capable of completely disappearing into a role. That's a major advantage for anyone taking on Bond, which, coupled with everything else Pattinson could bring to the role, surely makes him one of the most exciting candidates.

Josh O'Connor has all of the makings of a great James Bond, even if they're not as apparent on the surface. One might look at the star of "Challengers" and assume that he doesn't have the look to play 007, or that he's not muscular enough. However, virtually every Bond actor that came before had to live in the shadow of whoever preceded him. The worst thing the producers could do is to just try and replicate Daniel Craig.

Shifting to a guy like O'Connor would be an unexpected move, yet an exciting one. For one, he meets all of the James Bond requirements according to the casting director. He can look like a regular guy and, most importantly, he's a brilliant actor. He starred alongside Craig in last year's "Wake Up Dead Man," alongside some truly phenomenal, established actors, and went toe-to-toe with all of them. So much so that he came out of that film with quite possibly the best performance of them all. That's no small thing.

O'Connor is also responsible for some of the sexiest moments in "Challengers," while starring alongside Zendaya and Mike Faist. He can be sexy. He's a great actor. He's done action in movies like "Disclosure Day." He's also not so famous to have built up a fixed perception among audiences. He can make Bond his own and mold himself into the role, while clearly being a very different actor than the man who went before him. O'Connor is, using history as our guide, right for the job.

"Slow Horses" is one of the best spy shows on TV. While much of that is down to an unforgettable performance from Gary Oldman as the delightfully disheveled Jackson Lamb, as River Cartwright Jack Lowden has quietly been making a case for himself as one of Britain's best actors.

The Scottish star plays his misfit sleuth with an intriguing mix of world weariness and ambition, crafting a fully realized performance that is one of the best parts of "Slow Horses." His Season 6 relationship with Olivia Cooke's Sidonie Baker was one of the most surprisingly affecting aspects of the entire series — a testament to both actors' talent for convincingly emotional performances. He's also more than proven he has a razor sharp comedic sense that allows him to nail the sardonic wit of author Mick Herron, which originated in the "Slough House" novels and pervades the Apple TV series adaptation.

Bond is, obviously, a very different character. But Lowden has demonstrated such talent as River, clearly has major potential, and isn't yet a major A-lister. Add to that his ability to deliver darkly funny dialogue and his naturalistic sensibility which has made River feel so human, and Lowden is surely the most exciting Bond prospect. I'd be fascinated to see what he does as 007, more so than anybody else on this list, and that's why he's here at number one.

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.
