#3521. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3520. Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film

The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “Godzilla Minus Zero” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic), “Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.

#3519. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

Joining several returning season 1 cast members is prominent addition John Malkovich. Malkovich plays a Miami mob boss that Vaughn’s Yancy finds himself up against.

#3517. Black Doves' Spy Organization Explained: Every Member & Who They Work For

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for Black Doves season 2.Netflix’s spy action thriller Black Doves primarily focuses on the titular spy agency, but given the nature of their covert work, it can be hard to determine who's actually part of the Black Doves and what the company does. The cast of Black Doves, as well as the show itself, revolves around the titular organization. Even as the show focuses on Helen, Sam, and Reed's personal lives and history, everything circles back to the work of the Black Doves.

Black Doves season 1 revealed precious little about the organization, but by the end of Black Doves season 2, the company's lore and personnel list had increased exponentially. Now, the Black Doves are an international agency with a decades-long history that operates around the world. They've even gained a new rival in the form of Kestrel, the anarchist spy network founded in East Berlin and revived by Vita and Franz.

As the Black Doves have gotten larger and more important, it's gotten harder to keep track of who is actually part of the organization, who its enemies are, and why it even exists in the first place. Those distinctions are incredibly important, though, as Black Doves season 2 is filled to the brim with betrayals, double agents, and enemies both old and new. Here's everything we know about the Black Doves, including their leaders, agents, and history.

The Black Doves spy organization is an independent capitalist enterprise; as such, its primary goal is to earn money. As Reed explained to Helen when they first met, the organization’s employees retrieve information and sell it for the highest possible amount. The lack of ties to any particular government or country allows its spies to be hired by anyone, anywhere, regardless of the person or group’s ideological interests or country of origin. This likely bolsters its profit margins.

Black Doves, Netflix's action thriller starring Keira Knightley, included a twist that will create a huge problem for the show’s second season.

Though Black Doves season 1 only introduced the audience to four members of the spy agency (along with several freelance assassins and secret agents), season 2 drastically expanded the scope of the company. Previously, the Black Doves were thought to be an all-female organization based solely in Britain. Now, we know that the Black Doves have been in operation since at least the 1980s, that they operate throughout Europe, and that it has dozens of agents, executives, contractors, and analysts of every gender.

Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, is the show's protagonist and one of the top agents in the spy organization. While her past is shrouded in mystery (and Helen isn’t her real name), she was recruited into Black Doves, at least in part, due to her shady background. All that’s really known is that when interviewing for a translator job, the interviewer knew all about her mother’s death and stepfather’s murder at the hands of her stepsister. The interviewer refers her to Reed, who is immediately taken by her calculating manner and fierceness.

She is married to prominent politician Wallace Webb and publicly lives a domestic life with her husband and children. However, she’s been stealing government secrets from her husband the whole time and passing them on to the Black Doves organization. She also had an affair with a man named Jason (Andrew Koji), whose murder kicks off the events of the Black Doves series. By the end of season 1, Helen has avenged her lover, reconciled with her husband, and found a best friend in Sam Young (Ben Whishaw).

In season 2, Helen is tasked with discovering what happened to her handler, Mrs. Reed, and uncovering the truth of a past Black Doves operation she knows only as "Wildflower." By the end of the season, Helen is forced to reveal her identity as a spy to Wallace, putting her cover in jeopardy and likely ruining any chance of continuing to extract information out of him. Reed, however, offers Helen a chance to move up in the Black Doves organization and take on more responsibility besides being a "spy wife."

Dani is one of the newer members of the Black Doves, and she was originally embedded as Wallace's new assistant. Reed deployed Dani to seduce Wallace and replace Helen in season 1, as Reed felt Helen was getting uncontrollable. Helen, however, managed to defeat Dani in a brawl, though she spared her life. In season 2, Helen convinces Dani to search through the Black Doves' archives looking for Wildflower. Dani is then approached by Patrick and Kestrel, and she ultimately decides to betray the Black Doves by letting Kestrel into the building. Dani is then killed by Eleanor in the finale.

Marie was a Black Doves agent who was embedded in the Webb household as their nanny since the series began. In season 2, Reed revealed that she placed Marie there to keep an eye on Helen and her whereabouts. However, Marie was also turned by Kestrel and convinced to bring Helen's children to the London Zoo as hostages during the finale. Despite her protestations that she never would have harmed the children, Helen shot and killed Marie.

During a flashback to Mrs. Reed's youth in Black Doves season 2, the show revealed that the Black Doves organization has been in operation since at least the 1980s. There are presumably hundreds of former and deceased agents, but we know of at least three other operatives active in East Berlin in the 1980s and one from the modern day.

Much of Black Doves season 2 revolves around three former Black Doves agents who worked with Reed in her youth in East Berlin. The leader of the group, Peter Maddison, codename Thunder, engaged in a romantic relationship with Reed only to later be killed by her. Melanie Ambrose aka Spitfire and Erik Klein aka Zeus were there as hired muscle to support Reed's undercover work. As season 2 revealed, Sam killed Ambrose and Klein on Kestrel's behalf. In modern day, a Black Dove named Ida Povetkin was inserted as Alexi Chernov's maid, though she was killed off-screen.

In addition to dedicated agents and executives, the Black Doves also employ a wide range of hired guns on a contract basis. The most notable of these contractors is Sam Young, who met Helen through his work for Mrs. Reed. In season 2, Laila also worked for the Black Doves and did off-the-books work for Reed specifically. Additionally, Mr. Conteh mentions that the Black Doves send clean-up crews when their operatives make a mess, such as when Helen killed Marie.

As a private company, the Black Doves' leadership structure closely resembles that of a regular corporation. While there's no company charter to reference, the Black Doves did have an executive committee that was composed of at least five different people, as revealed in season 2. Unfortunately, it's only clear what two of those members actually did for the organization.

Elizabeth Reed spent her entire life as a Black Dove. As season 2 revealed through flashbacks, Reed spent much of the 1980s as an undercover agent embedded in an East Berlin anarchist spy network known as Kestrel. During her five years of undercover work, Reed gave birth to a daughter, Vita. Her mission ultimately ended when she fabricated a story about Kestrel planning to bomb an American checkpoint, causing the rest of her Black Doves team to execute the spy network's members. Reed then had to kill her boss and lover, Peter, after he discovered her lie.

By the time of Black Doves season 1, Elizabeth Reed had risen through the ranks of the organization and became Helen's handler in addition to serving on the company's executive committee. Reed managed several spies and assassins, and her work mainly focused on stealing government secrets and presumably selling them to the highest bidder. At the end of season 2, Reed expresses a desire to actually hunt down criminals and terrorists and make the world a better place.

The only other member of the Black Doves' executive committee who gets any attention is Mr. Conteh, a new addition to season 2. Much of Conteh's personal life is shrouded in mystery, though he seems to have an extended history with Reed. Conteh mentions that Reed never respected him, and he also delights in being able to take her down. It's not clear what Conteh does during normal times, but it's safe to assume he manages a different team of agents, considering how he was chosen to become Helen's new handler in Reed's absence.

As previously mentioned, there were several other members of the Black Doves executive committee who didn't survive Kestrel's attack. In addition to Conteh and Reed, the Black Doves were led by three other executives: Ms. Conduct, Mrs. Burkinshaw, and Mr. Rodgers. These three may have also handled agents personally, or they may have been more involved in executive functions like meeting clients and overall corporate strategy.

Though Netflix hasn't officially renewed Black Doves season 3 yet, the ending of the second season leaves the door wide open for its story to continue. If it does continue, the Black Doves will have quite a bit to do going forward. Helen will presumably move up in the ranks of the organization, either becoming a handler herself on the executive committee as the company rebuilds. Alternatively, she could simply gain more field work aside from her marriage to Wallace.

As Reed explained, the Black Doves are also presumably going to make it a point to hunt down what remains of Kestrel and its operatives. Patrick managed to escape the battle at Black Doves HQ, and Reed mentioned that he was seen boarding a plane to Tokyo. Even though Vita is dead, Kestrel has survived and remains a major threat. Where and how they strike next is impossible to predict, though it's safe to assume the Black Doves will attempt to stop them.

The Black Doves also may be expanding in season 3. Now that Kestrel has made itself known to the world, they've also made global enemies. The United Kingdom and MI6 will likely want retribution for a terrorist attack on its soil and an attempt on the Prime Minister's life. The United States will likely want retribution for the murder of a political delegate. In short, Black Doves season 3 may see the titular organization becoming a major player in global politics and among information agencies.

#3516. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3515. Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

“You Can See Everything,” an intimate look at Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has earned nearly $80 million at the domestic box office, becoming A24‘s third-highest-grossing release in North America. It bypasses “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and its $77 million haul to take its spot on the indie studio’s chart, and that film won the Oscar for Best Picture.

With $79.8 million stateside, “You Can See Everything” sits behind the summer blockbuster “Backrooms” ($197 million) and 2025’s “Marty Supreme” ($96 million) on the list of A24 releases. Other A24 films made more globally, with “Backrooms” earning more than $400 million, “Marty Supreme” grossing $192.4 million, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” netting $147.9 million. However, “You Can See Everything” has yet to be released in most international markets. It’s unclear if Holmes’ fraud will resonate with moviegoers so far from Silicon Valley. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t connect, because with a budget of $7 million, “You Can See Everything” is already wildly profitable. Its success means that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the directing duo behind the doc, are now in high demand.

“You Can See Everything” also jumped ahead of “March of the Penguins” ($77 million) on the list of highest-grossing documentaries in North America. Variety reports that makes it the second highest-grossing doc behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which earned $119 million domestically. That doesn’t account for music documentaries like “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ($267.1 million) and “Michael Jackson’s This is It” ($268 million), which were far more popular.

A24 is on a hot streak. In addition to “Backrooms,” the indie studio has released hits like “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Its latest film, “Club Kid,” grossed an impressive $390,583 this weekend when it opened on six screens in New York and Los Angeles. That’s a per-screen average of $65,097. A24 acquired the drama about a hard-living gay man and his son out of the Cannes Film Festival, where it debuted to raves. The studio hopes to position the film and its writer, director, and star Jordan Firstman in the Oscar race.

#3512. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3511. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

#3510. First macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 RCs now available [U]

Update, November 5: The release candidates are now available to public beta testers as well.

In addition to the release of macOS 27.3 beta 1, Apple is also rolling out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3. Here are the details.

Apple today released the first developer beta of macOS 27.3, which introduces several new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions, and may also bring support for additional Siri AI languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Additionally, the company rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3, continuing its support for older versions of macOS. Just last week, Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, which addressed more than 150 security vulnerabilities.

As usual, the release notes for both RCs only mention that “this update provides security fixes for your Mac,” with details about the specific vulnerabilities addressed expected to be published once the updates are officially released.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 is 24H314, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 is 25G416.

Did you spot anything new in today’s betas? Let us know in the comments.

#3509. Alan Ritchson's R-Rated Sci-Fi Thriller Is One Of Netflix's Best

Netflix has many exciting sci-fi movies and TV shows, but this one starring Alan Ritchson is easily one of the best when it comes to the popular genre on the streaming service. Ritchson has become one of the biggest names in the world. He was already popular with superhero fans, given that the actor's list of projects includes Smallville and Titans.

However, it was as Jack Reacher, the live-action take on the action hero from Lee Child's bestselling novels, in Prime Video's Reacher that Ritchson became a global star. Now, the actor has pretty much his choice of projects, with each new season of Reacher breaking records for Prime Video and Ritchson signing on for creative action movies of different tones outside his work on the thriller series.

Now take Netflix's slate of releases, which has quite a few major sci-fi projects, ranking from TV shows that have become forever linked to the streamer, such as Stranger Things and Black Mirror, and movies that dominated streaming for a time, like Sandra Bullock's Bird Box. Ritchson added to that sci-fi slate on Netflix in 2026 with one of its most action-packed releases.

The actor might have become famous for his work on Reacher on Prime Video, but Ritchson proved in 2026 that he could excel in other streamers without the built-in Jack Reacher audience. War Machine is a violent R-rated sci-fi thriller movie starring the actor, and while Netflix has released many exciting original movies over the years, it is safe to say that Ritchson's action flick is among the streamer's best.

Story-wise, War Machine is pretty straightforward, as it starts as a simple war movie, with Ritchson's 81, a US Army Staff Sergeant, in Afghanistan going through a traumatic encounter with the Taliban that leads to significant losses. However, when the movie switches genres, with a training exercise a couple of years later leading to the Reacher star's character and his new unit coming face to face with a deadly alien killing machine, the sci-fi thriller becomes one of the most intense films on Netflix's catalog. Ritchson is a mountain of a man, but even he is no match for a giant robot.

After seeing Ritchson play such a grounded hero in Reacher, it is exciting that Netflix merged that world, with Ritchson once again as a military character, only now going up against a massive and advanced killer robot. With the actor's Titans co-star Esai Morales and fellow DC actors Jai Courtney (Suicide Squad) and Keiynan Lonsdale (The Flash), among other names like Hollywood veteran Dennis Quaid and I Play Rocky's Stephan James, the Netflix sci-fi movie ensures that many viewers will already be connected to the characters through prior experiences watching these actors, given how most of the characters themselves are defined by numbers.

That is a smart tactic. With gritty sci-fi action and a commanding performance from Ritchson as a soldier desperately fighting for survival and to try to keep those next to him alive, War Machine became a global smash hit for Netflix. The R-rated sci-fi thriller is one of Netflix's most-watched movies of all time, racking up 139.9 million views in its first 91 days of availability on the streamer, ranking 10th all-time. It is one of the only two 2026 movies to do so, with the other being Michael B. Jordan's animated fantasy film Swapped, with 144.9 million views, at 8th.

War Machine was so good and such a massive action hit for Netflix that it marked the start of a new era for the streamer, with the franchise set to continue with a War Machine sequel that is currently in development. Alongside his work on future seasons of Reacher, with Prime Video already renewing the action thriller series for at least another two seasons, Ritchson has also signed a first-look deal to develop and star in movies at Netflix, continuing to build on the streamer and actor's successful War Machine partnership. If they are anything like War Machine, Alan Ritchson's next Netflix movies are worth keeping an eye on.
